passages.title: The quaking Hour and those who still dispute
passages.tafsir:
Sūrat al-Ḥajj opens by addressing the whole of humanity: an order to fear your Lord, and then a scene of the Hour so violent that the most unbreakable bond in creation — a mother and the child at her breast — simply snaps. Then, in ayat 3–4, the view turns from that terrifying horizon back to the present, to a man standing in the middle of it all, disputing about Allah with no knowledge at all.

**What holds these four ayat together** is the contrast between them. Ayat 1–2 describe a day whose sheer weight no one can bear. Ayat 3–4 describe the person who hears about that day and disputes rather than fears, and who follows a guide that leads him exactly where the first two ayat warned him not to go. The passage is a warning, and then a portrait of the one who ignores the warning.

## A sūrah unlike any other

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens with a note on the sūrah as a whole that is worth carrying into the passage. Commentators differ over whether al-Ḥajj is Makkan or Madani; Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) is reported to have expressed two views on different occasions. The majority of commentators hold that the sūrah is a combination of both Makkan and Madani verses, and this is the view Qurṭubī prefers.

Qurṭubī also mentions its other peculiarities: some of its verses were revealed at night and some during the day; some while the Prophet ﷺ was travelling and some while he was not; some in Makkah and others at Madinah; some in the middle of battle and others in peacetime. Some of its verses are *nāsikh* (verses of the Qurʼān that abrogate other verses) and some are *mansūkh* (verses that have been abrogated by others); some are *muḥkam* and others *mutashābih*. Indeed, as Maʿārif puts it, this one sūrah comprises all categories of revelation.

## The day the Prophet ﷺ raised his voice on the road

One of the most illuminating things about ayat 1–2 is *how* they were received, and both our sources dwell on it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that this verse was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ while he was travelling, and that he recited it **in a loud voice**, so that all his Companions gathered around him after hearing his voice.

Ibn Kathīr gives the same scene with more detail. Imām Aḥmad recorded that ʿImrān bin Ḥusayn said that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was on one of his journeys and some of his Companions had fallen behind, he raised his voice and recited these two ayat — "O mankind! Have Taqwā of your Lord! Verily, the earthquake of the Hour is a terrible thing…" — and when the Companions heard that, **they hastened to catch up with him, because they knew that he wanted to say something.** That last detail is worth pausing over: they had learned to recognise when something was coming that they could not afford to miss.

What he said when they reached him was this: *Do you know what Day that is? That is the Day when Ādam will be called. His Lord will call him and will say: "O Ādam, send forth those of your progeny who are to be sent to the Fire." He will say, "O Lord, how many are to be sent to the Fire?" He will say, "From every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine will be in the Fire and one will be in Paradise."*

Ibn Kathīr notes that this was also recorded by At-Tirmidhī and by An-Nasāʼī in the Book of Tafsīr in their Sunans, and that At-Tirmidhī said, "It is Ḥasan Ṣaḥīḥ." Al-Bukhārī recorded the same teaching in his Tafsīr, under this very ayah, from Abū Saʿīd — with the added detail that at that moment "every pregnant female will drop her load and children will turn grey," and that this will be so difficult for mankind to bear that their faces will change. Ibn Kathīr adds that Al-Bukhārī also recorded it elsewhere, and that it was recorded by Muslim and by An-Nasāʼī in his Tafsīr as well. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the incident from Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim on the authority of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him).

**The Companions' reaction is part of the tafsīr.** In Imām Aḥmad's version they were filled with despair and stopped smiling. In At-Tirmidhī's version, the Muslims started to weep. In Maʿārif's telling, they were frightened and asked outright: "O prophet of Allah! Who are those among us who will escape this terrible fate?" That is the honest response of a heart that has actually heard the verse.

## And then he consoled them

What follows matters as much as the warning, and it should never be quoted without it. Seeing their state, the Prophet ﷺ said: *Be of good cheer and strive hard, for by the One in Whose Hand is the soul of Muḥammad, you will be counted with two creations who are of immense numbers — Yaʼjūj and Maʼjūj, and those who have already died of the progeny of Ādam and the progeny of Iblīs.*

As Maʿārif puts it, among the nine hundred and ninety-nine the majority will be from those peoples. Then they felt happier, and he said: *Strive hard and be of good cheer, for by the One in Whose Hand is the soul of Muḥammad, in comparison to mankind you are like a mole on the flank of a camel, or a mark on the foreleg of a beast.* In Al-Bukhārī's wording: "Among mankind you are like a black hair on the side of a white bull, or a white hair on the side of a black bull."

In At-Tirmidhī's version he added a further instruction — *be close in your rank and be straightforward* — and explained that there was never any Prophet but that there was a time of ignorance (*jāhiliyyah*) just before his advent; the number will be taken from that time of ignorance, and if that is not enough, it will be made up from the hypocrites. Then he said, "I hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise," and they said, "Allāhu Akbar!" Then, "a third of the people of Paradise" — "Allāhu Akbar!" Then, "half of the people of Paradise" — "Allāhu Akbar!" The narrator said he did not know whether he went on to say two-thirds.

So the passage's emotional arc, as the Prophet ﷺ himself taught it, runs from terror to *striving with good cheer*. The verse is not designed to crush; it is designed to move you.

## "The earthquake of the Hour is a terrible thing"

Ibn Kathīr explains that here Allah commands His servants to have **taqwā** of Him — reverent fear of Allah and mindfulness of Him, guarding oneself against what He has forbidden — and then informs them of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, which will come to them with its earthquakes and other horrors. He gathers the parallel verses: *"When the earth is shaken with its final earthquake, and when the earth throws out its burdens"* (99:1–2); *"And the earth and the mountains shall be removed from their places, and crushed with a single crushing. Then on that Day shall the Great Event befall"* (69:14–15); *"When the earth will be shaken with a terrible shake, and the mountains will be powdered to dust"* (56:4–5).

The words *shayʼun ʿaẓīm* — "a terrible thing" — Ibn Kathīr renders as: a serious matter, a terrifying crisis, a horrendous event.

**A subtle point about the quaking itself.** Ibn Kathīr says this earthquake is what will happen to people when they are filled with terror, and he cites *"There, the believers were tried and shaken with a mighty shaking"* (33:11) — a verse about hearts and nerves under strain, not only about ground moving. The same root that shakes the earth shakes the human being standing on it.

## When does this quaking happen?

Both sources treat this as a genuine difference among the scholars, and neither settles it.

**View one: before the Hour, at the end of this world.** Ibn Kathīr notes it was said that this earthquake will come at the end of the life span of this world, at the outset of the Hour, and reports that Ibn Jarīr recorded ʿAlqamah's comment on *"Verily, the earthquake of the Hour is a terrible thing"* — that it is before the Hour. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presents this as the opinion that the earthquake will occur in this world before the Day of Judgment, among the last signs of its coming, and points to 99:1, 69:14 and 56:4 as support.

**View two: on the Day of Resurrection itself.** Others said this refers to the terror, fear, earthquakes and chaos that will happen on the Day of Resurrection, in the arena of Judgement, *after* the resurrection from the graves. Ibn Kathīr reports that this was the view favoured by Ibn Jarīr, who took the aḥādīth above as his evidence — since in them the scene of pregnant women dropping their loads is placed at the moment Ādam is called on the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif likewise notes that some have deduced this second view from that same hadith.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's own conclusion is stated plainly: **there is in fact no inconsistency between these two views**, because verses of the Qurʼān and aḥādīth of the Prophet ﷺ may be quoted in support of either. *Allah knows best.*

Maʿārif also offers a resolution of the obvious puzzle, on the authority of Qurṭubī. If the earthquake takes place in this world before the Day of Judgment, then pregnant women miscarrying and nursing mothers being diverted from their infants need no further explanation. But if the earthquake occurs after the Resurrection, then the explanation is that a woman who was pregnant would be raised on that Day in the same state, and a woman who died while breastfeeding her child will also be raised in the same condition along with her child. *Allah knows best.*

## The Arabic of ayah 2: a word chosen with terrible precision

One of Ibn Kathīr's finest observations in this passage rests on a single word.

Allah says *kullu **murḍiʿatin*** — "every nursing mother." Ibn Kathīr points out that He did **not** say a mother who merely *has* an infant of breastfeeding age. What the word describes is the woman caught in the act of suckling — as Ibn Kathīr puts it, her shock will make her neglect her infant *at the very moment of breastfeeding*.

And *ʿammā arḍaʿat* — "her nursling" — means, Ibn Kathīr says, her nursing infant that has not yet been weaned: the most dependent creature there is.

*Tadhhalu* — "will forget" — means she will be distracted by the horror of what she is seeing, which will make her forget **the one who is the dearest of all to her, and to whom she shows the most compassion.** That is the measure the ayah is giving you. Not "people will be frightened," but: the strongest instinct Allah placed in creation is overwritten in an instant.

*"And every pregnant one will drop her load"* — Ibn Kathīr: before the pregnancy has reached full term, because of the intensity of the horror.

*"And you shall see mankind as in a drunken state"* — because of the severity of their situation, when they will lose their minds, so that whoever sees them will think that they are drunk. Then Allah corrects the impression Himself: *"yet they will not be drunken, but Allah's torment is severe."* The stagger, the vacant eyes, the incoherence — all of it without a drop of wine. What has emptied them is not intoxication but the weight of what they are facing.

## Ayat 3–4: the man who disputes anyway

Against that horizon, ayah 3 introduces a figure: *"And among mankind is he who disputes about Allah, without knowledge, and follows every rebellious Shayṭān."*

**Who was it about?** As-Suddī reported that Abū Mālik said this ayah was revealed about An-Naḍr bin Al-Ḥārith, and Ibn Kathīr notes this was also the view of Ibn Jurayj. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the man's profile: he was a very quarrelsome person; he claimed the angels were Allah's daughters; he claimed the Qurʼān was a storybook containing fables about people of bygone ages; and he denied the Day of Judgment and the Resurrection of the dead. Maʿārif then states the principle that governs all such reports: although this verse relates to a particular person, **its message applies to all who are in a similar situation and practise such wickedness.**

**Ibn Kathīr widens it exactly that way.** He says Allah condemns those who deny the Resurrection and who deny that Allah is able to restore life to the dead; those who turn away from what Allah has revealed to His Prophets and, in their denial and disbelief, follow every rebellious Shayṭān among men and jinn. Note that: the "rebellious Shayṭān" of ayah 3 is not only the unseen devil. Ibn Kathīr says this is the state of the followers of innovation and misguidance, who turn away from the truth and follow falsehood, following the words of **the leaders of misguidance who call people to follow innovation and their own desires and opinions**. A human being who calls you to follow his whim in place of revelation is functioning as a *shayṭān marīd* in this ayah's sense.

*"Without knowledge"* — Ibn Kathīr glosses: meaning, without *sound* knowledge. The problem is not that the man has an opinion; it is that he has no sound basis for it and disputes about Allah regardless.

**Ayah 4 is the verdict on the guide, not only the follower.** *"For him it is decreed that whosoever follows him, he will mislead him, and will drive him to the torment of the Fire."* Mujāhid said that the one for whom it is decreed refers to **that Shayṭān** — meaning, says Ibn Kathīr, that this is a matter written in the decree. *"Whosoever follows him"* means: whoever takes him as a patron and imitates him. And then he will mislead him **in this world**, and **in the Hereafter** drive him to the torment of the Fire — which Ibn Kathīr describes as unbearably hot, painful and agonising. That is the whole return on the investment.

## Living it

The passage puts a simple question to the reader.

**One.** The command in ayah 1 is addressed to *an-nās* — humanity, not just believers — and its content is taqwā. Ibn Kathīr frames the whole passage as Allah commanding His servants to have taqwā of Him and then informing them of the terrors of the Day of Resurrection. The "why" is not an argument; it is a scene. Let it work on you the way it worked on the Companions, who wept, and then were told to strive with good cheer.

**Two.** Notice what the Prophet ﷺ prescribed against the fear he had just created: not despair, but *be of good cheer and strive hard* — along with being close in rank and straightforward. Fear of that Day is meant to convert into action, and it comes packaged with hope: *"I hope that you will be half of the people of Paradise."*

**Three.** Ayat 3–4 ask you to audit your sources. Who are you following on matters of Allah, His revelation and the Hereafter, and do they have sound knowledge — or are they calling people to innovation and to their own desires and opinions, as Ibn Kathīr describes? The verse does not condemn asking questions; it condemns **disputing about Allah without knowledge**, and Ibn Kathīr's reading pairs that disputing with a lead being taken from someone. Ayah 4 tells you where that lead ends.

passages.title: Embryo and dead earth prove the Resurrection
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form one sustained argument, addressed not to believers but to humanity at large: if you doubt that Allah will raise the dead, then look at two things you have already watched happen — how you yourself were made, and what dry ground does when rain falls on it. Ayah 5 lays out the two proofs; ayah 6 draws the conclusion about Allah; ayah 7 draws the conclusion about you.

Ibn Kathir names the logic of the passage plainly: when Allah speaks of disbelief in the Resurrection, He also mentions the evidence of His power and ability to resurrect that is evident from the way He initiates creation. In plain words — and this is my own way of putting Ibn Kathir's point, not his phrasing — the way Allah starts a thing is itself the evidence that He can bring it back.

## "O mankind, if you are in doubt"

The doubt in ayah 5 is doubt about *al-baʿth*, rendered here "the Resurrection." Ibn Kathir defines it precisely: the time when **souls and bodies** will be raised up on the Day of Resurrection. This matters for belief. What is promised is not the survival of a spirit somewhere; it is your body, this one, brought back.

Notice the shape of the reply. A doubt about the *end* is answered by a reminder of the *beginning*. Allah does not open with descriptions of the Last Day. He opens with the reader's own body.

## First witness: the making of a human being

**"We created you from dust."** Ibn Kathir explains: you were originally created from dust — which is what Adam, peace be upon him, was created from. Then the verse moves from the origin of the species to the origin of each individual: **"then from a *nutfah*"** — which Ibn Kathir glosses as Allah then making his offspring from despised water.

Then the stages, which Ibn Kathir describes as an eyewitness would: if the *nutfah* establishes itself in the woman's womb it stays like that for forty days; then more material is added to it and it changes into a red clot (*ʿalaqah*), by the leave of Allah, and it remains like that for forty days. Then it changes and becomes a lump of flesh (*muḍghah*), "like a piece of meat with no form or shape." Then it starts to take on a form and shape, developing a head, arms, chest, stomach, thighs, legs, feet and all its members. Sometimes a woman miscarries before the fetus is formed, and sometimes she miscarries after it has formed.

That is the point of the phrase **"some formed and some unformed"** — Ibn Kathir's comment on it is three words: *as you see*. This is not a hidden mystery. It is what human beings have always observed.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites, as recorded in the Two Sahihs, the report of Ibn Masʿud that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — "the true and truly inspired one" — said: *Every one of you is collected in the womb of his mother for the first forty days, and then he becomes a clot for another forty days, and then a lump of flesh for another forty days. Then Allah sends an angel to write four words: He writes his provision, his deeds, his life span, and whether he will be blessed or wretched. Then he blows the soul into him.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reproduces this same detailed hadith of Ibn Masʿud from the Sahih of Bukhari, by way of Qurtubi, in which the angel records how long it will live, how much sustenance it will receive, what acts it will do, and whether its end will be wretched or fortunate.

## Where the scholars differ: *mukhallaqah* and *ghayr mukhallaqah*

The phrase "formed and unformed" was read in more than one way, and both readings are held by serious authorities.

**The first reading** takes it as the difference between a pregnancy that runs its course and one that does not. Mujahid said it means the miscarried fetus, formed or unformed — and that when forty days have passed of it being a lump of flesh, Allah sends an angel to it who breathes the soul into it and forms it as Allah wills, handsome or ugly, male or female; then writes its provision, its allotted length of life, and whether it is to be one of the blessed or the wretched. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a narration related by Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir, also on the authority of ʿAbdullah ibn Masʿud: when the seed has become a lump of flesh, the angel charged with watching over it seeks guidance from Allah, asking *"O Lord — mukhallaqah or ghayr mukhallaqah?"* If Allah says *ghayr mukhallaqah*, the womb aborts the fetus and it does not reach the stages leading to a live birth. If Allah says *mukhallaqah*, the angel then asks whether it is to be a boy or a girl, wretched or fortunate, how long it will live, how it will spend its life, and when it will die — and is given all of it then and there. Ibn ʿAbbas is reported (via Qurtubi) to have interpreted these two words in a similar way.

**The second reading**, held by other commentators, takes *mukhallaqah* to mean a fetus that completes all the stages of growth and development, with limbs and organs healthy, normal and proportionate, and *ghayr mukhallaqah* to mean one whose limbs are deformed or disproportionate. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this second reading is the closer fit to the rendering it adopts — and then closes the discussion the way a scholar should: *Allah knows best*.

Either way, the lesson stands. Nothing here is automatic. **"And We cause whom We will to remain in the wombs for an appointed term"** — Ibn Kathir: meaning that sometimes the fetus remains in the womb and is not miscarried. Whether a pregnancy holds is a decision, not a mechanism. And for anyone who has lost a pregnancy, this passage is not cold: even that lump of flesh was known and decided upon by its Lord.

## From helplessness to strength, and back again

**"Then We bring you out as infants."** Ibn Kathir: weak in his body, hearing, sight, senses, stamina and mind. Then, he says, Allah gives him strength gradually — and causes his parents to treat him with tender kindness night and day. That last clause is easy to skim past. The love your parents felt for a creature who could do nothing for them was itself part of Allah's arrangement.

**"That you may reach your full strength"** (*ashuddakum*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes a fine point of Arabic: *ashudd* is the plural of *shiddah*, just as *anʿum* is the plural of *niʿmah* (blessing). And it describes what that maturing involves: the baby comes out a totally helpless thing — its body weak and so are its other faculties, hearing, vision, senses, brain function, and its physical movements including its grasp — and the process of gradual development continues until all the faculties reach their peak, which happens when a person is in the prime of his youth. Ibn Kathir: his strength increases until he reaches the vitality and handsomeness of youth.

Then the verse forks, and the fork is the sharpest thing in the passage. **"Among you is he who dies"** — Ibn Kathir: when he is young and strong. **"And among you is he who is brought back to the miserable old age"** (*arḍhal al-ʿumur*) — Ibn Kathir: advanced old age with its weakness in mind and body, in steady decline in comprehension, and disability to grasp. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the stage of life when human faculties and senses begin to degenerate. Then the devastating clause: **"so that he knows nothing after having known."**

Read ayah 5 whole and see what it has done. It has shown you a resurrection you already believe in, because you lived it: dust, to fluid, to clot, to flesh, to a helpless infant, to a strong adult. Then it shows the curve coming back down, so the climb cannot be mistaken for your own achievement. Ibn Kathir brings in another ayah that traces the same arc: *"Allah is He Who created you in (a state of) weakness, then gave you strength after weakness, then after strength gave (you) weakness and grey hair. He creates what He wills. And it is He Who is the All-Knowing, the All-Powerful"* (30:54).

**A duʿā for this.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records that the Prophet ﷺ sought Allah's protection from such a stage of life: Nasa'i has quoted Sayyidna Saʿd as saying that he ﷺ used to repeat this prayer very frequently (via Qurtubi): *"O Allah! I seek Your protection from miserliness, and I seek Your protection from cowardice, and I seek Your protection from that I am carried to the age of helplessness, and I seek Your protection from the seductions of this world and the chastisement of the grave."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also reproduces a long narration from Anas ibn Malik, quoted from the Musnad of Ahmad and the Musnad of Abu Yaʿla, listing what Allah grants a believer at forty, fifty, sixty and beyond. It should be handled with the caution its own commentator gave it: Hafiz Ibn Kathir judged this hadith *gharib jiddan* — reported by one narrator only — and extremely *munkar*, that is, reported by a weak narrator against the authentic traditions, while adding that in spite of all this Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal related it in his Musnad both as a saying of the Prophet ﷺ and as the saying of a Companion. Mention it as the scholars did, and build nothing on it.

## Second witness: the dead earth

Having taken you through your own body, ayah 5 turns you outward: **"And you see the earth *hāmidah*."** Ibn Kathir: this is another sign of the power of Allah to bring the dead back to life, just as He brings the dead, barren earth back to life — the lifeless earth in which nothing grows. Qatadah explained the word as the eroded, dusty earth; As-Suddi simply said: dead.

Then three verbs in quick succession, each a stage of the return to life. **It is stirred** (*ihtazzat*) — Ibn Kathir: when Allah sends the rain upon it, vegetation begins to grow and it comes alive after it was dead. **It swells** (*rabat*) — then it rises after the soil had settled. **And it puts forth every lovely kind** (*min kulli zawjin bahīj*) — its different kinds of fruit and crops with all their varied colours, tastes, fragrances, shapes and benefits; Ibn Kathir glosses *bahīj* as beautiful in appearance and with delightful fragrances.

Do not rush past that last word. Bare survival would have proved the point. The chosen proof of resurrection is not a grim reassembly of matter but an outbreak of colour and scent.

## Ayah 6: what the two witnesses prove

**"That is because…"** The whole display in ayah 5 exists in order to establish three things.

**Allah is *al-Ḥaqq* — the Truth.** Ibn Kathir explains the name here as: the Creator, the Controller, the One Who does as He wills.

**He gives life to the dead.** Ibn Kathir ties this straight back to the field: just as He gives life to the dead earth and brings forth from it all these kinds of vegetation. He quotes: *"Verily, He Who gives it life, surely is able to give life to the dead. Indeed He is able to do all things"* (41:39).

**He is able to do all things.** As for how it is done, Ibn Kathir answers with: *"Verily, His command, when He intends a thing, is only that He says to it, 'Be!' — and it is!"* (36:82). A Lord for whom creation costs a word is not slowed by graves.

## Ayah 7: the doubt is closed

**"And surely the Hour is coming — *no doubt about it*."** Ibn Kathir: it will inevitably come to pass. Note how the passage frames itself. It opened with *your* doubt — *rayb*, in "if you are in doubt" — and closes with that same word negated: *lā rayba fīhā*, there is no doubt about it. The doubt was never in the thing. It was only ever in you.

**"And certainly Allah will resurrect those who are in the graves."** Ibn Kathir: He will bring them back to life after they have become dust; He will create them anew after they have become nothing. With that, the circle closes on the word the passage started with. You began from dust; you become dust; and from dust you will be raised, by the One who did it the first time. Ibn Kathir seals it with Surah Ya-Sin: *"And he puts forth for Us a parable, and forgets his own creation. He says: 'Who will give life to these bones after they are rotten and have become dust?' Say: 'He will give life to them Who created them for the first time! And He is the All-Knower of every creation!' He Who produces for you fire out of the green tree, when behold you kindle therewith"* (36:78–80).

*And forgets his own creation* — that is the disease this passage treats. Doubt about the Resurrection is, at root, a failure of memory.

## Living it

**Answer doubt by looking.** The passage does not hand you an abstract proof. It sends you to a pregnancy, an infant, an ageing relative, and a field after rain. Faith here is built from ordinary sights most people walk past.

**Rest in what was written.** The angel wrote four things before you drew a breath: provision, deeds, lifespan, and blessed or wretched. Your provision and your lifespan are settled and out of your hands, which is reason enough to stop gnawing at them. Your deeds are the one item on that list your days are actually spent on.

**Take the duʿā seriously.** The Prophet ﷺ frequently sought refuge from being carried to the age of helplessness. Ayah 5 shows why: strength is a loan, briefly held, and it is repossessed.

**Let rain mean something.** Ibn Kathir's point is that the reviving earth is a sign of Allah's power to bring the dead back to life. So the next time green breaks out of ground that was dead, you have watched a sign of your own raising.

passages.title: The arrogant disputer and his fiery reward
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat sketch a single figure: the man who argues about Allah with nothing to argue from, who turns his body away in contempt when the truth is offered to him, and who drags others down the road he has chosen. Ayah 8 names his emptiness, ayah 9 shows his posture and his double sentence — disgrace here, burning there — and ayah 10 delivers the verdict spoken to his face: this is your own doing, and Allah has wronged no one. What holds the passage together is a straight line from a certain kind of pride to a certain kind of punishment.

## Two disputers, not one

Ibn Kathir opens by setting this figure beside another one Allah has already described. "Allah has already told us about the ignorant imitators who are led astray," he says, quoting: *"And among mankind is he who disputes about Allah, without knowledge, and follows every rebellious Shayṭān."* That is the ignorant follower — the imitator who is himself being led.

Here the same opening words return, *"And among men is he who disputes about Allah,"* but the ending is different, and so is the man. Ibn Kathir says that here Allah "tells us about those who call others to misguidance, the leaders of disbelief and innovation," and he titles the passage as a clarification of the state of "the leaders of the innovators and those who lead people astray."

That pairing is worth pausing over. The Qur'an does not lump the misguided together. There is the follower who has swallowed something he never examined, and there is the figurehead who calls others to it. Both are in error. But the second man carries a weight the first does not, and these three ayat are aimed at him.

## Three doors, all shut

Ayah 8 denies him three things: **ʿilm** (knowledge), **hudā** (guidance), and **kitāb munīr** — rendered as "a Book giving light." Ibn Kathir compresses this into a sharp formula: he has *"no correct rational thought, and no clear transmitted text; what they say is based only on their opinions and whims."*

Think of it as three doors by which a claim about Allah could legitimately enter. Sound reasoning is one. Guidance is another. A revealed scripture that gives light is the third. This man has none of the three, and yet he speaks — confidently, publicly, and about **Allah**, the subject on which human guesswork has the least purchase of any subject there is.

Whatever he produces, then, is not a third source of truth. It is, as Ibn Kathir says, opinion and whim wearing the clothes of argument.

## The body language of arrogance (ayah 9)

Then comes the phrase that gives the passage its physical vividness: **ثَانِيَ عِطْفِهِ**, *thāniya ʿiṭfihi*.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the vocabulary plainly: **ʿiṭf** means "the side of the body," and the expression means "to turn on one's side" — which is to say, **to oppose**. The Arabic captures a gesture anyone can picture: the shoulder that swivels away, the torso that turns as you are still speaking, the man who has physically closed himself off before you have finished your sentence.

Ibn Kathir gives two readings from the early authorities, and they complement rather than contradict each other:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās and others**: it means he is *"too proud to follow the truth when he is called to it."* This reads the phrase as a description of the heart's condition — the inner refusal.
- **Mujāhid, Qatādah and Mālik, narrating from Zayd ibn Aslam**: it means *twisting his neck* — turning away from the truth to which he is called, "bending his neck out of pride and arrogance."

So the phrase works on both levels at once: a neck that turns, and a soul that will not bend. Ibn Kathir then lines up a series of ayat that show the same turning away:

- **Firʿawn** in 51:38–39 — Mūsā was sent to him with a manifest authority, and *"(Firʿawn) turned away along with his hosts."*
- **The hypocrites** in 4:61 — invited to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger ﷺ, *"you see the hypocrites turn away from you with aversion."*
- **63:5** — invited to come so that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ may ask forgiveness from Allah for them, *"they twist their heads, and you would see them turning away their faces in pride."*
- **31:7** — *"And when Our verses are recited to him, he turns away in pride."*
- And from the other direction, **Luqmān's advice to his son** in 31:18: *"And turn not your face away from men with pride"* — which Ibn Kathir glosses as: do not turn away from them in an arrogant manner.

That last one is the quiet sting of the collection. The very gesture the Qur'an condemns in Firʿawn is the gesture a wise father warns his own son against in ordinary company. The arrogance of the great disputer and the arrogance of the man who cannot bear to be corrected at the dinner table are the same disease at different scales.

## Leading others astray

The ayah continues: *"and leading (others) too (far) astray from the path of Allah."* Ibn Kathir reports that this is read in one of two ways. It either refers to those who are **stubborn**; or it means that the person who does this "has been created like this so that he will be one of those who lead others astray from the path of Allah." On the second reading the ayah is not an excuse for the man — as ayah 10 will make unmistakable, the deed is still *his*, sent forward by his own hands.

Either way, the point that lands is this: private error does not stay private in a man who is followed. His arrogance becomes other people's misguidance. The sin is no longer his alone.

## Disgrace here, burning there

Ayah 9 hands down a sentence in two instalments.

**"For him there is disgrace in this worldly life."** Ibn Kathir explains *khizy* as humiliation and shame, and he draws out the fittingness of it: this comes about "when he is too arrogant to heed the signs of Allah, so Allah will send humiliation upon him in this world and will punish him in this world, before he reaches the Hereafter, because this world is all he cares about and all he knows."

That is a striking piece of divine justice. The punishment is delivered in the only currency he recognises. A man whose entire horizon is this life is disgraced within this life — hit where he actually lives. And the arrogance that made him unable to accept the truth is answered by a humiliation he cannot refuse.

**"And on the Day of Resurrection We shall make him taste the torment of burning."** The instalment in this world is not the whole account.

## "Because of what your hands sent forth" (ayah 10)

Ayah 10 does something the ear should catch. Through ayahs 8 and 9 the man has been spoken *about* — "he," "him," "for him." Now, suddenly, he is spoken *to*: **"that is because of what your hands have sent forth."** Ibn Kathir explains why: *"this will be said to him by way of rebuke."* The distance closes. The one who spent his life turning his side away is finally addressed face to face, and there is no side left to turn.

"What your hands have sent forth" is the Qur'anic image of deeds dispatched ahead of you, arriving before you do. He did not find the Fire waiting for him by accident; he sent it ahead himself, argument by argument, refusal by refusal.

Then: **"and verily, Allah is not unjust to the servants."** The whole passage has been building a case, and this is the seal on it. Nobody is punished for a thing he did not do. The disputer was not deprived of knowledge, guidance, or a Book giving light — he turned his shoulder to them. Every element of ayahs 8 and 9 is there to establish that the verdict of ayah 10 is exactly earned.

Ibn Kathir closes by placing beside it the scene of 44:47–50: *"Seize him and drag him into the midst of blazing Fire, then pour over his head the torment of boiling water. Taste you (this)! Verily, you were (pretending to be) the mighty, the generous! Verily, this is that whereof you used to doubt!"* The titles the man pretended to — *the mighty, the generous* — are read back to him there as his own indictment. It is the same logic that runs through our passage: what the arrogant man built his identity on is what is used to answer him.

## Living it

The passage is a portrait, but portraits in the Qur'an are also mirrors. Three things it asks of a believer:

**Check your sources before you speak about Allah.** Ayah 8 names exactly what a claim about Allah must rest on: knowledge, guidance, and a Book giving light. Ibn Kathir's warning is that what fills the vacuum when those are absent is not silence but "opinions and whims" delivered with confidence. Saying *I don't know* about a matter of religion is not a failure; it is the honest alternative to becoming the man in this ayah.

**Watch the shoulder.** By the reading of Ibn ʿAbbās, *thāniya ʿiṭfihi* is being too proud to follow the truth when you are called to it. That test does not wait for great theological occasions. It arrives when a spouse, a student, or a younger person points out that you were wrong — and something in you turns away before the sentence is finished. Luqmān's counsel in 31:18 puts it at exactly that everyday level.

**Remember who is watching the ripple.** The man in this passage is condemned not only for his own error but for where it carried others. Anyone who teaches, posts, leads, or is simply listened to should feel the weight of that clause.

And behind all of it stands the assurance of ayah 10 — *Allah is not unjust to the servants*. The same sentence that terrifies the arrogant reassures everyone else: no one is answered for more than what his own hands sent forth.

passages.title: Worshipping Allah on the edge of faith
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat draw a portrait of a particular kind of person: someone who does worship Allah, but only from the outer rim of faith — and whose religion therefore lasts exactly as long as his good fortune does. Ayah 11 shows us the man and how he falls; ayat 12 and 13 show us where he lands once he has fallen, calling on things that cannot help him and on a "friend" who only harms.

## The image in ayah 11: worship on a ledge

The Arabic phrase is `عَلَىٰ حَرْفٍ` — *ʿalā ḥarf*, "upon an edge." Ibn Kathir records two readings of it from the early authorities.

**Mujahid, Qatadah and others** said *ʿalā ḥarf* means **in doubt**. The man's worship rests on an unsettled mind; he has not made up his heart about Allah, so nothing he does is anchored.

**Others** took the word in its physical sense: an edge the way a mountain has an edge or a side. On that reading, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "this person enters Islam on the edge, and if he finds what he likes he will continue, otherwise he will leave."

Notice what the image is not saying. It is not saying he stands outside the religion. He is described as one who *worships Allah* — he is inside, he prays, he is counted among the Muslims. But he is standing on the rim rather than in the middle. Anyone standing on a ledge is one gust away from being off it, and that is precisely what the rest of the ayah describes.

## Who the ayah is describing

The commentaries fill in the human picture behind the image.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** relates — naming Bukhari and Ibn Abi Haim as its sources, from Sayyidna Ibn ʿAbbas — that when the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah, people flocked to him and accepted the new religion. But among them were some whose conversion was far from genuine, whose sole motive was self-advancement, and who lacked conviction. If, after becoming Muslims, circumstances turned favourable and their prosperity and children increased, they thought Islam a very good religion; and they were equally ready to condemn it if things went against their personal interests. The verse was revealed to describe such people: mere opportunists, easily swayed either way depending on where their selfish interests lay.

**Al-Bukhari recorded** from Ibn ʿAbbas the concrete version of this. People would come to Madinah to declare their Islam; if their wives gave birth to sons and their mares gave birth to foals, they would say, "This is a good religion" — and if their wives and their mares did not give birth, they would say, "This is a bad religion."

**Al-ʿAwfi reported** from Ibn ʿAbbas a fuller picture that adds a crucial detail: Madinah at that time was a land infected with a contagious disease. So the man arrives. If he stays healthy there, and his mare foals, and his wife bears him a boy, he is content and says, "I have not experienced anything but good since I started to follow this religion."

Sit with that sentence for a moment. It sounds like gratitude. It is in fact a verdict — he has been quietly assessing the religion against a private ledger of outcomes, and this time the ledger came out in profit.

## What "if a fitnah strikes him" means here

The ayah's second half turns: `وَإِنْ أَصَابَتْهُ فِتْنَةٌ` — "but if a fitnah strikes him." Ibn Kathir specifies that **fitnah here means affliction**, hardship that befalls a person.

And Ibn ʿAbbas, in Al-ʿAwfi's report, spells out exactly what that looked like for this man: the disease of Madinah befalls him, his wife gives birth to a baby girl rather than the son he wanted, and charity is delayed in coming to him. Small griefs, ordinary disappointments — nothing that touches the truth of the religion at all.

Then comes the decisive moment, and it is worth noticing that in this report the turning point is not the hardship itself but a voice: **the Shaytan comes to him and says, "By Allah, since you started to follow this religion of yours, you have experienced nothing but bad things."** Ibn ʿAbbas says: *this* is the fitnah. Ibn Kathir notes that Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj and others among the Salaf — the earliest generations of Muslims, whose understanding of the Qur'an carries special weight — explained the ayah along the same lines.

So the trial has two layers. There is the loss — and then there is the interpretation offered to him about the loss. The Shaytan does not tell him Allah is not real. He simply audits his life since the day he embraced the religion and presents the balance as evidence against it. Notice too that the whisper even swears by Allah. It arrives dressed as honest reckoning.

## "He turns back on his face"

`انْقَلَبَ عَلَىٰ وَجْهِهِ` — he turns back on his face. It is the language of a fall, which is what someone standing on an edge does. **Mujahid** said plainly of this phrase: "he becomes an apostate and a disbeliever."

That is the sober weight of ayah 11. The man did not gradually drift; he flipped. And what flipped him was not an argument against Allah but a run of bad luck.

## The double loss

`خَسِرَ الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةَ` — "He loses both this world and the Hereafter." Ibn Kathir unpacks both halves. **In this world**, he does not gain anything — the whole point of his bargain was worldly return, and he does not get it. **In the Hereafter**, he has disbelieved in Allah the Almighty, so he will be utterly doomed and humiliated.

Hence the verdict that closes ayah 11: `ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ الْخُسْرَانُ الْمُبِينُ` — "That is the evident loss." Ibn Kathir glosses it as **the greatest loss and the losing deal**. The commercial flavour is fitting: this man approached his religion as a transaction, so he is answered in the language of transactions. He was trading, and he came away with nothing on either side of the ledger.

## Ayat 12–13: where the edge leads

Having fallen, he does not fall into nothing. He falls into something.

**Ayah 12:** `يَدْعُو مِنْ دُونِ اللَّهِ مَا لَا يَضُرُّهُ وَمَا لَا يَنْفَعُهُ` — "He calls besides Allah unto that which can neither harm him nor profit him." Ibn Kathir identifies what he calls upon: **the idols, rivals, and false gods** whom he invokes for help, support and provision — and which can neither benefit him nor harm him.

Feel the irony against ayah 11. He abandoned the worship of Allah because it was not delivering benefit, and what he ran to cannot deliver benefit at all. It cannot even harm him — it is that inert. Of this the ayah says: `ذَٰلِكَ هُوَ الضَّلَالُ الْبَعِيدُ` — "That is a straying far away." He has not merely stepped off the path; he has wandered a long way from it.

**Ayah 13** then sharpens the description: `يَدْعُو لَمَنْ ضَرُّهُ أَقْرَبُ مِنْ نَفْعِهِ` — "He calls unto him whose harm is nearer than his profit." Ibn Kathir explains: **he is more likely to be harmed than benefited by it in this world, and in the Hereafter it will most certainly cause him harm.** The thing was useless in ayah 12; in ayah 13 it is worse than useless. There is nothing on the profit side to weigh, and the harm is not distant — it is *nearer*, already pressing on him.

## "An evil mawlā and an evil ʿashīr"

The passage ends with two words of judgement, and they are worth learning: `لَبِئْسَ الْمَوْلَىٰ وَلَبِئْسَ الْعَشِيرُ` — "certainly an evil mawlā and certainly an evil ʿashīr!" Of this phrase **Mujahid** said: "This means the idols."

**Mawlā** here carries the sense of the patron one turns to — Ibn Kathir gives the meaning as: "How evil a friend is this one upon whom he calls instead of Allah as a **helper and supporter**." A mawlā is the one you fall back on when you have nowhere else to go.

**ʿAshīr** Ibn Kathir defines as **the one with whom one mixes and spends one's time** — the constant companion, the one whose company shapes your days.

So the false object of worship is condemned in both of its roles at once: as the protector who cannot protect, and as the intimate whose company is ruin. Every function a person hopes to get from turning to something other than Allah — rescue in crisis, companionship in ordinary life — is named here and declared worthless.

## Living it

This passage is not really about mares and foals. It is about a way of holding one's faith, and the sources make the diagnosis precise enough to apply.

**Watch what your religion is resting on.** The man in ayah 11 was not lazy in worship; he worshipped. His problem was location — he stood at the edge, in doubt as Mujahid and Qatadah read it, ready to leave if things stopped going his way. The question is not only *do I worship?* but *what would it take to stop me?*

**Beware the private ledger.** "I have not experienced anything but good since I started to follow this religion" is a dangerous sentence, because the same accounting logic that produces it will one day produce its opposite. If good fortune is your evidence for the truth of Islam, misfortune becomes evidence against it. Islam is true because it is true, not because the year went well.

**Recognise the whisper for what it is.** In Ibn ʿAbbas's report, the fitnah is the moment the Shaytan totals up your hardships and hands you the sum as proof that faith has cost you. Name that accusation when it arrives.

**And do not misread ordinary hardship.** Illness in a new city, a daughter instead of a son, help that was slow to arrive — these were the afflictions that toppled a man's entire religion. The ayah's whole point is that he read them wrongly: he took ordinary hardship as a verdict on the religion, when it was only a test of whether he was standing in the middle of it or on its edge.

The alternative to the edge is the middle: worshipping Allah because He is Allah, so that when the affliction comes — and it will — there is nowhere to fall from.

passages.title: Rage cannot undo what Allah has decreed
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are read here as one passage, and its theme is that rage cannot undo what Allah has decreed. Ayah 14 tells us where believing and doing righteous deeds ends: Gardens underneath which rivers flow. Ayah 15 turns to the man who thinks Allah will not help His Messenger ﷺ and tells him, with devastating irony, to stretch out a rope and hang himself — and then see whether that changed anything. Ayah 16 closes the movement: this Qur'an has been sent down as clear signs, and it is Allah who guides whom He wills.

Notice the frame the passage builds. Ayah 14 ends **"Verily, Allah does what He wills."** Ayah 16 ends **"and surely, Allah guides whom He wills."** Between those two statements about Allah's will sits ayah 15 — the picture of a man raging against something he has no power to touch. Read the middle ayah without the two ends and it sounds merely strange; read it inside the frame and its point is unmistakable.

## Two destinies, set side by side

Ibn Kathir opens by pointing out the structure of the passage: the mention of the misguided who are doomed is followed by mention of the righteous who are blessed. The Qur'an rarely leaves a warning standing alone; it sets the two destinies beside each other so the reader can see which road he is on.

Notice how Ibn Kathir defines the second group. They are "those who believe firmly in their hearts and confirm their faith by their actions, doing all kinds of righteous deeds and avoiding evil actions." Two halves that must meet: an inward conviction, and an outward life that confirms it. That is why the ayah pairs *believed* with *did righteous deeds* — the deeds are faith's confirmation, not an optional extra bolted on afterwards. And because of this, says Ibn Kathir, "they will inherit dwellings in the lofty ranks of the gardens of Paradise."

Ibn Kathir then draws the two halves of the passage together: Allah tells us that He sends those astray and guides these, and says, **"Verily, Allah does what He wills."** He does not leave that phrase to stand as bare power — as we will see at ayah 16, he joins Allah's willing to His complete wisdom.

## Who the contrast was drawn against

The contrast lands harder when you know who the preceding ayat were describing. Commenting on **"And among men there is one who worships Allah (standing) on the verge"** (22:11), Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān reports that **Bukhari and Ibn Abi Haim** have related from Sayyidna Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) that when the Prophet ﷺ migrated to Madinah, people flocked to him and accepted the new religion — but among them were some whose conversion to Islam was far from genuine. Their sole motive was to seek self-advancement, and they lacked conviction. If, after becoming Muslims, favourable circumstances increased their prosperity and their children, they thought Islam a very good religion; but they were equally ready to condemn it if things went against their personal interests. The ayah was revealed to describe such people — mere opportunists, easily swayed either way depending on where their selfish interests lay.

So ayah 14 is the answer to that portrait. Against the man whose religion is a calculation, Allah sets the one whose belief is firm in the heart and confirmed by his actions — and it is the second whom Allah admits into the Gardens. The same divine will that leaves the calculating man on his verge admits the sincere man into Paradise.

## "Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him" — two readings of one word

This is the strangest-sounding ayah in the passage, and the commentators give two readings of it. Both turn on one Arabic word: **samā'** (سَمَاء), which normally means *sky* or *heaven*, but which some scholars here take to mean the ceiling of one's house.

**Reading one: the ceiling.** This is the reading Ibn Kathir carries. He narrates from **Ibn 'Abbas**: "Whoever thinks that Allah will not help Muhammad ﷺ in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch out a rope" — *to the ceiling*, that is, "to the ceiling in his house" — "and let him hang himself with it." Ibn Kathir notes that this was also the view of **Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', Abu Al-Jawza', Qatadah and others**: a solid weight of the early commentators.

The sense, as Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: whoever thinks that Allah will not support Muhammad ﷺ and His Book and His Religion, let him go and kill himself if it annoys him so much — for Allah will most certainly help and support him. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān records the same reading, attributing it to **Mazhari and others**: a person who entertains hostile feelings towards Islam and the Prophet ﷺ must realise that he can do them no harm, so the best thing left for him is to hang himself from the ceiling out of sheer mortification.

Read this the way the commentators read it — as a rhetorical challenge, not a religious instruction. The ayah is not telling anyone to take his own life; it is exposing the emptiness of his rage by naming the most extreme thing he could do to himself and then asking whether even *that* would remove what enrages him.

**Reading two: the sky.** Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān prefers a different reading, related in **al-Durr al-Manthūr from Ibn Zaid**, and calls it in his opinion the most appropriate one; **Qurtubi** also thinks it the best interpretation of this verse. On this reading the *samā'* is the actual sky, and the cutting is the cutting of the chain of revelation.

The reasoning runs like this. The enemies of Islam who put hurdles in its path desired that Allah should abandon the Prophet ﷺ and his religion. But that could only happen if — Allah forbid — he were deprived of the office of prophethood and ceased to receive *wahy* (revelation) from Allah. And it is well understood that when Allah bestows prophethood on someone and favours him with revelation, He also promises him full support in this world and in the Hereafter. So the only way to stop the advancement of a prophet and his mission would be to dispossess him of that mission, or to sever the sequence of revelation — which would mean going up to the sky and cutting off the chain of revelation. Since no such thing is possible, no amount of fire and fury can do any harm to Islam.

Both readings arrive at the same door from opposite sides. One says: your rage cannot be relieved even by destroying yourself. The other says: to stop this you would have to reach the sky, and you cannot. Either way the decree of ayah 14 — *Allah does what He wills* — stands untouched.

## The question put to the enraged man

**"Then let him see whether his plan will remove that whereat he rages!"** Two of the early authorities unpack the closing words. Of what it is that enrages him, **As-Suddi** said: "Meaning, in the case of Muhammad ﷺ." And **'Ata' Al-Khurasani** said: "Let him see whether that will cure the rage he feels in his heart."

That second comment deserves a pause, because it locates the rage precisely — *in his heart*. The ayah invites the man to run the experiment himself: put your plan to work, do your worst, and then look honestly and tell me whether the thing eating at you is gone. It will not be. His scheming changes nothing outside him, and by 'Ata' Al-Khurasani's reading it does not even cure what is inside him.

Behind the challenge stands a promise, and Ibn Kathir names it with another ayah: **"Verily, We will indeed make victorious Our Messengers and those who believe in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses will stand forth"** (40:51). Both times are named — this world's life, and the Day the witnesses stand forth.

## Clear signs, and guidance in Allah's hand

**"Thus have We sent it down"** — Ibn Kathir: this refers to the Qur'an.

**"as clear Ayat"** — Ibn Kathir explains: clear in its wording *and* in its meaning, evidence from Allah to mankind. Both halves matter. A text can be plain in its words but murky in what it asks, or profound in meaning but locked behind its expression. The claim here is that the Qur'an is clear in both, and that this is what makes it *evidence*: no one who rejects it can say the case was never properly put to him.

**"and surely, Allah guides whom He wills."** Ibn Kathir states it directly: He sends astray whomsoever He wills and He guides whomsoever He wills — "and He has complete wisdom and definitive proof in doing so." That last clause is the guard against misunderstanding, and it is what the earlier *Allah does what He wills* was pointing towards all along. Divine will is never presented here as bare power; it comes joined to wisdom and to proof. Ibn Kathir then cites **"He cannot be questioned about what He does, while they will be questioned"** (21:23), and comments that because of His wisdom, mercy, justice, knowledge, dominion and might, no one can overturn His ruling — and He is swift in bringing to account.

Hold those two together the way the source does. Allah is not answerable to His creation, and creation is entirely answerable to Him. And that is no licence for despair, because the same commentary names *mercy* and *justice* alongside dominion and might. We affirm what Allah has said of Himself — His will, His wisdom, His mercy, His justice — as the early generations did, without likening any of it to the will or the mercy of creatures, and without emptying the words of their meaning.

## What this passage asks of us

**Locate yourself in ayah 14.** The description is specific: belief firm in the heart, confirmed by actions — doing righteous deeds and avoiding evil ones. Set against it stands the portrait behind ayah 11: people whose verdict on the religion tracked their circumstances, good fortune making it look excellent and hardship making it look doubtful. That test still runs. The honest question is not whether you say you believe, but whether your practice moves when your circumstances move.

**Recognise what rage cannot do — including your own.** Ayah 15 is aimed at those hostile to the Prophet ﷺ, but 'Ata' Al-Khurasani's question is worth carrying into ordinary life: *will that cure the rage he feels in his heart?* When something Allah has decreed sits badly with us, scheming against it neither removes it nor soothes us. The passage's own answer to a decree we cannot touch is the frame it is built on: **Allah does what He wills.**

**Take the promise seriously.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 15 is not merely that opposition is futile, but that Allah "will most certainly help and support" His Messenger ﷺ, His Book and His Religion — in this world's life and on the Day when the witnesses stand forth (40:51). For a believer watching the religion mocked or squeezed, that is the settling thought.

**And ask for guidance rather than assume it.** If Allah guides whom He wills, then guidance is a gift to be begged for, not a possession to be smug about. The Qur'an has been sent down as clear Ayat, clear in wording and in meaning; the clarity is complete on Allah's side. What remains is a heart willing to receive it.

passages.title: All religions judged, all creation prostrating
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in brief.** These two ayat set the world's competing religions side by side and then answer the question they raise. Ayah 17 lists the great communities of faith — the believers, the Jews, the Sabians, the Christians, the Magi, and others who worship others alongside Allah — and declares that Allah Himself will settle the matter between them on the Day of Resurrection. Ayah 18 then lifts the reader's eyes off the human argument and shows creation — heavens, earth, sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees, animals — prostrating before Allah, before naming two groups among mankind: those who prostrate, and those on whom the punishment is justified.

**What holds them together.** The two ayat move from *dispute* to *submission*. Ayah 17 says the verdict is coming; ayah 18 shows what is being weighed. The question underneath every claim is whether a person submits to Allah, as the rest of creation already does. And the passage ends where the argument ends — the one whom Allah disgraces has no one left to honour him.

## Ayah 17: the sects and the settlement

Ibn Kathir opens by noting that Allah is here telling us about "the followers of these various religions" — the believers (Muslims) and others such as the Jews and the Sabians. He notes that a definition of the Sabians has already been seen in Sūrat al-Baqarah, and that people differ over who they are. He adds that there are also the Christians, the Majūs (Magi), and others who worship others alongside Allah. On the identity of the Sabians, then, Ibn Kathir reports the disagreement rather than settling it.

What is *not* left open is the outcome. Ibn Kathir explains **يَفْصِلُ بَيْنَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ** — "(judge between them on the Day of Resurrection)" — as judging *with justice*: "He will admit those who believed in Him to Paradise and will send those who disbelieved in Him to Hell." And he grounds that in Allah's knowledge: "He is a Witness over their deeds, and He knows all that they say and all that they do in secret, and conceal in their breast."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same link between the judgement and the knowledge: Allah will decide among the believers and non-believers of the different faiths on the Day of Resurrection **because He knows everything**. It adds that what that decision will be has been related in the Qur'an in several places — the good Muslims will enjoy a life of everlasting peace and comfort, while the disbelievers will be condemned to a life of eternal perdition.

**Notice what the ayah does not do.** It does not stage a debate between the groups it names, and it does not argue against each in turn. It names them and states that Allah will judge between them. And nothing said aloud, nothing done in secret, nothing concealed in a chest, is outside the knowledge of the One who will judge.

## Ayah 18: the sight that settles the argument

Then the address turns personal: **أَلَمْ تَرَ** — "See you not…". The eye is directed away from the sectarian quarrel and onto creation itself.

Ibn Kathir sums up the point in a sentence: Allah is telling us that **He alone, with no partner or associate, is deserving of worship**. Everything prostrates to His might, willingly or unwillingly, and — this is the key that unlocks the ayah — **everything prostrates in a manner that befits its nature**. He cites Allah's words about created things whose "shadows incline to the right and to the left, making prostration unto Allah, and they are lowly" (16:48), and Allah's words that "there is not a thing but glorifies His praise" (17:44).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same principle in plain terms: *sajdah* (prostration) is used here in the broader sense of **submission to the will of Allah and obeying His commands**, because all created things act upon this submission in their own way. Human beings perform sajdah by touching the ground with the forehead; in the case of other created things, their sajdah "constitutes their faithful performance of the functions assigned to them by Allah."

**Who is included.** Ibn Kathir explains "whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth" as "the angels in the regions of the heavens, and all the living creatures, men, Jinn, animals and birds." Then the ayah names specific things: **the sun, the moon, and the stars**. Ibn Kathir explains exactly why these three are mentioned by name — **"because they are worshipped instead of Allah, so Allah explains that they too prostrate to their Creator and that they are subjected to Him."** He connects it to the command: "Prostrate yourselves not to the sun nor to the moon, but prostrate yourselves to Allah Who created them" (41:37).

**From the Sunnah — the sun beneath the Throne.** In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs it was recorded that Abū Dharr said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me, "(Do you know where this sun goes?)" I said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "(It goes (sets) and prostrates beneath the Throne, then it awaits the command. Soon it will be told, 'Go back the way whence you came.')" The very body that Ibn Kathir says is worshipped instead of Allah is shown here going, prostrating, awaiting the command, and being told where to go.

**The prostrating tree.** Ibn Kathir records that Ibn ʿAbbās said: a man came and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I saw myself in a dream last night, as if I was praying behind a tree. I prostrated, and the tree prostrated when I did, and I heard it saying, 'O Allah, write down a reward for me for that, and remove a sin from me for that, store it with You for me and accept it from me as You accepted from Your servant Dāwūd.'" Ibn ʿAbbās said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ recited an Ayah mentioning a prostration, then he prostrated, and I heard him saying the same words that the man had told him the tree said." This was recorded by at-Tirmidhī, Ibn Mājah, and Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ. Those words are worth carrying into your own sujūd: a request for reward, for a sin lifted, for the deed to be stored with Allah and accepted.

**The animals — ad-Dawābb.** Ibn Kathir explains **الدَّوَابُّ** as "all the animals," and reports that it was mentioned in a hadith recorded by Imam Aḥmad that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade using the backs of animals as platforms for speaking, "for, perhaps the one who was being ridden was better and remembered Allah more than the one who was riding." Sit with that. The ayah has just told you the animal is prostrating; the hadith tells you not to stand on top of it to make a speech.

## The two groups among mankind

Ayah 18 sweeps through creation and then breaks its own rhythm. It does not say "and mankind." It says **وَكَثِيرٌ مِّنَ النَّاسِ** — "(and many of mankind)." Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning "they prostrate willingly, submitting themselves to Allah of their own free will." Then the counterweight: **وَكَثِيرٌ حَقَّ عَلَيْهِ الْعَذَابُ** — "(But there are many (men) on whom the punishment is justified.)" — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, "those who refuse prostration, are stubborn and arrogant."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the structure out: the ayah declares that all created things — living things, minerals, plants — are in obedience and submit to the supreme authority of Allah, and then mentions two groups *among humans*: one which obeys Allah and is therefore included amongst the creatures who prostrate to Him, and another which is rebellious and refuses to bow before Him, meaning refusing to submit to His will.

**Two kinds of submission.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes them carefully. The first is what it calls the guidance of *takwīn* — an inherently programmed guidance by which the entire universe and all created things in it are under the control of, and subject to, the will of their Creator. This submission is "pre-determined, involuntary and instinctive." No created being escapes this universal law of creation: Muslim or non-believer, living thing or dead, mineral or plant. "The smallest particle and the highest mountain cannot make the slightest movement without His Will." The second kind is when a person offers homage to Allah **voluntarily and without constraint** — and *this*, it says, is what distinguishes a believer from a non-believer: a believer is obedient and sincere in his submission to Allah, whereas a non-believer repudiates His existence.

Read together, the two kinds tell you something worth holding: the first kind of submission is not optional for anyone. What is refused is the second — the willing bow.

**Where the commentators go different distances.** Ibn Kathir reads the prostration of ayah 18 as everything prostrating to Allah's might "willingly or unwillingly," each in the way that befits its nature. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān argues for more: since this ayah deals with the difference between a Muslim and a *kāfir* (one who rejects faith), it is "more likely" that the sajdah mentioned does not refer to pre-destined and instinctive obedience alone but covers **voluntary** submission as well. It then warns the reader not to suppose that only humans and jinn, who possess intelligence, can offer voluntary submission while animals, plants and minerals cannot. It argues from the text of the Qur'an that every created thing has reason, intellect and intent, the difference lying only in degree: humans and jinn possess a perfect level of intelligence, which makes them liable to strict adherence to what is permissible and what is forbidden, while other creatures are given intelligence according to their needs — animals highest after humans, then plants, and last the minerals, whose share is so little and concealed that it is not easily discernible.

For evidence it cites the Qur'an's own words: of the sky and the earth, **قَالَتَا أَتَيْنَا طَائِعِينَ** — "They said, 'We come willingly'" (41:11) — that is, when Allah commanded the sky and the earth to submit to His will either by free choice or by force, both replied that they accepted His authority by their own voluntary choice. And of the rocks, **وَإِنَّ مِنْهَا لَمَا يَهْبِطُ مِنْ خَشْيَةِ اللَّـهِ** — "and there are still others which fall down in fear of Allah" (2:74). It adds that there are numerous traditions providing evidence of mountains conversing with one another, or other created things showing signs of intelligence. Its conclusion: except for humans and jinn, all other created things voluntarily and willingly submit to the Divine Authority; it is only humans and jinn who are divided into two factions — those who bow in submission to the will of Allah, and those who deny His authority and refuse to submit to Him and are therefore despised. And it closes, as a careful scholar should, with **"Allah knows best."**

We affirm what the sources affirm — that creation genuinely prostrates and glorifies Allah, each thing in the manner that befits its nature — without pressing beyond that into speculation about *how*.

## "Allah does what He wills"

The passage ends: **وَمَن يُهِنِ اللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُ مِن مُّكْرِمٍ ۚ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ ۩** — "(And whomsoever Allah disgraces, none can honor him. Verily, Allah does what He wills.)"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān has just described the faction that denies Allah's authority and refuses to submit to Him as being, for that reason, *despised*. The closing words of the ayah say where that leaves them: if Allah disgraces a person, there is no one who can honour him.

**From the Sunnah — the Shayṭān weeping.** It was recorded that Abū Hurayrah said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "(When the son of Adam recites the Ayat containing the prostration, the Shaytan withdraws weeping and says, 'Ah! Woe (to me)! the son of Adam was commanded to prostrate and he prostrated, so Paradise is his; I was commanded to prostrate and I refused, so I am doomed to Hell.')" This was recorded by Muslim. The refusal ayah 18 describes is not an abstraction — here is one who was commanded to prostrate and refused, weeping as he watches a human being do what he would not do.

## Living it: this ayah asks for a sajdah

Ayah 18 carries the sajdah symbol ۩ at its end, and the report from Abū Hurayrah above describes exactly this: the son of Adam recites the ayah containing the prostration, and he prostrates.

Ibn Kathir records two reports about the prostrations of this sūrah. In his book *Al-Marāsīl*, Abū Dāwūd recorded that Khālid bin Maʿdān, may Allah have mercy upon him, reported that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said: "(Sūrat al-Ḥajj has been favored over the rest of the Qur'an with two prostrations.)" And al-Ḥāfiẓ Abū Bakr al-Ismāʿīlī recorded from Abū al-Jahm that ʿUmar did the two prostrations of Sūrat al-Ḥajj when he was in al-Jābiyah, and said, "This Surah has been favored with two prostrations."

So the passage does not merely describe prostration — it asks for one. You read that the sun prostrates, that the mountains and trees and animals prostrate, that many of mankind prostrate and many refuse; and then the ayah invites you to put your own forehead on the ground.

**Three things to carry away.**

- **The verdict belongs to Allah.** Ayah 17 names the communities and states that Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection, with justice, because He knows everything. Our work is to be found in the right group.
- **You are never worshipping alone.** Ibn Kathir's picture in ayah 18 is of angels, living creatures, sun, moon, stars, mountains, trees and animals all prostrating. The believer who bows joins what the rest of creation is already doing; the one who refuses is, in Ibn Kathir's words, "stubborn and arrogant."
- **Honour has only one source.** "And whomsoever Allah disgraces, none can honor him. Verily, Allah does what He wills."

passages.title: Two adversaries: the boiling drink and the bracelets
passages.tafsir:
These six ayat take the whole history of human disagreement and reduce it to two parties standing before their Lord. Ayah 19 announces the case — "These are two opposing groups that disagree about their Lord" — and the rest of the passage delivers the verdict on each side: first the losing party (ayat 19–22), then the winning one (ayat 23–24). What holds the unit together is a sustained contrast carried by matched images — garments for one group and garments for the other, a drink poured on one and rivers running for the other, words of scorn spoken to one and words of peace to the other.

## "Two opposing groups"

Ibn Kathir renders the opening of the ayah, "These two opponents dispute with each other about their Lord." The word rendered "opponents" carries the sense of two adversaries in a dispute — and the passage that follows makes clear that each "opponent" is not one man but a whole side.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws exactly that conclusion: the verse "with its general words, deals with two sets of people, namely the Muslims and the infidels whether they belong to the earliest times or to later ages."

And notice what the quarrel is about: *fī rabbihim*, "about their Lord." Not about land, or honour, or trade. Ibn Kathir puts his finger on why these two parties can never be reconciled: "the believers want to support the religion of Allah, while the disbelievers want to extinguish the light of faith and to defeat the truth and cause falsehood to prevail." That is the fault line under everything else.

## The day the two sides walked out at Badr

The sources give this ayah an occasion of revelation that is unusually well attested, and it is worth telling properly.

Ibn Kathir reports that it was **recorded in the Two Sahihs** that Abu Dharr swore that this ayah was revealed concerning Hamzah and his two companions, and ʿUtbah and his two companions, on the day of Badr, when they came forward to engage in single combat. Ibn Kathir notes that this is the wording of Al-Bukhari in his Tafsir of this ayah.

Al-Bukhari also records the sub-narrator Qays naming the six men who came forward: on one side **ʿAli, Hamzah, and ʿUbaydah**; on the other **Shaybah bin Rabiʿah, ʿUtbah bin Rabiʿah, and Al-Walid bin ʿUtbah**. Ibn Kathir observes that this particular report was recorded only by Al-Bukhari.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in what happened. Hamzah and ʿUbaidah (may Allah be pleased with them) stepped out of the Muslim ranks, while ʿUtbah bin Rabiʿah, his son Walid and his brother Shaibah came out to challenge them. In the ensuing fight the three unbelievers were slain. Hamzah (may Allah be pleased with him) emerged unscathed. ʿUbaidah (may Allah be pleased with him) was mortally wounded, and died at the feet of the Prophet ﷺ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the revelation of this verse in relation to these warriors of the field of Badr is well established on the authority of traditions contained in Bukhari and Muslim.

Hold the scene in mind. Men step out of two armies into the open ground between them, and three of them do not walk back. And what Allah calls that scene, in the words He revealed about it, is a dispute *about their Lord*. Not a feud, not a raid — the two sides of a single argument over who the Lord is.

**ʿAli's words.** Al-Bukhari records that ʿAli bin Abi Talib said: "I will be the first one to kneel down before the Most Merciful so that the dispute may be settled on the Day of Resurrection." A man who came forward in that combat still spoke of the dispute as something yet to be settled. The sword had opened the case; it had not closed it. The real hearing is later, and he expected to be first to kneel for it.

## Badr, and everything after Badr

Alongside the Badr reports, Ibn Kathir records the broader readings. Ibn Abi Najih reported that **Mujahid** commented on this ayah, "Such as the disbeliever and the believer disputing about the Resurrection." According to one report **Mujahid and ʿAtaʾ** said simply, "This refers to the believers and the disbelievers."

Ibn Kathir then gives a fine piece of reasoning: the view of Mujahid and ʿAtaʾ "includes all opinions, the story of Badr as well as the others." A specific occasion does not shrink a verse; it illustrates it. He notes this was the view favoured by Ibn Jarir, "and it is good." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches the same place: the message "is not exclusive for them alone, but embraces the entire Muslim community of all times and ages."

## The verdict on the first party (ayat 19–22)

**"Garments of fire will be cut out for them."** Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning that pieces of fire will be prepared for them. Saʿid bin Jubayr said: "Of copper, for it is the hottest of things when it is heated." Clothing is what a person is seen in; here what they will be seen in has been prepared for them, and it burns.

**The boiling water.** Ibn Kathir defines *al-ḥamīm* as water that has been heated to the ultimate degree. It is not thrown at them; it is *poured down over their heads*.

Ayah 20 then says something the mind resists: *yuṣharu bihi mā fī buṭūnihim wa-l-julūd* — "melting whatever is in their bellies, along with their skin." The heat does not stop at the surface. Ibn Kathir's rendering is that with it will melt, or vanish away, what is within their bellies as well as their skins: the innermost and the outermost together, from a single pouring.

Ibn Jarir recorded from **Abu Hurayrah** that the Prophet ﷺ said: "The boiling water will be poured over their heads and will penetrate their skulls until it reaches what is inside, and what is inside will melt until it reaches their feet. This is the melting, then he will be restored to the state he was before." Ibn Kathir notes it was also recorded by **At-Tirmidhi**, who said it is *Hasan Sahih*, and also by **Ibn Abi Hatim**.

That last clause — *then he will be restored to the state he was before* — is the hinge of the scene. The punishment is not allowed to end the one being punished. It resets.

**The iron maces.** In ayah 21, *maqāmiʿ min ḥadīd*, which Ibn Kathir's text renders "hooked rods of iron." **Ibn ʿAbbas** said: "They will be struck with them, and with each blow, a limb will be severed, and they will cry out for oblivion." They do not cry out for rescue. They cry out to stop existing — and even that is denied.

**The closed door.** Ayah 22 says "every time": every time they seek to get away from it, out of anguish, they are driven back into it. Ibn Kathir here cites Al-Aʿmash reporting from Abu Zibiyan that **Salman** said, "The fire of Hell is black and dark; its flames and coals do not glow or shine" — and then Salman recited this very ayah. Fire that gives no light: burning without even the small mercy of being able to see.

And then the words: **"Taste the torment of burning!"** Ibn Kathir compares this to "and it will be said to them: 'Taste you the torment of the Fire which you used to deny'" (32:20), and draws out the point — "they will be humiliated by words and actions." The suffering is physical *and* verbal. What they mocked is now what mocks them.
