One further report: Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that **ʿAbdullah bin As-Sariy** said that an angel will come to him carrying the vessel with a pair of tongs because of its heat; when he brings it near his face he will shy away from it, and the angel will raise a hammer and strike his head with it. Ibn Kathir includes this as a commentator's description of ayah 20, not as words of the Prophet ﷺ, and it should be read that way.

## The verdict on the second party (ayat 23–24)

Ibn Kathir marks the turn beautifully. After describing the people of Hell — "we seek refuge with Allah from that state of punishment, vengeance, burning and chains" — Allah tells us of the people of Paradise, "we ask Allah by His grace and kindness to admit us therein."

Notice the sentence structure of ayah 23. The first party's fate was given in the passive: garments *are cut out*, water *is poured*. Here Allah names Himself as the actor: **"Truly, Allah will admit** those who believe and do righteous good deeds." And the two conditions are kept together — *believe* and *do righteous good deeds*. Neither stands alone.

**Rivers that obey.** On "Gardens underneath which rivers flow," Ibn Kathir says these rivers flow throughout its regions, beneath its trees and palaces, "and its inhabitants direct them to go wherever they want." In this world we build around water; there, water goes where you wish it.

**Bracelets — and why bracelets.** Ibn Kathir explains *yuḥallawna fīhā* as being adorned with jewelry, the bracelets of gold and pearls worn on their arms, and cites the **agreed-upon hadith** in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "The jewelry of the believer [in Paradise] will reach as far as his Wudu' reached." The ornament follows the exact reach of the water you washed with. Nothing of that quiet obedience was lost.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers the obvious objection — are bracelets not women's jewellery? Throughout the ages, it replies, monarchs have embellished their persons with costly jewellery, crowns and bracelets as symbols of their might and wealth. It recalls the well-known story of **Suraqah Ibn Malik** (may Allah be pleased with him), who before his conversion set out in pursuit of the Prophet ﷺ to apprehend him on the way from Makkah to Madinah; by Allah's will his horse sank in a piece of treacherous sand, and at that moment he expressed repentance for his error and begged the Prophet ﷺ to pray for his deliverance. When, through that prayer, his horse was freed, he was promised that when the bracelets of the King of Persia fell to the Muslims as spoils of war they would be given to him. Later, in the caliphate of ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), the Muslims conquered Persia, the Persian king's bracelets were brought to Madinah with the other spoils, and Suraqah claimed them and received them from ʿUmar. "Just as wearing a crown is a royal privilege and not a common practice among men," writes Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, "similarly wearing bracelets by men is a royal privilege" — so the men admitted to Paradise will wear them as a symbol of honour and Divine favour. It adds that since this ayah and Surah Fatir mention gold while Surah An-Nisaʾ mentions silver, commentators hold that the bracelets of the pious in Paradise will be of three kinds: gold, silver and pearls — and pearls are named in this very ayah.

**Silk against fire.** Ibn Kathir sets the two wardrobes side by side deliberately: "in contrast to the garments of fire worn by the inhabitants of Hell, the people of Paradise will have garments of silk," and quotes 76:21–22 on green *Sundus* and *Istabraq*, bracelets of silver, and a pure drink given by their Lord — the answer, drink for drink, to the boiling water of ayah 19.

He then cites, **in the Sahih**: "Do not wear fine silk or gold embroidery in this world, for whoever wears them in this world, will not wear them in the Hereafter." ʿAbdullah bin Az-Zubayr commented that those who do not wear silk in the Hereafter are those who will not enter Paradise, since Allah says here that the garments of the people of Paradise are silk.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles the same warning at more length. On the authority of Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him), **Imam Nasaʾi** relates that the Prophet ﷺ said: "He who wears silk in this world will not wear it in the Hereafter; he who drinks wine in this world will be deprived of the sacred nectar in the Hereafter; he who uses utensils made of precious metals for food and drink in this world will be denied their use in the Hereafter." Then he ﷺ added that these three things are exclusively for the people of Paradise (cited by Qurtubi from Nasaʾi). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the sense: this concerns one who spent his life amid these three luxuries *and did not show contrition*. It also relates, on the authority of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri (may Allah be pleased with him) — reported by Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi in his Musnad, with Qurtubi saying its chain is sahih — that "He who wore silk in the world will not wear it in the Hereafter even if he is admitted to Paradise. All other people of Paradise will wear silk, but not he."

That raises a real difficulty: if a person in Paradise remains deprived of something, will he not feel sorrow — and Paradise is no place for grief? **Qurtubi's** answer, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls very convincing, is that the people of Paradise will be given different grades and places at different levels, according to how they stood in Allah's favour; everyone will be aware of these differences, but Allah will fill their hearts with tranquility and contentment so that they feel no grief or sorrow about them. And Allah knows best.

Two further notes from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: the silk of Paradise and the silk of this world have only the name in common — in quality there is no comparison between the two. And it relates from ʿAbdullah Ibn ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him), through **Imam Nasaʾi, Bazzar and Baihaqi**, that the Prophet ﷺ once said that the clothes of the people of Paradise will be made from silk extracted from a fruit growing there; and there is a statement of Jabir (may Allah be pleased with him) that there would be a tree in Paradise producing silk from which the people of Paradise would wear dresses (from Mazhari).

## Ayah 24: the last gift is speech

The passage does not end with jewelry. It ends with words — and that is the sharpest contrast of all. The last thing the first party hears is "Taste the torment of burning." The last thing said of the second party is that **"they have been guided to the best of speech."**

Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels: "their greeting therein will be: Salam" (14:23); angels entering from every gate with "Peace be upon you, for you persevered in patience" (13:23–24); "No evil vain talk will they hear therein, nor any sinful speech, but only the saying of Peace, Peace" (56:25–26); "Therein they shall be met with greetings and the word of peace and respect" (25:75). They will be guided, he says, to a place in which they will hear good speech — set expressly against the scorn heaped upon the people of Hell by way of rebuke, when they are told, "Taste the torment of burning!" (3:181).

**"And they are guided to the path of Him Who is Worthy of all praises."** Ibn Kathir explains this as being guided to a place in which they will give praise to their Lord for all His kindness, blessings and favours towards them — and cites the **Sahih hadith**: "They will be inspired with words of glorification and praise, just as they are inspired with breath." Praise as effortless as breathing: not a duty performed but a nature received.

**What "goodly speech" means.** Ibn Kathir reports that some scholars of Tafsir said it refers to the Qur'an; and it was said that it means *La ilaha illallah*, or words of remembrance prescribed in Islam. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records from **Ibn ʿAbbas** (may Allah be pleased with him) that it refers to the *kalimah tayyibah*, لا إله إلا الله, while some others say it means the Qur'an (from Qurtubi) — and concludes that the meaning includes all these things. Ibn Kathir similarly notes that "guided to the path of Him Who is Worthy of all praises" was also explained as the straight path *in this world*, and adds that these interpretations do not contradict one another. And Allah knows best.

That last reading is worth pausing on. If the goodly speech is *La ilaha illallah* and the guidance is to the straight path in this world, then ayah 24 is not only describing a future reward — it is also describing what happened to you the day you were given the words of tawhid to say. The guidance to good speech begins here; Paradise is where it finishes.

## Living it

**The dispute is still open, and you are in it.** Mujahid and ʿAtaʾ read the two opponents as simply the believers and the disbelievers, in every age. There is no third party in this ayah.

**The verdict is not the fight.** ʿAli came forward at Badr and still said he would be the first to kneel before the Most Merciful for the dispute to be settled on the Day of Resurrection. Outcomes in this world — who won, who was killed, who prospered — are not the ruling. The ruling comes later.

**Your wudu is being recorded as ornament.** The jewelry of the believer will reach as far as his wudu reached. Small, unwitnessed acts of worship are being turned into something you will wear.

**Restraint here buys the real thing there.** The warnings about silk, wine and vessels of gold and silver all point one way: what a believer forgoes in this world is not lost, but returned in a form this world has only the name of.

**Guard your speech now.** The people of Paradise are rewarded with speech — peace, greeting, praise. Train the tongue toward *La ilaha illallah*, dhikr and the Qur'an, and you are already walking the path the ayah describes.

passages.title: The Sacred House barred, and the call to pilgrimage
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The Quraysh had shut the believers out of the Sacred Mosque. Ayah 25 condemns those who bar people from His path and His House; ayahs 26–29 go back to the beginning of that House: who was shown its site, on what condition it was built, and who was called to it. The unit hangs on one argument: *the House was never yours to close.* It was founded on the worship of Allah alone and opened by Him to near and far alike, and every pilgrim walking toward it is answering a call Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) made at Allah's command.

## The moment behind ayah 25

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places the verse: the previous ayah spoke of the hostility between believers and disbelievers, and here one face of it is named — the people who turned back the Prophet ﷺ and his Companions when they came wanting to enter the Sacred Mosque in the pilgrim's garb. The place was never their property, and they had no right to refuse entry to anyone.

Ibn Kathir sees in this proof that the ayah came down in Madinah, and links it to Sūrat al-Baqarah, where the same crime is weighed: fighting in the sacred months is grave, "but a greater transgression with Allah is to prevent mankind from following the way of Allah… and to drive out its inhabitants" (2:217). He also recalls Allah's verdict on their claim to guardianship: "and they are not its guardians. None can be its guardians except those who have Taqwa" (8:34).

**A grammatical detail worth feeling.** Ibn Kathir notes the shape of the phrase: *those who disbelieved* (past tense) *and hinder* (present tense) — it is not merely that they disbelieve; on top of that they continuously block others from Allah's path and His House. He compares it with 13:28: not merely believers, but believers whose hearts also find rest in Allah's remembrance. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that *sabīl Allāh*, "the way of Allah", means Islam itself, and that *al-Masjid al-Ḥarām* — strictly the mosque around the Kaʿbah — stands here, as in 48:25, for the whole sacred precinct of Makkah, since the Quraysh shut the Muslims out of the sanctuary as a whole; al-Durr al-Manthūr reports this wider sense from Ibn ʿAbbās.

## "The dweller and the visitor are equal there"

Allah describes the House as one He Himself made open to all people, "the dweller in it and the visitor from the country are equal there". Ibn ʿAbbās said, "Both the people of Makkah and others can stay in Al-Masjid Al-Haram"; Mujāhid said the same, and Qatādah said, "Its own people and others are equal therein."

**Where the scholars differed.** Ibn Kathir records that this was the question over which ash-Shāfiʿī and Isḥāq bin Rāhwayh disagreed in the Masjid of al-Khayf, with Aḥmad bin Ḥanbal present. Ash-Shāfiʿī held that property in Makkah may be owned, inherited and rented, citing the hadith of Usāmah bin Zayd in the Two Sahihs — he asked the Prophet ﷺ whether he would stay in his house in Makkah, and he replied, "Has ʿAqīl left us any property?"; he also cited ʿUmar's purchase of a Makkan house from Ṣafwān bin Umayyah. Isḥāq bin Rāhwayh held they may not be inherited or rented — the view of Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ and a number of the Salaf — citing the report recorded by Ibn Mājah from ʿAlqamah bin Naḍlah, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, Abū Bakr and ʿUmar died and nobody claimed property in Makkah except the grazing animals. Imam Aḥmad took a middle path, as his son Ṣāliḥ narrated: they may be owned and inherited but not rented, reconciling all the proofs.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān marks where there is no dispute at all: the whole Ummah and all the jurists agree that the ground of the essential rites — between Ṣafā and Marwah where pilgrims do *saʿy* (the walking back and forth between the two hills), and the open areas of Minā, ʿArafāt and Muzdalifah — is *waqf*, meaning permanently dedicated to the benefit of all Muslims, never owned by individuals and never able to be. On private houses both views are reported from Imam Abū Ḥanīfah, and the Ḥanafī jurists gave the fatwa that ownership, sale and rent are valid (Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī). But the places this ayah speaks of are *waqf* by consensus — no one can be denied access to them.

## "Whoever intends deviation there, wrongfully"

*Ilḥād* literally means deviation from the straight path. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Mujāhid and Qatādah read it as disbelief and denial of Allah's oneness, while others keep its broad literal sense, wide enough to include even hurling abuse at one's servant.

The added *bi-ẓulm*, "wrongfully", matters: Ibn Kathir explains that the person deliberately aims at wrong rather than erring by misunderstanding — as Ibn Jurayj related from Ibn ʿAbbās, "someone whose actions are intentional." Ibn ʿAbbās said it is shirk, and in another report, permitting inside the Ḥaram what Allah forbade — wronging those who never wronged you, killing those who never fought you. ʿAṭāʾ widened it to entering the Ḥaram without iḥrām, or hunting or cutting its trees. Ibn ʿAbbās also gives an occasion of revelation: ʿAbdullāh bin Unays, sent out by the Messenger of Allah ﷺ with two men, quarrelled over lineage, killed the Anṣārī among them, then left Islam and fled to Makkah — so the words came down about him, meaning whoever flees to the Ḥaram in order to do evil. Ibn Kathir judges that such reports name instances while the meaning is broader — as with the owners of the Elephant, destroyed by the birds Allah sent (105:4-5) as a warning to anyone intending evil there.

**The sobering detail.** Mujāhid drew from this ayah something unique to the Ḥaram: a person may be held to account for *intending* an evil action there, before he has begun it. Ibn Masʿūd is reported to the same effect — if a man intends an evil action therein, Allah will make him taste a painful torment — recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim and Aḥmad; Ibn Kathir notes its chain is Ṣaḥīḥ by al-Bukhārī's conditions, though more likely a saying of Ibn Masʿūd himself than one traced back to the Prophet ﷺ — in the language of hadith scholars, *mawqūf* (a report that stops at a Companion) rather than *marfūʿ* (one raised to the Prophet ﷺ). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that al-Qurṭubī took this view from Ibn ʿUmar and supported it, and preserves the practice behind it: on Hajj Ibn ʿUmar pitched two tents, one inside the Ḥaram and one outside, and if he had to rebuke a member of his household he did it in the outside tent — because even words blurted out in anger, he said, count as *ilḥād* inside the sanctuary. Mujāhid's balancing note: what is forbidden is forbidden everywhere; naming the Ḥaram signals that a good deed there is richly rewarded and a sin there draws the severest punishment.

## Ayah 26: the House was founded on tawhid

The Arabic *bawwaʾnā* literally means to assign someone a place to settle (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān) — itself a hint that Ibrāhīm was not already living there, having migrated from Syria. Ibn Kathir reads it as Allah showing him the site of the ʿAtīq House: guiding him to it, entrusting it to him, and permitting him to build.

**Was Ibrāhīm the first builder?** Ibn Kathir reports that many scholars took this ayah as evidence that he was, and that the House had no earlier structure; their support includes the hadith in the Two Sahihs from Abū Dharr, who asked the Prophet ﷺ which mosque was built first. He said, "Al-Masjid Al-Haram." "Then which?" "Bayt Al-Maqdis." "How long between them?" "Forty years." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it the other way: *the place of the House* suggests it pre-existed Ibrāhīm's arrival, since by reliable traditions its foundations were laid around the time Adam (peace be upon him) was sent to the earth, and the prophets after him circled it; at the Flood in the time of Nūḥ (peace be upon him) the upper structure was removed while the foundations remained, and Ibrāhīm was brought to raise it again on them.

**The two commands.** "Associate not anything with Me" means, Ibn Kathir says, *build it in My Name alone*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the obvious — Ibrāhīm could not have committed shirk; he had suffered at the hands of idolaters for destroying their idols — so the command reaches past him to humanity, warning against the one sin that would empty this House of meaning. The second command, "sanctify My House", Qatādah and Mujāhid explain as purifying it *from shirk*. The House was not standing at that moment, but *Baytullāh* is not merely bricks: the term covers that whole piece of sacred ground, where al-Qurṭubī records that Jurhum and the Amalekites had set up idols; another view is that the command binds later generations too.

## Ayah 27: the call that is still being answered

"And proclaim to mankind the Hajj" means, Ibn Kathir explains, announce it and call people to make pilgrimage to this House you have been commanded to build. Ibrāhīm said, "O Lord, how can I convey this to people when my voice will not reach them?" He was told: *Call them, and We will convey it.* So he stood — at Maqām Ibrāhīm, or as it is also related, on Mount Abū Qubays — put his fingers in his ears, turned to the four directions and called: "O mankind! Your Lord has established a House, so come on pilgrimage to it." It is said the mountains lowered themselves so his voice reached every region of the earth, and that those still in their mothers' wombs and their fathers' loins heard it; and the answer came back from everyone Allah has decreed will make the pilgrimage until the Day of Resurrection: *Labbayk Allāhumma labbayk* — "At Your service, O Allah, at Your service."

Ibn Kathir gives this as a summary of narrations from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others among the Salaf, recorded by Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates it from Ibn Abī Ḥātim from Ibn ʿAbbās, who said the pilgrims' *talbiyah* — that answering cry of *labbayk* — has its origin in that response.

**"On foot and on every lean camel."** Some scholars argued from the word order — "on foot" first — that Hajj on foot is better for those able, since it shows keenness and resolve; Ibn ʿAbbās said, "I do not regret anything except that I wish I had performed Hajj on foot, because Allah says, *They will come to you on foot*." But the majority hold riding better, following the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who performed Hajj riding though physically able to walk. *Ḍāmir* is the lean camel — lean, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, from the distance covered — and *ʿamīq*, per Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, as-Suddī and Qatādah, means *distant*.

## Ayah 28: why they come

"That they may witness things that are of benefit to them." Ibn ʿAbbās: "Benefits in this world and in the Hereafter" — of the Hereafter, Allah's pleasure; of this world, the sacrificial animals and trade, which Ibn Kathir ties to "There is no sin on you if you seek the bounty of your Lord" (2:198). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the grammar: *manāfiʿ*, "benefits", is indefinite, taking in benefits of every kind rather than one narrow category. For the spiritual gain it cites a hadith of Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ said whoever performs Hajj seeking Allah's pleasure and avoids sin and obscenity returns as pure as a newborn child (Bukhari and Muslim).

**Mentioning Allah's Name.** The second purpose is "that they may mention the Name of Allah on appointed days over the beast of cattle He has provided." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the sharp point: the object of the sacrifice is not the meat but the Name of Allah pronounced over the animal — that is the worship, and the meat being lawful is an added gift. The cattle are camels, cattle and sheep, the words covering every sacrifice, obligatory or voluntary. As for the "appointed days", Ibn ʿAbbās said they are the ten days of Dhul-Ḥijjah — al-Bukhārī cited this approvingly, with a disconnected chain, and similar comes from Mujāhid, Qatādah, ʿAṭāʾ and al-Ḥasan — while Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes them as the 10th, 11th and 12th, the days on which sacrifice may be offered.

On the merit of those ten days Ibn Kathir gathers: from Al-Bukhari, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Prophet ﷺ said, "No deeds are more virtuous than deeds done on these days"; they asked, "Not even Jihad for the sake of Allah?" and he said, "Not even Jihad for the sake of Allah, unless a man goes out risking himself and his wealth for the sake of Allah, and does not come back with anything." From Imam Ahmad, from Ibn ʿUmar: "There are no days that are greater before Allah or in which deeds are more beloved to Him than these ten days, so increase your Tahlil, Takbir, and Tahmid during these days." And in Sahih Muslim, from Abū Qatādah, the Prophet ﷺ was asked about fasting on the day of ʿArafah and said, "I hope by Allah that it will be an expiation for the previous year and the coming year."

**Eating and feeding.** In "Then eat thereof and feed therewith the poor having a hard time", the imperative is permission, not obligation — Mujāhid compared it to "But when you finish the Ihram, you may hunt" (5:2), the view Ibn Jarīr favoured and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shares. It is recorded that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ offered his sacrifice he had part of each animal cooked, ate of the meat and drank of the broth. *Al-bāʾis al-faqīr*, in ʿIkrimah's words, is the one in desperate need whose poverty is visible, and the poor person too proud to ask. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a distinction: the meat of a sacrifice offered to atone for a violation of the sacred limits — what the jurists call *dam al-jināyah*, *dam* meaning literally "blood", an animal slaughtered as compensation for an offence — is for the poor alone, by agreement of the jurists, whereas the sacrifices this ayah is about may be eaten by the offerer and his family too.

## Ayah 29: closing the rites

**"Then let them complete their prescribed duties."** *Tafath*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, means the dirt that gathers on the body — in iḥrām a person may not shave, trim or pluck hair, pare nails or use perfume, so it accumulates. Ibn ʿAbbās, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujāhid and ʿIkrimah glossed the phrase as coming out of iḥrām: shaving the head, putting on ordinary clothes, trimming the nails.

Note the order: sacrifice first, then removing the *tafath*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a ruling from that sequence — shaving or paring nails before the obligatory sacrifice is not allowed, and whoever does so must slaughter an animal as *dam*, the compensatory offering described above. Keeping the rites in their transmitted order is *sunnah* by consensus; whether it is also obligatory is disputed — Abū Ḥanīfah and Mālik held the order binding, so that deviating from it requires *dam*, while ash-Shāfiʿī held it only *sunnah*, deviation lessening the reward without obliging a sacrifice.

**"And fulfil their vows."** A *nadhr* is a commitment spoken aloud, to win Allah's pleasure, to do something not otherwise obligatory; fulfilling it then becomes binding by consensus — provided the act is not itself sinful. If someone vows something sinful he must not carry it out, but must make atonement for the unfulfilled vow; and a resolve made silently in the heart is no vow at all (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). A pilgrim is moved to pile up good deeds, and vowing extra sacrificial animals was common — Ibn ʿAbbās took *nadhr* here to mean exactly that. There is a resemblance too: a vow makes obligatory what was not and forbids what was permitted, and iḥrām does the same.

**"And circle the ʿAtīq House."** Mujāhid: this is the ṭawāf obligatory on the Day of Sacrifice — *ṭawāf az-ziyārah*, performed on the 10th after the stoning and the sacrifice, the second obligatory rite after standing at ʿArafāt, and after which iḥrām is entirely lifted (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān). Ibn ʿAbbās, quoting this ayah, said: "The end of the rituals is the Ṭawāf around the ʿAtīq House." Ibn Kathir confirms it from the Prophet's ﷺ practice: returning from Minā on the Day of Sacrifice he stoned the Jamrah with seven pebbles, offered his sacrifice, shaved his head, then circled the House. And in the Two Sahihs, Ibn ʿAbbās said the people were commanded to make their last act at the Kaʿbah the ṭawāf around it, menstruating women being excused.

**Why "ʿAtīq"?** Several senses are offered, each true of the House: al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, because it is the first House established for mankind; ʿIkrimah, because it was set free (*uʿtiqa*) from the flood in the time of Nūḥ; Khuṣayf, because no tyrant ever conquered it. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives it the sense of "liberated house", reporting from the Prophet ﷺ that it has been freed from the domination of disbelievers and tyrants and will never again be ruled by them — a hadith it traces to at-Tirmidhī (graded *ḥasan*), al-Ḥākim (graded *ṣaḥīḥ*), Ibn Jarīr and aṭ-Ṭabarānī. Its other sense is simply "ancient".

## Living it

Guard the sanctuary in your own conduct: Ibn ʿUmar's two tents show a man who feared a hasty word inside those limits. Do not privatise what Allah levelled: the strangers pressing around you at the House have exactly the claim on it that you do. And when you say *labbayk*, remember you are answering a call Ibrāhīm made into an empty valley, trusting Allah to carry his voice.

These four ayat sit inside the Qur'an's passage on the Hajj, and they turn from the rites themselves to the *heart* that performs them. Ibn Kathir frames the opening of ayah 30 as Allah saying: "This is what We have commanded you to do in the rituals (of Hajj), and this is the great reward that the person who does that will gain." What binds the four ayat together is a single phrase repeated at two hinges — *wa man yuʿaẓẓim*, "and whoever honours": honouring the *ḥurumāt* (the sacred things) of Allah in ayah 30, and honouring the *shaʿāʾir* (the symbols) of Allah in ayah 32. Between and around those two hinges the passage sets out what dishonouring looks like — the idol, which is called filth, and false speech, which is set beside idolatry itself — and then, in ayat 32 and 33, what honouring looks like when it becomes visible in an animal chosen, cared for, and finally offered at the Ancient House. Read as one unit, the passage teaches that pilgrimage is not a set of movements but a trained reverence, and that reverence shows in what a person refuses to touch, refuses to say, and refuses to skimp on.

## Ayat 30–31: honouring what Allah made sacred, and fleeing what dishonours Him

**"And whoever honours the sacred things (*ḥurumāt*) of Allah, then that is better for him with his Lord."** The two commentaries approach the phrase from two sides, and together they give a full picture.

- **Ibn Kathir** reads it as restraint: it means "whoever avoids disobeying Him and does not transgress that which is sacred, and regards committing sin as a very serious matter." Note that last clause — it is not only about not sinning, but about the *inward weight* a person gives to sin. A believer who treats a small trespass as a small thing has already lost some of this honouring.
- **Maʿārif ul Qurʾān** reads it more broadly: the *ḥurumāt* of Allah "are the things sanctified by Allah Taʿālā, that is the religious laws," and they are "a source of welfare in this world and in the Hereafter for those pious Muslims who seek to learn them and act upon them." So honouring them has two limbs — *learning* the sacred law, then *acting* on it.

On "then that is better for him with his Lord," Ibn Kathir draws out a principle that is easy to miss: "he will attain much good and a great reward for doing that. Just as the one who does acts of obedience will earn a great reward, so too, the one who avoids sin will earn a great reward." We instinctively picture reward as attached to things we *do* — prayer, charity, pilgrimage. Here it is attached to things we *don't* do. The restraint of a person who holds back from what Allah made inviolable is itself being recorded.

**"And the cattle are lawful to you, except those mentioned to you."** *Anʿām* — as Maʿārif ul Qurʾān specifies — covers camels, cows, goats, sheep and the like, and these "are made lawful at all times and even when one is in the state of *iḥrām*." So the ayah reassures the pilgrim: the sanctity he has entered does not strip him of his ordinary lawful food. Ibn Kathir adds a further note on what the permission excludes: "We have made permissible for you all the *Anʿām*," he writes, "and Allah has not instituted things like *Baḥīrah* or a *Sāʾibah* or a *Waṣīlah* or a *Ḥām*." The lesson that stands on its own is the one the ayah makes: what Allah permitted stays permitted, and no one else's ruling adds to the list of what He has instituted.

Then the exception — "except those mentioned to you" — points to prohibitions detailed elsewhere in the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir lists them, reporting this as the view of Ibn Jarir, who recorded it from Qatadah: carrion (*al-Maytah*), blood, the flesh of swine, and that over which Allah's Name was not pronounced at slaughter — that is, slaughtered as a sacrifice for other than Allah, or slaughtered for idols — and the animal killed by strangling, by a violent blow, by a headlong fall, by the goring of horns, or partly eaten by a wild animal, unless you are able to slaughter it before its death; and that which was slaughtered on *an-Nuṣub*. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān gives a shorter list to the same effect and supplies the key contrast: the permitted cattle are lawful in every state, whereas these are "unlawful in all circumstances, whether one is in the state of *iḥrām* or not."

**"So shun the *Rijs* of the idols, and shun false speech."** Twice in one breath the ayah says *shun* — first an object, then a sentence.

*Rijs*, explains Maʿārif ul Qurʾān, "means filth or moral impurity," and *awthān* "is the plural of *wathan* which means idol." Why call a carved stone *filth*? Because "idols have been described as filth, because they fill a man's heart and soul with moral impurity." The uncleanness is not a property of the object; it is what the object does to the one who bows to it. Ibn Kathir points the same way: "from this it is clear what *ar-Rijs* means, i.e., avoid the abomination, which means idols" — the idols *are* the filth being named.

Then, without pause, comes *qawl az-zūr* — the word of falsehood. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān defines it widely: "Anything which is contrary to truth is a lie and false, whether it is corrupt beliefs and practices or whether it is false evidence." Ibn Kathir observes that *shirk* is mentioned in conjunction with false speech, and gives an instance: *"Say: the things that my Lord has indeed forbidden are Al-Fawāḥish… joining partners with Allah for which He has given no authority, and saying things about Allah of which you have no knowledge"* (7:33) — and this, he says, includes bearing false witness.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites, from the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, a report of Abū Bakrah that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"Shall I not tell you about the worst of major sins?"* We said, "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." He said, *"Associating others with Allah, disobeying one's parents."* He had been reclining; then he sat up and said, *"and indeed giving false statements, and indeed bearing false witness…"* — "and he kept on repeating it until we wished that he would stop." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān narrates the same teaching, attributing it to Bukhari, in a wording that includes "giving false evidence and telling lies in general talk," and notes that he ﷺ used the phrase *qawl az-zūr* repeatedly.

Do not read past the physical detail. He ﷺ was lying at ease; he sat up to say this, and would not let the sentence go. The posture is part of the teaching: a sin that people treat as ordinary conversation — and Maʿārif's wording names ordinary talk explicitly — is being lifted into the company of the greatest sins.

Ibn Kathir then records from Imam Ahmad that Khuraym bin Fātik al-Asadī said: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ prayed aṣ-Ṣubḥ (al-Fajr), and when he had finished he stood up and said, *"Bearing false witness is on a par with the association of others with Allah"* — and then he recited this very ayah. The report says no more than that. But the sequence is worth sitting with: the sentence about false witness is followed immediately by the ayah that puts shunning the idol and shunning the lie side by side.

**"*Ḥunafāʾ Lillāh*, not associating partners unto Him."** Ibn Kathir glosses *Ḥunafāʾ Lillāh* as "sincerely submitting to Him Alone, shunning falsehood and seeking the truth." There are two motions in that gloss — away from the false, toward the true — and the ayah itself is built the same way, as a positive and a negative: devote yourself wholly, *and* attach nothing to Him. Both are required; sincerity that still keeps a rival in reserve is not sincerity.

**The parable of the man falling out of the sky.** Ibn Kathir says that Allah now "gives a likeness of the idolator in his misguidance and being doomed and being far away from true guidance": *"and whoever assigns partners to Allah, it is as if he had fallen from the sky, and the birds caught him in midair, or the wind had thrown him to a far off place."*

Sit with the image. The one who commits *shirk* is not drifting slowly off a path; he is in free fall from a height with nothing beneath him, and two ends await, both destroying — birds snatching him apart in the air, or a wind carrying him to *makān saḥīq*, which Ibn Kathir explains as "remote and desolate, dangerous for anyone who lands there." Faith, in this picture, is the ground under a man's feet; take it away and no gentler descent is on offer.

Ibn Kathir joins this to what he calls the Ḥadīth of al-Barāʾ, concerning the disbeliever at death: when the angels of death take his soul and ascend with it to the heaven, the gates of heaven are not opened for him; on the contrary, his soul is thrown down from there — and, Ibn Kathir notes, the Prophet ﷺ then recited this ayah. (Ibn Kathir does not name a collection at this point, saying only that the ḥadīth has already been quoted in his explanation of Sūrah Ibrāhīm.) In his handling, then, the falling of the parable is not merely a figure for a confused life.

And beside it he places a second parable of the idolaters from Sūrat al-Anʿām: *"…like one whom the Shayāṭīn have made to go astray in the land in confusion, his companions calling him to guidance, saying: Come to us. Say: Verily, Allah's guidance is the only guidance"* (6:71). Between the two images you have the whole condition — bewildered on the earth, and unanchored in the sky.

## Ayat 32–33: honouring the signs, and the offering that makes it visible

**"And whosoever honours the *Shaʿāʾir* of Allah, then it is truly from the taqwa of the hearts."** Here the passage returns to its first word — *whoever honours* — with a new object, and the second half of the unit unfolds from it.

Ibn Kathir's gloss is compact: the *Shaʿāʾir* of Allah means "His commands." Maʿārif ul Qurʾān opens the word up linguistically: *shaʿāʾir* is the plural of *shaʿīra*, meaning "a symbol, a distinctive sign," and it refers to "those things which are considered as the specific emblems of certain groups of people or certain faiths." So the *Shaʿāʾir* of Allah are "those special laws which are generally taken to be the identifying features of a Muslim," and "most of the rules of Ḥajj fall in this category."

Now the turn of the ayah. It does not say that honouring these signs *produces* taqwa. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān is precise: "respect for the *Shaʿāʾir* of Allah is an evidence of the piety of heart… taqwa is a quality which rests in one's heart. When the heart is equipped with this quality, it is reflected in all his actions." The outward act is the *readout*, not the source. Which means the ayah works in two directions at once: it dignifies the small physical rites of Hajj by tracing them back to something invisible, and it quietly warns that a rite performed with a careless heart has lost the very thing that made it worth counting.

**What honouring looks like in practice.** Ibn Kathir shows that this "also includes obeying His commands in the best way when it comes to offering sacrifices." Al-Ḥakam narrated from Miqsam, from Ibn ʿAbbās: "Honouring them means choosing fat, healthy animals (for sacrifice)." Abū Umāmah bin Sahl said, "We used to fatten the *Uḍḥiyyah* in Al-Madīnah, and the Muslims used to fatten them" — recorded by al-Bukhari. In Sunan Ibn Mājah it is recorded from Abū Rāfiʿ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sacrificed two castrated, fat, horned rams; Abū Dāwūd and Ibn Mājah recorded the same from Jābir.

And the reverse side: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ "commanded us to examine their eyes and ears, and not to sacrifice the *Muqābilah*, the *Mudābirah*, the *Sharqāʾ*, nor the *Kharqāʾ*" — recorded by Ahmad and the Sunan compilers, and at-Tirmidhī graded it Ṣaḥīḥ. Ibn Kathir defines them: the *Muqābilah* is the one whose ear is cut at the front, the *Mudābirah* the one whose ear is cut at the back, the *Sharqāʾ* the one whose ear is split (as ash-Shāfiʿī said), and the *Kharqāʾ* the one whose ear is pierced with a hole. It was recorded that al-Barāʾ said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: *"Four are not permitted for sacrifice: those that are obviously one-eyed, those that are obviously sick, those that are obviously lame and those that have broken bones, which no one would choose."* This too was recorded by Ahmad and the Sunan compilers, and graded Ṣaḥīḥ by at-Tirmidhī.

Read that list back against the ayah and it becomes a spiritual diagnostic. Nobody's heart is visible; but the animal a man selects is visible. Choosing the sound, well-fed beast when a defective one would technically discharge the duty is the taqwa of the heart becoming something you can see. The closing phrase is telling — "which no one would choose" — the rejected animal is the one a person would not want for himself. What is not good enough for you is not good enough as an offering.

**"For you in them are benefits until an appointed term; then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House."** Ayah 33 keeps the animal in view and adds a mercy. Ibn Kathir explains the *manāfiʿ*: in the *budn* (the sacrificial camels) "you find benefits such as their milk, their wool and hair, and their use for riding." And the appointed term? Miqsam reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "Until you decide to offer them as a sacrifice."

He then cites, from the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, the report of Anas: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw a man driving his sacrificial camel and said, *"Ride it."* The man said, "It is a sacrificial camel." He said, *"Ride it, woe to you!"* — the second or third time. And in a report recorded by Muslim from Jābir, he ﷺ said, *"Ride it gently according to your needs."*

The man's scruple was sincere — he had dedicated the animal and did not want to take anything from it. The Prophet ﷺ pushed back, and pushed back again. Reverence is not measured by inventing hardship for oneself; Allah Himself named these benefits as *yours* for a term.

Here the two commentaries place their emphasis differently, and the reader should know both. Ibn Kathir, with Ibn ʿAbbās, reads the term as running until the owner decides to offer the animal. Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws a tighter line around the animal already designated: it is lawful for Muslims to take benefit from livestock — milk, riding, transport — "unless the animals have been made *hady* by reserving them for sacrifice to be offered within the precincts of the *ḥaram*." Once a person takes an animal along for the specific purpose of sacrificing it within the *ḥaram*, it is described as *hady*, and "no benefit may be derived from it, except in extreme emergency. A person leading a camel after it has been nominated as *hady* may lawfully ride it only if he is unable to walk and no other mount is available." Both are attentive to the same fact — the animal is on its way to Allah — and they differ over how early that claim takes full hold.

**"Then their place of sacrifice is at the Ancient House."** Ibn Kathir: they are eventually brought to the *Bayt al-ʿAtīq*, "which is the Kaʿbah," and he supports this with *"an offering, brought to the Kaʿbah"* (5:95) and *"and detained the Hady, from reaching their place of sacrifice"* (48:25).

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān adds the juristic detail: here *al-Bayt al-ʿAtīq* "includes the entire precincts of *ḥaram*," as was the case in the previous verse where *al-Masjid al-Ḥarām* stood for the whole area of the *ḥaram*, and *maḥill* means the place of slaughtering the animals of *hady*. So "the entire *ḥaram* is declared as the slaughtering place of the animals of *hady*" — the *hady* may be slaughtered within, and not outside, the area of the *ḥaram*, which includes Minā and all other places of Makkah. (Maʿārif ul Qurʾān cites *Rūḥ ul Maʿānī* for this.)

## Living it

Across the four ayat the movement is: an inward posture of honouring (30), the two things that corrode it — false objects of worship and false words (30) — the alternative of belonging wholly to Allah and the vertigo of refusing it (31), then the same verb of honouring turned outward to the visible signs (32), and finally an animal that is milked, ridden, kept, and then walked to the House and given up (33). Three things it asks of a believer:

1. **Weigh sin properly.** Ibn Kathir's gloss makes "regarding sin as a very serious matter" part of the honouring itself — and reminds us that the reward for what you *refrain from* is as real as the reward for what you perform.
2. **Guard the tongue as you guard your creed.** Maʿārif ul Qurʾān stretches *qawl az-zūr* to cover "corrupt beliefs and practices" and "false evidence" alike, and its wording of the ḥadīth reaches "lies in general talk"; the Prophet ﷺ sat up from reclining to repeat it, and, in the report Ibn Kathir takes from Imam Ahmad, said that bearing false witness is on a par with associating others with Allah, then recited this ayah. The lie told in court and the lie told in ordinary talk are not from different worlds.
3. **Let the outward be honest about the inward.** The best animal, the sound eye and ear, the unhurried care — this is how an unseen taqwa becomes visible. And the reverse holds: if the outward rite is being done grudgingly or shabbily, ayah 32 invites us to look at the heart it is reporting on.

passages.title: Sacrifice, the humble-hearted, and true piety
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take an ancient, universal, physical act — animal sacrifice — and show what Allah actually wants from it. Ayah 34 places sacrifice in every nation's history and ties it to the oneness of Allah; ayah 35 describes the heart that offers it; ayah 36 gives the offering its practical shape; and ayah 37 delivers the verdict that holds the unit together: what rises to Allah is not flesh or blood but taqwa.

## Ayah 34: sacrifice is not a Muslim novelty

"For every community We appointed a rite" (*mansak*). Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us that sacrifice and the shedding of blood in the Name of Allah has been prescribed for all nations.

**The word *mansak*.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *mansak* and *nusuk* carry several senses in Arabic — the sacrifice of animals, the rites of pilgrimage, and the worship of Allah generally — and that in this context the word can bear all three. The early scholars divided along those lines: Mujahid and some other commentators took it as the sacrifice of animals, in which case the obligation to offer sacrifice laid on this Ummah is nothing new, because earlier peoples were likewise bound to it. Qatadah took it as the rites of pilgrimage, made obligatory on the people of earlier ages too. Ibn ʿArafah took it as worship of Allah — made obligatory on all the peoples of bygone ages, and though the forms of worship differed, in essence it remained unchanged. Ibn Kathir preserves further readings: ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported that Ibn ʿAbbas glossed *mansak* as "festivals"; ʿIkrimah said "sacrifices"; Zayd bin Aslam said it means Makkah — that Allah did not appoint religious ceremonies anywhere else for any nation.

**Why mention the Name?** "So that they may mention the Name of Allah over the beast of cattle He has provided them." The slaughter is not the point; the *invocation* is. Ibn Kathir cites what was recorded in the Two Sahihs, that Anas said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ brought two fat, horned rams, said *Bismillah* and *Allahu Akbar*, then put his foot on their necks. And the animal is described as what "He has given them for food" — already His own provision.

**Then the pivot to tawhid.** "Your deity is One Deity, so submit to Him alone." Ibn Kathir draws out the logic: your deity is One, even though the laws of the prophets may vary and may abrogate one another. All of the prophets called mankind to worship Allah alone with no partner or associate — he cites Allah's word, "And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: none has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me" (21:25). And *fa-lahu aslimu*, "so submit to Him alone," means, in Ibn Kathir's words, submit to His commands and obey Him in all sincerity.

## The *mukhbitin*: the people to whom good news is given

Ayah 34 ends with a command to the Prophet ﷺ: "And give glad tidings to the *mukhbitin*." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that *khabt* means a depressed tract of land, and that *mukhbit* means a person who deems himself humble and lowly.

Mujahid said the *mukhbitin* are those who find contentment in their faith. Ath-Thawri said they are those who find contentment in their faith, accept the decree of Allah, and submit to Him. ʿAmr bin Aws said they are people who do not wrong others, and if somebody wrongs them, they do not seek revenge. Sufyan observed that they are the people who are contented with Allah's will and remain agreeable in all circumstances — comfort or trouble, poverty or affluence.

Ibn Kathir adds that rather than settle on one lexical gloss, it is better to interpret *mukhbitin* by what comes next — the Qur'an defines its own term in ayah 35.

## Ayah 35: four marks of a humbled heart

**"Those whose hearts tremble when Allah is mentioned."** The verb is *wajilat*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *wajil* as a feeling of awe inspired by something majestic and sublime; these words describe the state of pious people who are overwhelmed by deep awe whenever the name of Allah is mentioned in their presence. Ibn Kathir puts it simply: their hearts fear Him.

**"And the patient in whatever befalls them"** — Ibn Kathir specifies: of afflictions.

**"And those who establish the prayer"** — Ibn Kathir: they fulfil the duties which Allah has enjoined upon them, the duty of performing the obligatory prayers.

**"And who spend out of what We have provided them"** — from the good provision Allah has given them. Ibn Kathir describes where it goes: they spend on their families and servants, and on the poor and needy; they treat people kindly while remaining within the limits set by Allah. He closes with a pointed contrast: this is in contrast to the hypocrites, who are the opposite of all this.

## Ayah 36: the offering, done properly

**"The *budn* We have made for you among the symbols of Allah."** On *budn*: Ibn Jurayj reports that ʿAtaʾ said cattle and camels, and a similar view was reported from Ibn ʿUmar, Saʿid bin al-Musayyib and al-Hasan al-Basri; Mujahid said *al-budn* means camels. Ibn Kathir frames the ayah as a reminder of blessing: Allah created these animals for His servants and made them one of His symbols, decreeing that they should be brought to His Sacred House — indeed they are the best of what may be offered as a sacrifice to Allah. He connects this to Allah's word, "Violate not the sanctity of the *shaʿaʾir* of Allah, nor of the Sacred Month, nor of the animals brought for sacrifice, nor the garlanded..." (5:2). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that *shaʿaʾir* are those special forms of rites and worship which are the symbols of Islam; sacrifice of animals is one of them, which must be observed with due importance.

According to Muslim, Jabir bin ʿAbdullah and others said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ commanded them to share in offering the sacrifice: a camel for seven people, and one cow for seven people.

**"Wherein you have much good"** — Ibn Kathir: this means reward in the Hereafter.

**"So mention the Name of Allah over them as they are lined up" (*sawaff*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains *sawaff* as *masfufa*, standing in a row, and reports that according to ʿAbdullah ibn ʿUmar the camel to be slaughtered should stand on three legs with one foreleg bent and tied up — a better way of slaughtering a camel, and according to sunnah; other animals should be slaughtered lying down, which is likewise sunnah. Al-Aʿmash narrated from Abu Zabiyan from Ibn ʿAbbas the same picture: they stand on three legs with the left foreleg tied up, and he says *Bismillah, Allahu Akbar, la ilaha illallah, Allahumma minka wa laka* — "In the Name of Allah, and Allah is Most Great; there is no god but Allah. O Allah, from You and to You." And it was recorded in the Two Sahihs that Ibn ʿUmar came to a man who had made his camel kneel down in order to sacrifice it, and told him: "Make it stand up fettered — the Sunnah of Abu al-Qasim ﷺ."

**What the Prophet ﷺ said as he slaughtered.** It was reported from al-Muttalib bin ʿAbdullah bin Hantab that Jabir bin ʿAbdullah said: "I prayed with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on ʿId al-Adha. When he finished, he brought a ram and slaughtered it, saying, '*Bismillah*, and *Allahu Akbar*. O Allah, this is on behalf of me and anyone of my Ummah who has not offered a sacrifice.'" This was recorded by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi. Muhammad bin Ishaq recorded from Yazid bin Abi Habib from Ibn ʿAbbas that Jabir said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sacrificed two rams on the day of ʿId, and when he laid them down to sacrifice them he said: "I turn my face to the One who created the heavens and the earth, being true and sincere in faith, submitting myself to Him alone, and I am not of the idolaters. Verily my prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying are for Allah, the Lord of all that exists, with no partner or associate for Him. Thus am I commanded, and I am the first of the Muslims. O Allah, from You and to You, on behalf of Muhammad and his Ummah." Then he said *Bismillah* and *Allahu Akbar* and slaughtered them. And it was reported from ʿAli bin al-Husayn from Abu Rafiʿ that when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ wanted to offer a sacrifice he would buy two fat, horned, fine rams; after praying and addressing the people he would bring one of them to where he stood in the prayer place and sacrifice it himself with a knife, saying, "O Allah, this is on behalf of all of my Ummah — whoever bears witness to Your Oneness and bears witness that I have conveyed," then bring the other and sacrifice it himself, saying, "This is on behalf of Muhammad and the family of Muhammad." He would give them to the poor, and he and his family would eat from them as well. This was recorded by Ahmad and Ibn Majah.

**Mercy in the manner of slaughter.** "Then when their flanks fall down" — Ibn Abi Najih reported that Mujahid said this means when it has fallen to the ground; this was narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and a similar view from Muqatil bin Hayyan. ʿAbdur-Rahman bin Zayd bin Aslam said it means when they have died. Ibn Kathir reconciles them: this is what was meant by Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid, for it is not permitted to eat from the sacrifice until it has died and its movements have ceased. He cites a *marfuʿ* wording (a report raised to the Prophet ﷺ), "Do not rush until you are sure that the animal is dead," which ath-Thawri narrated in his *Jamiʿ* as a saying of ʿUmar bin al-Khattab, and which he supported with the hadith of Shaddad bin Aws in Sahih Muslim: "Allah has prescribed proficiency in all things. If you kill, kill well; and if you slaughter, slaughter well. Let each one of you sharpen his blade and let him spare suffering to the animal he slaughters." And it was recorded that Abu Waqid al-Laythi said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whatever is cut from an animal while it is still alive is *maytah* (dead flesh)" — recorded by Ahmad, Abu Dawud and at-Tirmidhi, who graded it Sahih.

**"Eat from them, and feed the *qaniʿ* and the *muʿtarr*."** Ibn Kathir notes this is a command which implies that this is permissible. Two readings are transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbas himself: al-ʿAwfi reported from him that *qaniʿ* is the one who is content with what he is given and stays in his house, and *muʿtarr* the one who comes to you and rubs shoulders with you so that you will give him some meat, but does not ask for it — also the view of Mujahid and Muhammad bin Kaʿb al-Qurazi; while ʿAli bin Abi Talhah reported from him that *qaniʿ* is the one who is too proud to ask and *muʿtarr* the one who does ask — also the view of Qatadah, Ibrahim an-Nakhaʿi, and Mujahid in one report narrated from him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Mazhari) explains that *qaniʿ* applies to a needy person who does not solicit and is content with what people offer him voluntarily, while *muʿtarr* is a person who goes where he expects to receive something, whether he solicits verbally or not. Either way the ayah names two kinds of poor — the one who hides his need and the one who presents himself. Both must be fed.

**On dividing the meat into thirds.** This ayah has been quoted as evidence by scholars who said the sacrifice should be divided into three: a third for the one offering it to eat from, a third as gifts to friends, and a third in charity to the poor. But Ibn Kathir states plainly, "there is no evidence in this Ayah for this view." What is established is the freedom Allah gave: according to a Sahih hadith, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "I used to forbid you to keep the meat of the sacrifice for more than three days, but now eat from it and keep it as you see fit," and in other reports, "Eat some, keep some, and give some in charity," and "Eat some, feed others, and give some in charity." As for the skins, it was recorded in Musnad Ahmad from Qatadah bin an-Nuʿman: "Eat and give in charity, and make use of the skins, but do not sell them."

**Timing.** It was recorded that al-Baraʾ bin ʿAzib said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The first thing that we should do on this day of ours is to pray, then we return and offer the sacrifice. Whoever does that will have followed our Sunnah. Whoever slaughters his animal before the prayer, this is just meat which he has brought for his family; it is not a sacrifice at all" — recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim. And in Sahih Muslim it is mentioned that one is not to offer the sacrifice until the Imam has offered his. It is prescribed to offer the sacrifice on the day of Nahr and the following three days of Tashriq, because of the hadith of Jubayr bin Mutʿim, who said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "The days of Tashriq are all (for) sacrifice" — recorded by Ahmad and Ibn Hibban.

**"Thus have We subjected them to you, that you may be grateful."** Ibn Kathir explains *sakhkharnaha*: We have subjugated them to you, made them submissive towards you, so that if you wish you can ride them, or milk them, or slaughter them — connecting it to Allah's words, "Do they not see that We have created for them of what Our Hands have created, the cattle, so that they are their owners... will they not then be grateful?" (36:71–73).

## Ayah 37: what actually reaches Allah

"Neither their meat nor their blood reaches Allah; rather it is the taqwa from you that reaches Him."

**The background.** Ibn Kathir explains that this sacrifice is prescribed so that you will remember Allah at the time of slaughter, for He is the Creator and Provider; nothing of its flesh or blood reaches Him, for He has no need of anything other than Himself. During the time of Jahiliyyah, when they offered sacrifices to their gods, they would put some of the meat of their sacrifices on their idols and sprinkle the blood over them. Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Ibn Jurayj said the people of the Jahiliyyah used to put the meat of their sacrifices and sprinkle the blood on the House — and the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "We have more right to do that." Then Allah revealed this ayah. What Allah accepts and rewards is the taqwa behind the act.

**What Allah looks at.** Ibn Kathir supports this with what is "mentioned in the Sahih": "Allah does not look to your appearance or your colours, but He looks to your hearts and deeds."

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān generalises the principle.** The sacrifice of animals is a very high form of worship, but their meat and blood do not reach Allah, nor are these two things the real object of sacrifice; its real aim is to recite the Name of Allah and to comply with His commands with true devotion. This rule, it says, applies to all forms of worship: the object of prayer is not just the movement of limbs, nor of fasting merely a denial of food and drink. Yet it insists that these forms remain very important, because Allah Himself has prescribed them. Devoid of sincerity, the rites of worship are like a body without a soul.

**"That you may proclaim Allah's greatness for having guided you."** Ibn Kathir: that you may glorify Him for guiding you to His religion and His way, which He loves and is pleased with, and for forbidding you all that He hates and rejects.

**"And give glad tidings to the doers of good (*muhsinin*)."** Notice the symmetry: the passage opened in ayah 34 with glad tidings to the *mukhbitin*, the humbled, and closes in ayah 37 with glad tidings to the *muhsinin*, those who do good. Ibn Kathir defines them: those whose deeds are good, who remain within the limits prescribed by Allah, who follow what has been prescribed for them, who believe in the Messenger ﷺ and follow what he has conveyed from his Lord.

## Practical rulings the sources attach here

Ibn Kathir notes that the *udhiyyah* (the sacrifice) is *sunnah mustahabbah* — a strongly encouraged practice — and that one animal is sufficient on behalf of all the members of one household. Ibn ʿUmar said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ continued to offer sacrifice for ten years" (recorded by at-Tirmidhi). Abu Ayyub said: "At the time of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, a man would sacrifice a sheep on behalf of himself and all the members of his household, and they would eat from it and feed others, until the people started boasting and things reached the stage that you see now" — recorded by at-Tirmidhi, who graded it Sahih, and by Ibn Majah. ʿAbdullah bin Hisham used to sacrifice one sheep on behalf of his entire family, recorded by al-Bukhari. On the animal's age, Muslim recorded from Jabir that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Do not sacrifice any but mature animals, and if that is not possible, then sacrifice a young sheep."

Abu Ayyub's complaint is the passage in miniature. The moment sacrifice becomes a display of how much you can afford, the meat has grown and the taqwa has shrunk — and only one of those two ever reaches Allah.

## Living it

Say the Name and mean it. Sharpen the blade. Feed both the poor man who asks and the one too proud to ask. Keep the Prophet's ﷺ order: prayer first, then slaughter. And carry ayah 37 out of ʿId into prayer, fasting, charity and Hajj: each has a body of prescribed actions that must be kept, but what ascends from all of it is the taqwa in you.

passages.title: Permission granted to the wronged to fight back
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat are the turning point at which a persecuted community was finally permitted to defend itself. Ayah 38 promises that Allah defends the believers; ayah 39 grants permission to fight to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged; ayah 40 names the wrong and sets it against Allah's checking of one people by means of another; ayah 41 says what these same people will do once power is in their hands. One question threads them together: **when Allah defends His servants, what part are the servants asked to play?**

## Ten years of restraint

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the situation: the Makkan idolaters intensified their aggression against the Muslims, and every day people arrived in Madinah bearing marks of the ill-treatment they had suffered. In the days before the Hijrah the number of the faithful had grown considerably, and they sought permission to defend themselves against the oppression they were constantly subjected to; but the Prophet ﷺ counselled them patience, because he had not yet received Allah's permission to resist with force of arms. Citing Qurtubi, Maʿārif adds that this situation persisted for about ten years. Maʿārif also notes that in more than seventy earlier verses armed resistance had been forbidden.

It is a community that had been told "not yet" for a decade.

## Ayah 38 — "Indeed, Allah defends those who believe"

Ibn Kathir reads this as good news given before the command: Allah defends His servants who put their trust in Him and turn to Him in repentance. He protects them from the worst of evil people and from the plots of sinners — He protects them, guards them, and supports them. Ibn Kathir sets the tone with *"Is not Allah sufficient for His servant?"* (39:36) and *"whosoever puts his trust in Allah, then He will suffice him"* (65:3).

The second half — *"Verily, Allah likes not any treacherous ingrate"* — is explained by Ibn Kathir as meaning that He does not like any of His servants who bear these characteristics: **treachery** in covenants and promises, whereby a person does not do what he says; and **ingratitude**, which is to deny blessings, so that one neither acknowledges nor appreciates them. That is the moral portrait of the oppressors the believers were about to face.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 38 against the preceding verses, which recall how the idolaters of Makkah prevented the Prophet ﷺ and his companions from entering the Haram and the Holy Mosque to perform ʿUmrah when, having put on ihram, they had reached as far as Hudaybiyah. Here, says Maʿārif, Allah consoled the Muslims with the promise that He would deprive the disbelievers of their power to harm them any more — and Maʿārif notes that this incident took place in the year 6 AH, after which the power and morale of the idolaters suffered continuous decline until the Muslims conquered Makkah in the year 8 AH.

## Ayah 39 — the first ayah of jihad

**"Permission (to fight) is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged."**

**Udhina** — "permission *is given*" — is passive: the believers are not seizing a right, a right is being granted to them. **Yuqātalūna** is likewise passive: *those who are fought against* — the permission is described from the receiving end, these are people already under attack. And the clause that follows gives the ground: **bi-annahum ẓulimū**, *because they have been wronged*.

### The moment it was revealed

Al-ʿAwfi reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said this was revealed about Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions when they were expelled from Makkah. Mujahid, ad-Dahhak and others among the Salaf — such as Ibn ʿAbbas, ʿUrwah bin az-Zubayr, Zayd bin Aslam, Muqatil bin Hayyan and Qatadah — said: **this is the first ayah which was revealed about jihad.**

Ibn Jarir recorded that Ibn ʿAbbas said: when the Prophet ﷺ was driven out of Makkah, Abu Bakr said, *"They have their Prophet. Truly, to Allah we belong and truly, to Him we shall return; surely they are doomed."* Then Allah revealed *"Permission (to fight) is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged…"* — and Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: **"Then I knew that there would be fighting."** Imam Ahmad's version adds Ibn ʿAbbas's words, "This was the first ayah to be revealed concerning fighting." Ibn Kathir notes that this was also recorded by at-Tirmidhi and an-Nasaʼi in the Book of Tafsir of their *Sunans*, and that at-Tirmidhi said: "It is a *hasan* hadith." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Tirmidhi, Nasaʼi, Ibn Majah, Ibn Hibban, Hakim and others reported on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas that this is the first verse permitting the Muslims to offer armed resistance.

Maʿārif also records that as the Prophet ﷺ set out from Makkah accompanied by Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: *"They have expelled their Prophet ﷺ and the time has come when they will perish."* When he arrived at Madinah, this verse was revealed. Maʿārif cites Nasaʼi and Tirmidhi, from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Qurtubi for this report.

### "And surely Allah is able to give them victory"

It means, says Ibn Kathir, that **He is able to grant victory to His believing servants without any fighting taking place** — but He wants His servants to strive their utmost in obeying Him. He supports this with *"if it had been Allah's will, He Himself could certainly have punished them. But (He lets you fight) in order to test some of you with others"* (47:4-6) and *"Fight against them so that Allah will punish them by your hands… and heal the breasts of a believing people"* (9:14-15).

So fighting is never because Allah needs it: it is for the servants' sake — as obedience, as test, and as the healing of believing hearts.

### Why the permission came when it did

Ibn Kathir explains the timing with striking practicality. Allah prescribed jihad **at an appropriate time**, because when the Muslims were in Makkah the idolaters outnumbered them by more than ten to one; were they to engage in fighting then, the results would have been disastrous. It was when the idolaters went to extremes in persecuting the Muslims, driving out the Prophet ﷺ and resolving to kill him; when they sent his Companions into exile here and there, some to Ethiopia and some to Madinah; when those Companions had settled in Madinah and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had joined them there, and they gathered around him and lent him their support, so that they had **a place where Islam prevailed and a stronghold to which they could retreat** — then Allah prescribed jihad against the enemy.

Divine permission is not only a matter of right; it is also a matter of ripeness.

## Ayah 40 — "only because they said: Our Lord is Allah"

Ayah 40 identifies the wronged: *"Those who have been expelled from their homes unjustly only because they said: 'Our Lord is Allah.'"* Al-ʿAwfi reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said: they were driven out of Makkah to Madinah unjustly — that is, Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions.

Ibn Kathir dwells on the exception clause **illā an yaqūlū rabbunā Allāh**. It means, he writes, that they had not done anything to their people or committed any wrongs against them, apart from the fact that they believed in the Oneness of Allah and worshipped Him alone, with no partner or associate. But for the idolaters, this was the worst of sins. He cites *"and have driven out the Messenger and yourselves because you believe in Allah, your Lord!"* (60:1). The construction is jarring by design: it introduces their sole "offence" as though it were a crime.

### The law of repelling

*"For had it not been that Allah checks one set of people by means of another…"*

Ibn Kathir explains: were it not for the fact that He repels one people by means of another, and restrains the evil of people towards others by means of whatever circumstances He creates and decrees, **the earth would have been corrupted and the strong would have destroyed the weak.** His wording is general: not a comment on one grievance but a statement about how evil is held in check at all.

### Four kinds of sanctuary

Without this checking, *"Ṣawāmiʿ, Biyaʿ, Ṣalawāt and Masjids, wherein the Name of Allah is mentioned much, would surely have been pulled down."*

Ibn Kathir records the early scholars' readings:

- **Ṣawāmiʿ** — the small temples used by monks, according to Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Abu al-ʿAliyah, ʿIkrimah, ad-Dahhak and others. Qatadah said this refers to the places of worship of the Sabians; according to another report from him, the ṣawāmiʿ of the Zoroastrians. Muqatil bin Hayyan said they are houses along the roads.
- **Biyaʿ** — larger than the ṣawāmiʿ and accommodating more worshippers; the Christians also have these, according to Abu al-ʿAliyah, Qatadah, ad-Dahhak, Ibn Sakhr, Muqatil bin Hayyan, Khusayf and others. Ibn Jubayr reported from Mujahid and others that this referred to the synagogues of the Jews, known to them as *Salut*. And Allah knows best.
- **Ṣalawāt** — al-ʿAwfi reported that Ibn ʿAbbas said this means churches; ʿIkrimah, ad-Dahhak and Qatadah said it referred to the synagogues of the Jews; Abu al-ʿAliyah and others said the places of worship of the Sabians; Ibn Abi Najih reported that Mujahid said it refers to places of worship of the People of the Book and of the people of Islam along the roads.
- **Masjids** — these belong to the Muslims.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the words their lexical sense: ṣawāmiʿ is the plural of a word meaning a monastery, a place of worship for Christian monks and hermits; biyaʿ the plural of a word meaning a Christian church; ṣalawāt the plural of a word meaning a Jewish synagogue; and masājid, the places of worship of the Muslims.

On *"wherein the Name of Allah is mentioned much"* — it was said that the pronoun refers to the masjids, because this is the closest of the words mentioned, while ad-Dahhak said, "In all of them the Name of Allah is often mentioned." **Ibn Jarir said the correct view is that the monasteries of the monks, the churches of the Christians, the synagogues of the Jews and the masjids of the Muslims would all have been destroyed**, because this is the usual usage in Arabic. Some of the scholars said this is a sequence listing the smallest to the greatest, because the masjids are more frequented by more worshippers who have the correct intention and way.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the reasoning: the command to take up arms against the unbelievers is nothing new, because the earlier prophets and their followers had received similar orders, and the wisdom behind the command was that without armed resistance **no religion would have felt safe** and its places of worship would have been destroyed. Maʿārif adds a qualification: many religions were founded and built up by means of revelation, and though in time their basics were altered, before that happened they were true religions whose followers had a duty to respect and defend their places of worship — and it is such places the verse refers to, not the sacred places of religions that were never founded on prophethood and revelation. Citing Qurtubi, Maʿārif concludes that if the believers had not been permitted at different times to fight, no true religion would have felt secure, and in the times of Musa and of ʿIsa (peace be upon them) and of the Prophet ﷺ the places of worship of their respective religions would have been destroyed.

Sit with that: the first verse permitting the Muslims to fight justifies itself by naming, alongside the mosque, the monastery, the church and the synagogue.

### "Allah will help those who help His cause"

Ibn Kathir places this beside *"O you who believe! If you help (in the cause of) Allah, He will help you, and make your foothold firm"* (47:7-8).

Then the two names sealing the ayah: **Qawiyy** (All-Strong) and **ʿAzīz** (All-Mighty). Ibn Kathir affirms them as Allah's description of Himself: by His strength He created everything and measured it exactly according to its due measurements; by His might nothing can overpower Him or overwhelm Him — rather everything is humbled before Him and is in need of Him. Then the conclusion the exiled believers most needed: **whoever is supported by the All-Strong, the All-Mighty is indeed supported and helped, and his enemy will be overpowered.** He cites *"And, verily, Our Word has gone forth of old for Our servants, the Messengers, that they verily would be made triumphant"* (37:171-173) and *"Allah has decreed: 'Verily, it is I and My Messengers who shall be the victorious'"* (58:21).

## Ayah 41 — what they will do with power

*"Those who, if We give them power in the land, establish the Salah, enforce the Zakah, and they enjoin the good and forbid the evil. And with Allah rests the end of (all) matters."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that "those" in ayah 41 refers back to "those who were expelled from their homes without any just reason" in ayah 40. The refugees of one ayah are the rulers of the next. If they are placed in authority in this world, says Maʿārif, they will use it to promote good deeds — setting up prayers, paying the obligatory charity, enjoining people to do good and to abstain from evil.

Maʿārif observes that these verses were revealed soon after the Hijrah, at a time when the Muslims did not exercise dominion anywhere on earth — which means Allah had already made known what they would do with an authority they did not yet hold. Sayyidna ʿUthman, may Allah be pleased with him, said of this verse that it **praises these people before they actually perform the praiseworthy deeds**.

Ibn Kathir records that Ibn Abi Hatim reported ʿUthman bin ʿAffan saying of this ayah: *"It was revealed concerning us, for we had been expelled from our homes unjustly only because we said: 'Our Lord is Allah.' Then we were given power in the land, so we established regular prayer, paid the Zakah, enjoined what is good and forbade what is evil, and with Allah rests the end of all matters. This is about my companions and I."* Abu al-ʿAliyah said simply: "They were the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ."

Maʿārif, citing Ruh ul-Maʿani, reports that many scholars hold this verse to be clear evidence that the accession to power of the four Rightly Guided Caliphs was a direct fulfilment of Allah's prophecy, and that the system of caliphate they established was in accordance with His will — for when they and the Muhajirun established their government and held sway over vast territories, they used that power in setting up prayers, strengthening the system of Zakah, and enjoining good and forbidding evil.

But the verse is not confined to them. Maʿārif states the principle that where the Qurʼān uses general words and phrases, their purpose is not restricted to a particular situation but applies to all similar situations — and reports from ad-Dahhak (citing Qurtubi) that this verse contains an **injunction for all those whom Allah grants power and authority** to do what the four Caliphs did when they held rule.

### Power as a duty, not a prize

As-Sabah bin Suwadah al-Kindi said he heard ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAziz recite *"Those who, if We give them power in the land…"* and then say: **this is not obligatory only for those who are in authority, it also applies to those who are governed by them.** The people's rights over their governor, he said, are that he should check on them with regard to their duties towards Allah, restore the rights they have over one another, and guide them to the straight path as much as possible; their duties towards him are to obey him without cheating and without resentment, both in secret and openly.

ʿAtiyah al-ʿAwfi said this ayah is like *"Allah has promised those among you who believe and do righteous good deeds, that He will certainly grant them succession in the land"* (24:55). And the closing phrase, **"and with Allah rests the end of all matters"**, Ibn Kathir likens to *"And the good end is for those who have Taqwa"* (28:83); Zayd bin Aslam explained it as: with Allah will be the reward for what they did.

## Living it

**Confidence comes from the Protector.** Ayah 38 comes before the permission: the believers were told Who was defending, guarding and supporting them before they were told they could lift a hand.

**Restraint is not weakness, and permission is not appetite.** About ten years of "not yet", more than seventy verses forbidding armed resistance, then a permission granted on the stated ground that they had been wronged. Ibn Kathir's note that Allah is able to grant victory with no fighting at all keeps it in place: He wants His servants to strive their utmost in obeying Him.

**Standing against oppression protects worship itself** — ayah 40 measures what would be lost in monasteries, churches, synagogues and mosques, not only in one's own sanctuary.

**If power ever comes, ayah 41 is the invoice.** Prayer established, Zakah enforced, good enjoined, evil forbidden — and on ad-Dahhak's reading, that is an injunction on everyone Allah grants power and authority. ʿUmar bin ʿAbdul-ʿAziz added the other half: the ayah binds the governed too, whose duty is obedience without cheating and without resentment, in private as in public. And the passage ends by taking the outcome out of our hands entirely: *and with Allah rests the end of all matters.*

passages.title: Earlier peoples who denied their messengers
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The Prophet ﷺ was being called a liar by his own people, and these five ayat answer that pain not with an argument but with a roll-call of history: every one of these great messengers was denied too. Ibn Kathir opens his comment on the whole block with exactly this: "Here Allah consoles His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ for the disbelief of those among his people who opposed him."

**What holds the unit together.** Ayat 42–44 list the deniers, one nation after another, and then state what Allah did with them — a delay, then a seizure. Ayah 45 shows what the seizure left behind: ruins, an abandoned well, a sturdily built castle standing empty. Ayah 46 turns and speaks to the living: walk out among those ruins, and see whether your heart is capable of taking the lesson. The movement is from *history* to *evidence* to *the organ that is supposed to perceive it*.

## The roll-call of denial (42–44)

The list is deliberately long: the people of Nuh, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Ibrahim, the people of Lut, the dwellers of Madyan — and then, breaking the pattern, "and denied was Musa."
