Notice the shift in the wording. Six times the Qur'an names a *people*; then it names the *messenger* and puts the verb in the passive: **wa kudhdhiba Mūsā**, "and denied was Musa." The rejection is stated as a bare fact, without even naming who did it — as if to say the denying is the point, not the identity of the deniers.

Ibn Kathir's comment on the whole sequence, from "the people of Nuh" through "and denied was Musa," is one short, weighty line: it happened **"despite all the clear signs and evidence that they brought."** That is the heart of the consolation. These were not messengers whose case was weak. They came with proofs, and were called liars anyway. So when the Prophet ﷺ is denied by his own people, that says nothing whatsoever about the truth of what he brought; denial has never been a verdict on evidence.

## "I granted them respite" — the most unsettling word in the passage

Then comes the turn in ayah 44:

**فَأَمْلَيْتُ لِلْكَافِرِينَ ثُمَّ أَخَذْتُهُمْ ۖ فَكَيْفَ كَانَ نَكِيرِ**
*"But I granted respite to the disbelievers for a while, then I seized them, and how (terrible) was My punishment!"*

Ibn Kathir glosses **amlaytu** simply: **"I delayed and postponed."** Not "I overlooked," not "I forgave" — I *deferred*. The rope was let out.

And **nakīr** he explains as: **"how great was My vengeance against them and My punishment of them!"** The words are an exclamation of enormity, not a request for information — the reader is being made to feel the size of what fell.

The two verbs sit side by side on purpose: *I delayed* … *then I seized*. The delay was never a reprieve; it was part of the seizure. Ibn Kathir brings a hadith that says precisely this. **In the Two Sahihs it is reported from Abu Musa that the Prophet ﷺ said:**

> **"Allah lets the wrongdoer carry on until, when He seizes him, He will never let him go."**

Then the Prophet ﷺ recited:

> *"Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the towns while they are doing wrong. Verily, His punishment is painful (and) severe."* (Hud 11:102)

Two things are worth pausing over here. First, the Arabic of the hadith uses the very same root as the ayah — *layumlī li-ẓ-ẓālim*, "Allah lets the wrongdoer carry on," matching **amlaytu**, "I granted respite." The Prophet ﷺ is describing the exact mechanism this ayah names. Second, the verse he recited (11:102) speaks of Allah seizing the towns *wa hiya ẓālimah*, "while they are doing wrong" — the identical phrase that ayah 45 is about to use of the townships He destroyed.

**Why this matters.** The most dangerous misreading of prosperity is to treat it as approval. A wrongdoer who is left alone, expanding, unpunished, may be experiencing not Allah's pleasure but the *imlāʾ* this ayah names — the lengthening of the rope. And the hadith closes the door on any hope in the delay: when the seizure comes, there is no slipping out of it.

## The ruins as courtroom evidence (45)

**فَكَأَيِّن مِّن قَرْيَةٍ أَهْلَكْنَاهَا وَهِيَ ظَالِمَةٌ**
*"And many a township did We destroy while they were given to wrongdoing…"*

Do not read **ẓālimah** ("wrongdoing") vaguely here. Ibn Kathir defines it from the context: **"meaning, they were rejecting their Messengers."** In this passage, the wrongdoing that brought down whole civilisations *is* the denial of the messengers. That is what ties ayah 45 back to the roll-call in 42–44 — these ruined towns are those same nations.

Then three images, each a picture of a life that stopped mid-sentence:

**1. فَهِيَ خَاوِيَةٌ عَلَىٰ عُرُوشِهَا — "so that it lie in ruins."** Ad-Dahhak said this means **"[Levelled to] their roofs"** — that is, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "their houses and cities were destroyed." The image is of walls collapsed down onto the roofs they once held up. Architecture turned inside out.

**2. وَبِئْرٍ مُّعَطَّلَةٍ — "and (many) a deserted well."** Ibn Kathir: **"they draw no water from it, and no one comes to it, after it had been frequented often by crowds of people."** Notice where he puts the weight: not on the water, but on the crowds. The well is described by who is missing from it. Its silence is the loudest detail in the ayah.

**3. وَقَصْرٍ مَّشِيدٍ — "and castle Mashid!"** Here the early scholars gave two readings, and Ibn Kathir reports both rather than choosing:

- **ʿIkrimah said: "This means whitened with plaster."** Ibn Kathir adds that something similar was narrated from **ʿAli bin Abi Talib, Mujahid, ʿAtaʾ, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Abu Al-Mulayh and Ad-Dahhak** — a remarkable weight of early authority for the reading "plastered, gleaming white."
- **Others said** it means **high and impenetrable fortresses.**

Ibn Kathir's verdict is generous and instructive: **"All of these suggestions are close in meaning and do not contradict one another"** — because whichever you take, the point is the same. **"This sturdy construction and great height did not help their occupants or afford them any protection when the punishment of Allah came upon them."** He then cites:

> *"Wheresoever you may be, death will overtake you even if you are in Buruj Mushayyadah!"* (an-Nisaʾ 4:78)

Ibn Kathir's text leaves that last phrase in Arabic rather than translating it. *Burūj mushayyadah* are towers built up high and strong — and *mushayyadah* comes from the same root as *mashīd* in our own ayah, "castle *Mashid*." The verse he quotes is describing the very kind of structure ayah 45 has just shown standing empty.

So the passage sets two monuments side by side: the well that crowds once thronged to and now no one visits, and the fortified castle that is still standing and no longer shelters anyone. The strong walls did not slow anything down for even a moment.

## Ayah 46: travel with your eyes open

**أَفَلَمْ يَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَتَكُونَ لَهُمْ قُلُوبٌ يَعْقِلُونَ بِهَا أَوْ آذَانٌ يَسْمَعُونَ بِهَا**
*"Have they not travelled through the land, and have they hearts wherewith to understand and ears wherewith to hear?"*

Ibn Kathir reads the travelling on two levels at once: **"have they not travelled in the physical sense and also used their minds to ponder?"** Then: **"Walk through their ruins, see what they did and what became of them"** — that is, look at "the punishments and divine wrath that struck the nations of the past who belied." And the purpose clause, "hearts wherewith to understand and ears wherewith to hear," he sums up in one line: **"let them learn a lesson from that."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the ruling implicit in this: **travels undertaken to acquire insight into things and to learn lessons from the past are one of the religious objectives.** But it attaches a condition — the verse "encourages travel, **provided the person travelling keeps his eyes wide open and imbibes in his mind the lessons of history.**" And it reads the phrase *"so that they should have hearts"* as suggesting that a person can genuinely **gain wisdom and intelligence by a careful study of the history of bygone times** and of the people who inhabited this world in different ages. As it puts it: **every event of history holds a lesson for a person who has insight and who does not regard history as a mere record of episodes and occurrences.**

Maʿārif also relates, from Ibn Abi Hatim's book *at-Tafakkur*, quoting **Malik ibn Dinar**, that Allah commanded Sayyidna Musa (peace be upon him) to wear shoes made of iron and hold a staff of iron in his hand and travel around the earth until the shoes wore out and the staff broke down. Maʿārif is careful with this report — **"if this narration is true"** — and reads it as an image of what the command means: to acquire knowledge and lessons from the past.

**How to keep a heart alive.** On this ayah Ibn Kathir quotes Ibn Abi Ad-Dunya's book *At-Tafakkur wal-Iʿtibar*, where "some of the wise people" said:

> "Give life to your heart with lessons, illuminate it with thought, kill it with asceticism, strengthen it with certain faith, remind it of its mortality, make it aware of the calamities of this world, warn it of the disasters that life may bring, show it how things may suddenly change with the passing of days, tell it the stories of the people of the past, and remind it what happened to those who came before."

Read that slowly: it is a regimen. The heart is treated as something that can be fed, lit, disciplined, and reminded — and history is one of its staple foods.

## The closing diagnosis: which blindness is real

**فَإِنَّهَا لَا تَعْمَى الْأَبْصَارُ وَلَٰكِن تَعْمَى الْقُلُوبُ الَّتِي فِي الصُّدُورِ**
*"Verily, it is not the eyes that grow blind, but it is the hearts which are in the breasts that grow blind."*

This is the sentence the whole passage has been building to. Ibn Kathir: **"the blind person is not the one whose eyes cannot see, but rather the one who has no insight. Even if the physical eyes are sound, they still cannot learn the lesson."**

The ayah is not denying that people go blind in the ordinary sense. It is saying that *this* is not the blindness that ruins a person. Two people can stand in the same ruined town, see the same fallen roofs and the same empty well, and one of them walks out changed while the other photographs it and moves on. The eyes reported identically. The hearts did not.

Note also the phrase **"the hearts which are in the breasts."** The Qur'an specifies the location, as if to forestall any thought that "heart" here is a figure of speech for something vague — the seat of understanding is named, and it is failing.

## Living it

- **Never read a delay as an acquittal.** Ayah 44 and the hadith of Abu Musa in the Two Sahihs together teach that Allah's *imlāʾ* — His letting a wrongdoer carry on — is not indifference. Apply it first to yourself: if you are persisting in something wrong and nothing has happened yet, that is not evidence of safety.
- **Take the consolation for what it is.** If you are ridiculed, disbelieved, or dismissed for holding to this faith, ayat 42–44 put you in the company of Nuh, Ibrahim, Lut and Musa, and of the messengers sent to ʿAd, Thamud and Madyan. Being denied has never meant being wrong; the messengers came with "all the clear signs and evidence," and were denied anyway.
- **Travel as an act of religion, not tourism.** Maʿārif's condition is the whole thing: eyes wide open, the lessons of history taken in. A ruin, a museum, an abandoned town, an old family story — each is raw material for *iʿtibār*, the taking of a lesson.
- **Check for the blindness that counts.** After you read history or walk through it, the honest question from ayah 46 is not "did I see it?" but "did anything in me move?" If nothing moves, the problem is not the evidence. The evidence has been lying in the open for centuries.
- **Do not put your trust in what you have built.** The plastered castle and the impenetrable fortress are in ayah 45, and 4:78 is quoted alongside it: height and thickness of wall changed nothing. Security is from Allah, not from structures.

passages.title: They demand the punishment be hastened
passages.tafsir:
Some people had begun treating the delay of the promised punishment as a joke — daring the Prophet ﷺ to produce it. These five ayat answer that dare, and they answer it as one connected argument rather than five separate remarks. First the timetable is lifted out of human hands and set on a scale we do not measure with (47). Then the same point is proved from the record of towns that were left alone for a long while and then seized (48). Then the Prophet ﷺ is told plainly that he was never the one holding the switch (49). And finally the two ends that the whole warning is pointing towards are named (50–51). One idea runs through all five: the timing belongs to Allah alone, and it is not negotiable — not by mockery, and not by the Messenger ﷺ himself.

## The dare, and who made it

**"And they ask you to hasten on the torment!"**

Ibn Kathir identifies who "they" are: the disbelievers who disbelieve in Allah and in His Book and in His Messenger ﷺ and in the Last Day. Their words are not a question about timing. They are a demand that the punishment be brought forward — and Ibn Kathir shows this was a settled way of speaking among them by pointing to two other places where the Qur'an quotes them:

- *"O Allah! If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down stones on us from the sky or bring on us a painful torment"* (8:32) — a prayer made against themselves.
- *"Our Lord! Hasten to us Qittana (our punishment) before the Day of Reckoning!"* (38:16).

There is something worth pausing on here. A person who thought for a moment that the punishment might be real would never invite it upon his own head. The dare is itself the confession: they were certain enough that nothing was coming that they were willing to stake their own destruction on it.

## "And Allah fails not His promise"

The reply does not argue with the dare. It simply names what will happen.

Ibn Kathir explains **"And Allah fails not His promise"** as His promise to bring about the Hour, to wreak vengeance upon His enemies, and to honour His close friends. Notice that the one promise has two faces. The appointed moment that settles accounts with those who mocked is the same moment that raises the standing of those who stayed faithful to Him. So if you are on the receiving end of the mockery rather than making it, this half of the ayah is addressed to you exactly as much as the first half is addressed to them.

## A day with your Lord

**"And verily a day with your Lord is as a thousand years of what you reckon."**

This is the heart of the answer, and Ibn Kathir draws out its logic: *He does not hasten*. What is counted as a thousand years by His creation is as one day with Him. He delays, and waits, and postpones — and none of that is weakness or forgetfulness, because He knows that He is able to exact retribution and that not one thing will escape Him.

Understand what is being corrected. The mockers were reading the gap between the warning and its arrival as evidence that there was nothing behind the warning. The ayah says the gap only looks enormous from inside the human way of counting — "of what *you* reckon". The One who set the appointment is not working from our calendar. Delay of this kind is what power can afford; it is haste that betrays a fear of losing the chance.

## Two readings of "a thousand years"

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* records that this phrase can be understood in two ways, and treats both as available.

**The first**: that it refers to the Day of Resurrection, and that the events of that Day will be so horrifying and of such extreme severity that the day will appear never to end — as if it were a thousand years by our reckoning. *Maʿārif* notes that many commentators have interpreted the verse this way.

**The second**: that the Day of Resurrection will in actual fact be that long, stretching to a thousand years of this world.

For the second reading, *Maʿārif* cites a saying of the Prophet ﷺ reported in the *Musnad* of Ahmad and in Tirmidhi on the authority of Sayyidnā Abū Hurayrah, that the Prophet ﷺ once addressed the poor among the Muhājirīn (those who had migrated from Makkah) and gave them good news of full radiance on the Day of Resurrection, and that they would be admitted to the Garden half a day before the rich and the wealthy — and since a day in the Hereafter is a thousand years, the poor will enter five hundred years before the wealthy. Tirmidhi classified this hadith as *hasan*. (*Maʿārif* attributes the citation to Mazharī.)

Ibn Kathir brings the same teaching at this passage by another route: **Ibn Abi Hatim** recorded from **Abu Hurayrah** that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, *"The poor among the Muslims will enter Paradise half a day before the rich — five hundred years."* Ibn Kathir adds that this was recorded by **At-Tirmidhi** and **An-Nasa'i** from the hadith of Ath-Thawri from Muhammad bin ʿAmr, and that At-Tirmidhi said, *"Hasan Sahih."*

And he brings a second, quieter report: **Abu Dawud** recorded at the end of the Book of Al-Malāhim in his *Sunan*, from **Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas**, that the Prophet ﷺ said, *"I hope that it will not be too much for my Ummah if Allah delays them for half a day."* Saʿd was asked what half a day meant. He answered: five hundred years. (*Ummah* here means the community that follows him.)

That last report is worth sitting with. The unit of time being handled so calmly in it — "half a day" — is five centuries of ours. The people demanding that the punishment be rushed forward had no idea what scale of time they were making demands about.

## "But another verse says fifty thousand years"

*Maʿārif ul Qurʼān* raises the obvious difficulty and answers it. Sūrah al-Maʿārij says of the Day, *"Whereof the measure is fifty thousand years"* (70:4). How does that sit with a thousand?

**On the first reading** — that the number describes how the Day is experienced — there is no difficulty at all. Every person will suffer different levels of severity: to some it will appear as though they have endured a thousand years, while to others the period will seem equal to fifty thousand.

**On the second reading** — that the length is literal — the two figures do appear to clash. Here *Maʿārif* reports the reconciliation offered by Sayyidnā Ashraf ʿAlī Thānawī in his commentary *Bayān ul-Qurʼān*: the difference may be due to different horizons. Even in this world the length of day and night differs on different horizons — at zero latitude a day is twenty-four hours, while at the pole it runs to a year. It is likewise possible that the Day of Resurrection will have different lengths on different horizons, so that areas falling fifty times distant from where it measures a thousand years may have a day fifty times longer. *Maʿārif* closes the discussion the way such matters should be closed: **and Allah knows best.**

Two things to take from this. First, the scholars did not paper over an apparent tension in the Book; they named it plainly and worked at it honestly. Second, where a matter of the unseen genuinely admits more than one defensible reading, the honest position is to hold both with attribution rather than to force one of them into certainty.

## The same answer, proved from below

**"And many a township did I give respite while it was given to wrongdoing. Then I seized it. And to Me is the final return."**

Ayah 47 answered the dare from above — the scale on which Allah measures time. Ayah 48 answers it from below, from the record of what has already happened to whole towns. Ibn Kathir places the two side by side deliberately: it is *because* He does not hasten, and delays and waits and postpones while remaining fully able to exact retribution, that "hence He then says" — and the ayah about the towns follows.

The sequence in the ayah is exact: the respite was granted **while** the township was still given to wrongdoing. That is the whole point. The wrongdoing did not stop the clock, and the long run of untroubled prosperity was never a verdict of approval.

Then the seizure arrives with no warning built into the wording at all: **"Then I seized it."** And notice that the whole ayah is in the first person singular — *I* gave the respite, *I* seized, and to *Me* is the return. Nothing in this is handed to anyone else, which is precisely why the demand in ayah 47 was addressed to the wrong person.

The closing phrase — **"and to Me is the final return"** — carries the warning past the worldly seizure. Even where no seizure was ever visible in this life, the return is still to Him. There is no exit from the account.

## The messenger is not the timekeeper

Having established whose the timing is, the passage turns to the man they were making the demand of. Ibn Kathir is explicit that this instruction comes as Allah's word to His Prophet ﷺ *when the disbelievers asked him to hasten on the punishment for them*: **"Say: 'O mankind! I am sent to you only as a plain warner.'"**

Ibn Kathir unfolds the meaning as the Prophet's own words: Allah has sent me to you to warn you ahead of the terrible punishment, but I have nothing to do with your reckoning. Your case rests with Allah. If He wills, He will hasten the punishment for you; and if He wills, He will delay it for you. If He wills, He will accept the repentance of those who repent to Him; and if He wills, He will send astray those who are decreed to be doomed. He is the One who does whatever He wills and wants and chooses. Ibn Kathir then seals it with another ayah: *"There is none to put back His judgement, and He is swift at reckoning"* (13:41).

We affirm this as it is stated, without twisting it into something else and without imagining His will to be like ours: He wills, and it is as He wills.

This is one of the great humbling ayat for anyone who carries a message. The demand had been put to the Prophet ﷺ himself — *they ask **you** to hasten it*. The answer removes the ground the demand was standing on: he was never the one who decides. Two words define the entire commission — *nadhīr*, a warner, and *mubīn*, plain and clarifying. Not an enforcer. Not a scheduler of punishments. A clear warning, delivered.

Notice also how wide the address becomes: **"O mankind."** The demand came from a particular group of disbelievers, but the response is turned towards everyone. The warning has no shortlist.

## What the warning is pointing towards

The passage does not end on the refusal. Having taken the timing out of human hands, it names the two ends that all this waiting is heading for — and it is significant that the ayah of mercy comes first.

**"So those who believe and do righteous good deeds, for them is forgiveness and *rizq karīm*."**

Ibn Kathir's definition of these believers is worth committing to memory: **those whose hearts believe and whose actions confirm their faith.** Not a claim in the chest with nothing behind it, and not busy activity with an empty heart. Each authenticates the other.

Their reward has two parts, and Ibn Kathir separates them cleanly:

- **Forgiveness** — for their previous bad deeds. The past is dealt with.
- **A generous provision** — which he glosses as *a great reward in return for a few good deeds*. Muhammad bin Kaʿb Al-Qurazī said: when you hear Allah's words *rizq karīm*, this means Paradise.

Feel the exchange rate in that. Their sins are wiped, and their small handful of good deeds is paid out at a rate no work of theirs could ever have earned. Set it beside ayah 47: the same Lord whose delay was being read as absence is the Lord whose generosity runs this far beyond what is done for Him.

**"But those who strive against Our Ayat to frustrate them, they will be dwellers of the Hellfire."**

The early authorities Ibn Kathir cites read this as something more active than private unbelief:

- **Mujahid**: it means "to discourage people from following the Prophet ﷺ."
- **ʿAbdullah bin Az-Zubayr** held the same view — "to discourage."
- **Ibn ʿAbbas**: "to frustrate them means to resist the believers stubbornly."

So those condemned here are not merely people who did not accept. The ayah speaks of *striving* — effort spent to pull others away from following the Messenger ﷺ and to stand against the believers with stubborn resistance.

Their destination is named as *al-Jaḥīm*, which Ibn Kathir describes as the agonizingly hot Fire with its severe punishment — and he adds, *may Allah save us from it*. He closes with the ayah that shows why this is weightier than private refusal: *"Those who disbelieved and hinder men from the path of Allah, for them We will add torment to the torment because they used to spread corruption"* (16:88). Blocking the road for others carries an added weight, over and above one's own refusal to walk it.

## Living it

**Do not read delay as absence.** This is the discipline the whole passage is teaching, and it cuts both ways. The wrongdoer who is prospering should hear ayah 48 and be alarmed rather than reassured — respite was granted to those towns *while* they were wronging, and it ended. And the believer watching wrongdoing go unanswered should hear ayah 47 and steady himself: Allah fails not His promise, and He is not running on our calendar.

**Keep your role straight.** If the Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself was told he had nothing to do with people's reckoning, then no one calling to Allah today owns anyone's outcome. Deliver the warning plainly, and leave the hastening, the delaying, the accepting of repentance and the sending astray to the One who does whatever He wills.

**Let heart and limbs agree.** Ibn Kathir's definition at ayah 50 is the standard to measure yourself against: hearts that believe, actions that confirm it. That is the doorway to forgiveness for what is past, and to a provision no deed of ours could ever purchase.

**Guard against the sin named in ayah 51.** Discouraging people from following the Prophet ﷺ, and resisting the believers stubbornly, is singled out here for torment added upon torment. May Allah save us from it.

passages.title: Satan's interference in what prophets recite
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat answer a wound that every carrier of truth feels: *why does the message I bring get twisted, doubted, and fought the moment I open my mouth?* Allah tells His Prophet ﷺ that this is not new and not a sign of failure — it has happened to every messenger and prophet before him (ayah 52) — and then explains the wisdom in Allah permitting it: it sorts hearts (ayat 53–54), and those who refuse the sorting stay in doubt until doubt is no longer possible (ayah 55).

What holds the passage together is a single movement: **interference, then correction, then purpose, then outcome.** Something is thrown in; Allah lifts it away and makes His verses firm; the residue becomes a test that exposes diseased hearts and deepens knowing hearts; and the disbelievers remain suspended in doubt until the Hour or the punishment arrives.

## "A messenger or a prophet" — why both words?

Ayah 52 says *min rasūlin wa lā nabiyy* — "any messenger and any prophet." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the two words carry different meanings, though there is no consensus as to the precise nature of the difference. For our purposes, it explains: a **nabī** (prophet) is someone Allah designates with a mission to reform his people and who receives revelation from Him. He may receive a Scripture and a code of laws, or he may be commanded to convey the message of an earlier Book and code of laws. Mūsā and ʿĪsā (peace be upon them) belong to the first category; Hārūn (peace be upon him), who was directed to propagate the teachings of the Torah and the Mosaic laws, falls in the second. A **rasūl** (messenger) is one who receives from Allah a Scripture and a code of laws. So every messenger is necessarily a prophet, but not every prophet is a messenger.

Maʿārif adds two clarifications: these distinctions are applicable to human beings only, and the fact that an angel who carries *waḥy* (revelation) from Allah is also named a *rasūl* does not contradict this position.

The point of naming both categories is scope. **No one who ever carried revelation was spared this.** The Prophet ﷺ is being placed in the longest and most honourable line in history precisely at the moment his message is being attacked.

## The key phrase: "when he recited"

The Arabic in ayah 52 is *idhā tamannā alqā al-shayṭānu fī umniyyatih* — literally, "when he *tamannā*, Shayṭān threw into his *umniyya*." The verb *tamannā* normally suggests wishing or desiring, so the early scholars had to settle what it means here. Ibn Kathir preserves several readings, and it is worth keeping each attached to the person who said it:

- **Al-Bukhārī said that Ibn ʿAbbās said**, commenting on *fī umniyyatih* ("in his recitation"): "When he spoke, the Shayṭān threw (some falsehood) into his speech, but Allah abolished that which the Shayṭān threw in."
- Separately, **ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥa reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said** of the phrase "when he did recite, Shayṭān threw (some falsehood) in it": "When he spoke, the Shayṭān threw (some falsehood) into his speech."
- **Mujāhid** said of "when he did recite": "When he spoke."
- **Al-Baghawī and the majority of the scholars of tafsir** said *tamannā* means **"reciting the Book of Allah,"** and that what was thrown in was thrown **"in his recitation."**
- **Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk** read it simply: "When he recited." **Ibn Jarīr** said of this: "This comment is more akin to interpretation."

Ibn Kathir also notes a related usage: "it was said that it refers to his recitation," whereas in 2:78 the Qur'an speaks of those who have nothing but *amānī* — which, he reports, means "they speak but they do not write."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reaches the same conclusion cleanly: here *tamannā* is used as a synonym for *qara'a* (he recited), so *umniyyatih* means *qirā'ah* — **his recitation**.

## What was actually "thrown in"?

Two complementary explanations sit in the sources, and it is worth holding both.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah as being about **the doubts Shayṭān casts into the hearts of the hearers**: the disputes raised by the disbelievers regarding Allah's message are not something new, because similar doubts were raised by earlier people when their prophets presented them the message of Truth, and Shayṭān cast doubts about it in the hearts of disbelievers. Maʿārif calls this explanation "quite clear and straight-forward," and notes it has been adopted by many commentators including **Abū Ḥayyān in his Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ**.

Ibn Kathir's presentation stays close to the wording of the transmitted reports: something is thrown in around the prophet's recitation or speech, and Allah abolishes it. Either way, **the decisive half of the ayah is the second half** — what Allah does about it, which is where the passage is going next.

## The story of the Gharānīq — and why both commentators set it aside

Ibn Kathir writes that at this point many of the scholars of tafsir mentioned the story of the *Gharānīq*, along with the account of how many of those who had migrated to Ethiopia came back when they thought the idolaters of the Quraysh had become Muslims. His verdict is explicit: **"these reports all come through Mursal chains of narration and I do not think that any of them may be regarded as Ṣaḥīḥ. And Allah knows best."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is, if anything, firmer. It says the incident, known as *ḥadīth al-gharānīq*, "is not proved by authentic sources"; that **some scholars have held that it is invented by some heretics and enemies of Islam**; and that even those who believe the tradition to be worthwhile have taken pains to remove the doubts its words raise about the categorical and undisputed laws of the Qur'an and Sunnah. Its conclusion is worth stating plainly: the alleged incident **in no way affects** the plain and simple meaning of the ayah, and making it "part and parcel of the commentary on this verse, thereby creating unnecessary doubts, and then attempting to answer those doubts is an exercise in futility and absolutely undesirable."

So the honest position for a believer is: the ayah does not depend on that story, and the ayah's own words carry a complete and coherent meaning without it. *Wa Allāhu subḥānahu wa taʿālā aʿlam.*

## Allah cancels, then Allah makes firm

The heart of ayah 52 is what Allah does next: *fa-yansakhu Allāhu mā yulqī al-shayṭān thumma yuḥkimu Allāhu āyātih* — "But Allah abolishes that which Shayṭān throws in. Then Allah establishes His revelations."

Ibn Kathir explains the vocabulary: **the meaning of the word *naskh* in Arabic is to remove or lift away.** ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥa reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said this means, **"Allah cancels out that which the Shayṭān throws in."** Feel the two verbs together: first the removal, then the establishing — Allah does not merely delete the interference, He leaves His revelations standing firm afterwards. Shayṭān's throw is never the last move.

The ayah then closes on two of Allah's names, and Ibn Kathir gives each its weight:

- **ʿAlīm (All-Knower)** — "He knows all matters and events that will happen, and nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him." Nothing Shayṭān attempts catches Allah unprepared.
- **Ḥakīm (All-Wise)** — "in His decree, creation and command, He has perfect wisdom and absolute proof."

That second name is the hinge into ayah 53. Ibn Kathir moves straight from it to the next ayah with the words "hence He says" — the wisdom named at the end of ayah 52 is what the purpose clause of ayah 53 unfolds.

## Why Allah permits it: the sorting of hearts (ayat 53–54)

Ayah 53 opens with *li-yajʿala* — "that He may make" — a purpose clause. What Shayṭān throws in becomes **a *fitna* (a trial, a test)** for two groups:

**"Those in whose hearts is a disease."** Ibn Kathir defines the disease as **doubt, shirk (associating partners with Allah), disbelief and hypocrisy**. Ibn Jurayj, commenting on this description, said it means **the hypocrites**.

**"And whose hearts are hardened."** Ibn Jurayj said this means **the idolaters**.

The distinction is worth pausing on. A *diseased* heart is one carrying doubt and hypocrisy inside it; a *hardened* heart has gone stiff and cannot receive. Read against the purpose clause of the ayah, the insinuation is not what creates either condition — it is what turns the condition into a visible test. A doubt only lodges where there is already a place for it.

Then the verdict: *wa inna al-ẓālimīna la-fī shiqāqin baʿīd* — "and certainly, the wrongdoers are in an opposition far-off." Ibn Kathir explains: **far away in misguidance, resistance and stubbornness — that is, far from the truth and the correct way.**

## The other half of the sorting: "those who have been given knowledge" (ayah 54)

Ayah 54 is the mirror image, and it is the most consoling ayah in the passage. The very same event that unsettles the diseased heart *settles* the knowing heart. Ibn Kathir unpacks the phrase carefully:

Those "given knowledge" are **those given beneficial knowledge with which they may differentiate between truth and falsehood**, those who believe in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ. What they come to know is that "what We have revealed to you is the truth from your Lord" — the Lord **"Who has revealed it by His knowledge and under His protection, and He will guard it from being mixed with anything else."**

That last clause is the direct answer to any anxiety this passage might raise. Ibn Kathir seals it with another ayah: *"Falsehood cannot come to it from before it or behind it, (it is) sent down by the All-Wise, Worthy of all praise"* (41:42). The Book is under guard from every direction.

Then the ayah names what real knowledge produces, in two stages:

- ***fa-yu'minū bihi*** — "so that they may believe therein." Ibn Kathir: **"that they may believe that it is true and act upon it."** Belief here is not an opinion held; it is a conviction acted on.
- ***fa-tukhbita lahu qulūbuhum*** — "and their hearts may submit to it with humility." Ibn Kathir: **"that their hearts may humble themselves and accept it."** Knowledge that does not make the heart bow is not the knowledge this ayah is praising.

And the closing promise: *"And verily, Allah is the Guide of those who believe, to the straight path."* Ibn Kathir extends this over both worlds — **in this world**, He guides them to the truth and helps them to follow it and to resist and avoid falsehood; **in the Hereafter**, He will guide them to the straight path which leads to the degrees of Paradise, and He will save them from the painful torment and the dismal levels of Hell.

Notice the logic: the guidance is promised to *"those who believe."* Faith comes first, and guidance is given to it. That is why the same doubt that wrecks one man deepens another.

## Ayah 55: doubt that lasts until doubt is impossible

*"And those who disbelieved will not cease to be in doubt about it until the Hour comes suddenly upon them, or there comes to them the torment of Yawm ʿAqīm."*

Ibn Kathir says Allah is telling us **the disbelievers will remain in doubt concerning this Qur'an** — this was the view of Ibn Jurayj and the view favoured by Ibn Jarīr. The wording is relentless: *lā yazālu*, "they will not cease." Their doubt has no natural endpoint. Only an event ends it, and by then it is too late for it to help them.

**"Suddenly" (*baghtatan*).** Mujāhid said: "By surprise." Qatāda said it means the command of Allah will catch the people unaware — **"Allah never seizes a people except when they are intoxicated with pride, enjoying a life of luxury, and they think that the punishment will never come upon them, but Allah does not punish anyone except the evildoers."** That is a description of a mood, not just a moment: the confidence that consequences are for other people.

**"The torment of Yawm ʿAqīm."** The early authorities differed, and Ibn Kathir reports the difference rather than resolving it:

- Mujāhid said that **Ubay bin Kaʿb** said: *Yawm ʿAqīm* means **the day of Badr**.
- **ʿIkrima and Mujāhid** said: *Yawm ʿAqīm* means **the Day of Resurrection, following which there will be no night.** This was also the view of **Ad-Ḍaḥḥāk** and **Al-Ḥasan Al-Baṣrī**.

The commentary records both views without adjudicating between them, and both stand as an end to the doubt the ayah describes.

Ibn Kathir then reads the ayah that follows into the same thought — *"The sovereignty on that Day will be that of Allah. He will judge between them"* — comparing it with *"The Only Owner of the Day of Recompense"* (1:4) and *"The sovereignty on that Day will be the true sovereignty, belonging to the Most Gracious, and it will be a hard Day for the disbelievers"* (25:26). The doubt of ayah 55 dissolves the moment the true ownership of that Day becomes visible.

## Living it

**Doubt arriving is not the same as faith leaving.** The passage takes the most alarming possible scenario — interference around revelation itself — and shows Allah abolishing it and then establishing His revelations. If that is how Allah handles interference at the level of prophethood, an intrusive thought in your own prayer is not the catastrophe it feels like.

**Judge yourself by what doubt does to you, not by whether it comes.** Ayah 53 and ayah 54 describe two responses to the same trial. One heart is destabilised — the heart Ibn Kathir describes as carrying doubt, shirk, disbelief and hypocrisy, or as hardened. The other is confirmed, because it has the *beneficial* knowledge that distinguishes truth from falsehood.

**Ask for the knowledge that humbles.** Ayah 54 sets the standard: know it is the truth, believe that it is true, *act upon it*, and let the heart humble itself and accept it. Knowledge that leaves the heart unbowed has, by this ayah's measure, not yet done its work.

**Do not build your religion on unverified stories.** Ibn Kathir would not treat as authentic a report whose chains he judged not to be Ṣaḥīḥ, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the incident is not proved by authentic sources and calls building the commentary on it "an exercise in futility." That instinct — check what you are told before you carry it — sits close to what "those who have been given knowledge" means here.

**Take the warning about comfort seriously.** Qatāda's description of the people Allah seizes suddenly is not a description of criminals; it is a description of the proud, the comfortable, and the self-assured. And with it stands the mercy in the same sentence: **Allah does not punish anyone except the evildoers.**

passages.title: Sovereignty that Day and the reward of emigrants
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat move from the courtroom to the reward. Ayat 56 and 57 announce who holds authority on the Day of Judgement and split all of humanity into two outcomes; ayat 58 and 59 then single out one group from the believing side — those who left their homes in the cause of Allah — and promise, twice over, that they will be provided for and brought into a place that satisfies them. What holds the passage together is the theme of **final ownership**: on that Day the only kingdom is Allah's, the only verdict is His, and the only provision worth counting is the one He gives.

## The doubt that ayah 56 answers

To feel the force of ayah 56 you have to hear the ayah just before it. Ibn Kathir explains that in ayah 55 Allah tells us the disbelievers "will remain in doubt concerning this Qur'an" — this was the view of Ibn Jurayj, and the view favoured by Ibn Jarir. Their doubt is not a passing phase they will reason their way out of. It runs, as the ayah says, "until the Hour comes suddenly upon them" — that is, until the moment it becomes useless.

That moment is described with the word **baghtatan** — rendered "suddenly." Mujahid glossed it simply: "By surprise." Qatadah drew out the pattern behind it: the command of Allah will catch the people unaware, and "Allah never seizes a people except when they are intoxicated with pride, enjoying a life of luxury, and they think that the punishment will never come upon them" — yet, Qatadah adds, Allah does not punish anyone except the evildoers. The sense of safety is itself part of the trap; the very comfort that made doubt feel affordable is what makes the arrival so shocking.

**"The torment of Yawm 'Aqim."** Here the early authorities genuinely differed, and Ibn Kathir reports both readings without collapsing them:

- Mujahid reported that Ubay bin Ka'b said: "Yawm 'Aqim means the day of Badr."
- 'Ikrimah and Mujahid said it means the Day of Resurrection, "following which there will be no night." Ad-Dahhak and Al-Hasan Al-Basri held the same view.

Both readings serve the passage. On either understanding, the doubter's position is the same: he does not get to keep doubting.

## "All authority on that Day is for Allah alone" (ayah 56)

The ayah opens by naming the sovereignty itself — translated here as "All authority on that Day is for Allah alone," and rendered by Ibn Kathir as "The sovereignty on that Day will be that of Allah." He links this to two other places in the Qur'an where the same claim is made: *"The Only Owner of the Day of Recompense"* (1:4), and *"The sovereignty on that Day will be the true sovereignty, belonging to the Most Gracious, and it will be a hard Day for the disbelievers"* (25:26).

Notice what that second ayah adds: the sovereignty on that Day is called *the true* sovereignty. Not that Allah's kingship begins then — it never lapsed — but that on that Day nothing else will be standing next to it to be mistaken for it. Every rival claim that made doubt seem reasonable in this world is simply absent from the scene.

And immediately: **yahkumu baynahum**, "He will judge between them." Sovereignty here is not an abstract title; it issues at once in a verdict. The One who owns the Day is the One who decides the case, and there is no appeal above Him.

## The two verdicts (ayat 56–57)

The passage then divides everyone in two, and Ibn Kathir's comment on each half is worth reading slowly, because he describes not only what these people receive but what they *were*.

**"So those who believed and did righteous good deeds"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning "their hearts believed in Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, and they acted in accordance with what they knew; their words and deeds were in harmony." Three things are packed in there: belief seated in the heart, action that matches what one actually knows, and integrity between speech and conduct. That is the Qur'an's ordinary pairing — faith and righteous deeds — unpacked into a portrait of a whole person.

Their outcome is **jannat al-na'im**, "Gardens of Delight." Ibn Kathir's gloss: "they will enjoy eternal bliss which will never end or fade away." The two verbs matter. Worldly delight either ends or, worse, stays while your capacity to enjoy it fades. This delight does neither.

**"And those who disbelieved and denied Our Ayat"** — Ibn Kathir explains this as meaning "their hearts rejected and denied the truth; they disbelieved in it and resisted the Messengers and were too proud to follow them." Again the heart comes first, and again the description ends in a posture: pride.

Their outcome is **'adhab muhin**, a *humiliating* torment. Ibn Kathir is precise about why this adjective and not another: it is "in recompense for arrogantly turning away from the truth." The punishment is shaped to fit the sin. Those who were too big to bow are made small. He cites as proof: *"Verily, those who scorn My worship they will surely enter Hell in humiliation!"* (40:60) — the same pairing of arrogance with humiliation, stated there as an explicit rule.

So ayat 56 and 57 are not two unrelated announcements. They are one judgement seen from both sides, and in each case the outward result grows out of an inward condition: harmony of heart and limb produces unfading delight; pride of heart produces humiliation.

## The emigrants (ayat 58–59)

Now the passage narrows to a particular group, and the tone changes from verdict to reassurance.

**Who they are.** Ibn Kathir describes them as those who migrate for the sake of Allah, "seeking to earn His pleasure and that which is with Him, leaving behind their homelands, families and friends, leaving their countries for the sake of Allah and His Messenger to support His religion." Maarif ul Quran puts it in one warm phrase: people "who had left their hearth and homes in the cause of Allah."

Read that list again — homeland, family, friends, country. This is not a small sacrifice made once; it is the dismantling of an entire life. And notice what makes it worship rather than mere displacement: Ibn Kathir's insistence that it is done "for the sake of Allah," seeking His pleasure and what is with Him.

**"Then are killed or died."** This is the mercy at the heart of ayah 58, and Ibn Kathir marks it carefully. *Killed* means "in Jihad"; *died* means "they pass away without being involved in fighting." Both are named, and of both he says: "they will have earned an immense reward." The emigrant who falls in battle and the emigrant who dies in his bed of illness or old age are placed in the same ayah, under the same promise. He connects this with *"And whosoever leaves his home as an emigrant unto Allah and His Messenger, and death overtakes him, his reward is then surely incumbent upon Allah"* (4:100). The reward is tied to the setting out, not to how the story happens to end. Maarif ul Quran draws the plain conclusion: if they did not benefit from their sacrifice in this world, their reward will be there in the Hereafter.

**The language of certainty.** Read the promise as it stands: "*surely*, Allah will provide a good provision for them. And verily, it is Allah Who *indeed* is the Best of those who make provision. *Truly*, He will make them enter an entrance with which they shall be well-pleased." For people who had lost house, land, income and kin, this is exactly the register they needed: not that they may be compensated, but that they certainly will be.

**"A good provision."** Ibn Kathir explains *rizqan hasanan* as meaning that "He will reward them from His bounty and provision in Paradise with that which will bring them joy." Provision is precisely what these emigrants had walked away from — and provision is exactly the word Allah answers them with, promising it from **khayr al-raziqin**, "the Best of those who make provision." The one who left his living behind did not lose a provider; he changed providers.

**"An entrance with which they shall be well-pleased"** (ayah 59). Ibn Kathir says plainly: "This means Paradise," and cites *"Then, if he be of those brought near to Allah, rest and provision, and a Garden of Delights"* (56:88–89) — rest, provision, and a garden, which he notes is what is promised here too. What is striking in ayah 59 is the measure Allah chooses: not a place He merely describes, but a place *they will be pleased with*. Their own satisfaction is the standard, which means nothing they gave up will be left unanswered in their own reckoning.

**'Alim, Halim.** Ayah 59 closes with two of Allah's names, and Ibn Kathir shows that each answers a different worry of the emigrant.

- **All-Knowing** — "He is All-Knowing about those who migrate and strive in Jihad for His sake and who deserve that reward." No sacrifice went unrecorded because no one important was watching. He was watching.
- **Most Forbearing** — "He forgives and overlooks their sins, and He accepts as expiation for their sins, their migration (Hijrah) and their putting their trust in Him." This answers the second fear: *but I was not a perfect person.* The emigrant's sins are not brushed aside as though they did not matter; his hijrah and his reliance on Allah are accepted as the atonement for them.

## The martyrs, and those who simply died

Ibn Kathir adds that those killed for the sake of Allah — whether emigrants or not — "are alive with their Lord and are being provided for," quoting *"Think not of those as dead who are killed in the way of Allah. Nay, they are alive, with their Lord, and they have provision"* (3:169). And as for those who die for the sake of Allah, whether emigrants or not, he states that this ayah and the Sahih Hadiths guarantee that they will be well provided for and that Allah will show them kindness.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Shurahbil bin As-Simt said: "We spent a long time besieging a stronghold in the land of the Romans. Salman Al-Farisi, may Allah be pleased with him, passed by me and said, 'I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: Whoever dies guarding the borders of Islam, Allah will give him a reward like that reward of martyr, and will provide for him, and keep him safe from trials. Recite, if you wish: *Those who emigrated in the cause of Allah and after that were killed or died…*'" — and he recited our two ayat, 58 and 59, in full.

Note where that exchange takes place: soldiers stationed far from home, holding a long siege, being handed an ayah about people who left their homes for Allah.

**A Companion at two graves.** Ibn Abi Hatim also recorded that 'Abdur-Rahman bin Jahdam Al-Khawlani was with Fadalah bin 'Ubayd when they accompanied two funerals — one man had been struck by a catapult, the other had passed away. Fadalah sat by the grave of the man who had passed away. Someone said to him, "Are you neglecting the martyr and not sitting by his grave?" He replied, "I would not mind which of these two graves Allah would resurrect me from," and recited these two ayat, then said: "What should I seek, O you servant, if I were to enter an entrance to His pleasure, and be provided good provisions? By Allah, I would not mind which of these two graves Allah would resurrect me from."

That is a Companion reading these ayat exactly as they are written. The ayah said *killed or died*, so he refused to rank the two graves.

## Living it

**Doubt has an expiry date.** Ayah 55 into 56 makes the point without argument: the doubter is not settling into a permanent, comfortable position. Qatadah's warning is aimed at anyone whose sense of security comes from comfort — being "intoxicated with pride, enjoying a life of luxury," and thinking the punishment will never come.

**Check the harmony.** Ibn Kathir's definition of the saved is worth measuring yourself against: heart believing, action matching knowledge, words and deeds in harmony. It is possible to know a great deal and act on very little; the ayah rewards the ones who "acted in accordance with what they knew."

**Watch for the pride.** The humiliating punishment of ayah 57 is aimed at those who "were too proud to follow" the Messengers — punishment "in recompense for arrogantly turning away from the truth." Refusing a correction because of who is giving it belongs to the same family of sin, in miniature.

**Sacrifice is measured by the leaving, not by the ending.** The single most consoling word in ayat 58–59 is *or*: "killed **or** died." Whoever leaves something behind for Allah — a place, an income, a comfort, a circle of people — and then never sees the outcome he hoped for, is covered by this promise. Maarif ul Quran states it in one line: if they have not benefited in this world, their reward will be there in the Hereafter.

passages.title: Just retaliation and Allah's power to help
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat answer a very practical worry in the heart of a believer who has been wronged: *if I defend myself instead of quietly forgiving, does Allah still stand with me?* Ayah 60 answers yes — and then ayat 61 and 62 tell you **why** that promise is worth anything: because the One making it is Allah, who merges night into day, who hears and sees His servants, who alone is the Truth while everything else people call upon is false.

## The thread that ties the three together

Notice the small word that opens ayah 60: **ذَٰلِكَ — "That is so."** It is a hinge. It looks back at what came before — the promise of a good provision and an entrance they will be well-pleased with, for those who migrated in the cause of Allah and were then killed or died — and it opens a new case: the one who is wronged, hits back within limits, and is then attacked all over again.

Then ayah 61 opens with **ذَٰلِكَ بِأَنَّ — "That is because…"**, and ayah 62 opens the same way. This is a chain of grounding. The help promised in ayah 60 rests on the sovereignty described in ayah 61, and that sovereignty rests on the reality described in ayah 62: Allah is *al-Ḥaqq*, the Truth. Read the three together and you are reading a promise with its foundations laid bare beneath it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points the reader further back still, to ayah 39 of this same sūrah — *"Allah is powerful to give them victory"* (22:39). That earlier ayah, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, mentions that Allah helps those who are wronged unjustly. Ayah 60 extends the promise to a case that might have seemed excluded.

## Ayah 60: the exactness of a just response

The Arabic is worth pausing on:

> **وَمَنْ عَاقَبَ بِمِثْلِ مَا عُوقِبَ بِهِ ثُمَّ بُغِيَ عَلَيْهِ لَيَنصُرَنَّهُ اللَّهُ**
> *"And whoever has retaliated with the like of that which he was made to suffer, and then has again been wronged, Allah will surely help him."* (Ibn Kathir's rendering)

The measure is written into the promise: *bi-mithli mā ʿūqiba bihi* — "with the like of that which he was made to suffer." The response the ayah has in view is not a fresh act of aggression; it is equivalent to the injury received.

And then: **"then he was wronged again" (ثُمَّ بُغِيَ عَلَيْهِ)**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the scenario precisely. Some people bear their sufferings patiently and do not seek vengeance from their oppressors. Others retaliate and serve a full measure of retribution — which should place the two sides on even terms, as being quits. But if the oppressor, *incensed at the retaliation*, attacks him again, then this person once again becomes the victim of oppression. It is that second round the ayah is about. And this verse, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, promises Allah's help for such a person also.

## What actually happened: the fight in the sacred months

Ibn Kathir preserves an occasion of revelation for this ayah. **Muqatil bin Hayan and Ibn Jurayj** mentioned that it was revealed about a skirmish in which the Companions encountered some of the idolaters. The Muslims urged them not to fight during the Sacred Months. The idolaters insisted on fighting and initiated the aggression. So the Muslims fought them, and Allah granted them victory.

Hold that scene next to the wording of the ayah. The Muslims did not choose the fight; they urged that it be avoided. The aggression was initiated against them. And Allah's response was not merely to permit their fighting but to grant them victory.

## The tension the ayah resolves

Here is where this passage becomes spiritually delicate, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān handles it beautifully.

The Qur'an repeatedly praises the person who does *not* hit back. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers the verses:

- *"But whoso pardons and puts things right, his wage falls upon Allah"* (42:40)
- *"And that you forgive is closer to Taqwa"* (2:237)
- *"But surely he who bears patiently and forgives — surely that is true constancy"* (42:43)

In all these verses, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says, it is encouraged not to retaliate for revenge but rather to forgive and forget — a magnanimous way of dealing with fellow human beings. This is the way Qur'anic teachings stand, and they call it a supreme and superior trait.

So a doubt arises, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states it plainly: it may perhaps be argued that the person who retaliates against the wrongs done to him, and so conducts himself contrary to the course of action preferred by Allah, will be deprived of His support and help. Has he not forfeited his claim on Allah's help?

**The end of ayah 60 answers exactly that doubt:** *"Verily, Allah indeed is Oft-Pardoning, Oft-Forgiving"* — إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَعَفُوٌّ غَفُورٌ. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, explains: Allah will not punish him for this lapse, and will help him if he is subjected to injustice by his oppressors ever again.

Sit with how gentle that is. The ayah does not scold the man for taking his right. It does not withdraw the promise. It closes by naming Allah as *ʿAfuww* and *Ghafūr* — Oft-Pardoning, Oft-Forgiving — so that the man who fell short of the preferred road is not left wondering whether he has been dropped. The higher road remains the higher road; but the one who took the permitted road is still under Allah's care.

That is a rare and precious combination: a text that holds up an ideal without weaponising it against the people who did not reach it.

## Ayat 61–62: why this promise can be trusted

Now the passage lifts its eyes from the human quarrel to the One who is over it.

**"That is because Allah merges the night into the day, and He merges the day into the night."**

Why bring up night and day in the middle of a discussion about being wronged? Ibn Kathir's heading tells us the answer: *The Creator and Controller of this World is Allah.* Allah tells us that He is the Creator who directs the affairs of His creation as He wills. Ibn Kathir reads the ayah alongside 3:26–27, which pairs the very same image with the giving and taking of power:

> *"Say: 'O Allah! Possessor of the power, You give power to whom You will, and You take power from whom You will, and You endue with honour whom You will, and You humiliate whom You will. In Your Hand is the good. Verily, You are able to do all things. You make the night to enter into the day, and You make the day to enter into the night…'"*

That pairing is the key. The same hand that shifts the lengths of night and day is the hand that raises one people and brings another low. Ibn Kathir explains the "merging" plainly: it means the one encroaches upon the other, and vice versa — sometimes the night is long and the day short, as in winter; sometimes the day is long and the night short, as in summer.

So when you are the wronged one and the oppressor looks permanently on top, the ayah says: look at the sky. The one who is currently expanding does not own the sky. The turns belong to Allah, and He shifts them.

**"And verily, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Seer."** These are two of the names the ayah gives — *as-Samīʿ* and *al-Baṣīr*. Ibn Kathir's gloss: He hears what His servants say, and He sees them; nothing about them or their movement is hidden from Him whatsoever.

For the wronged person, this is not abstract theology. Every insult spoken about you was heard. Every blow struck at you was seen. Nothing needs to be reported to Allah; He was already there.

**Ayah 62: "That is because Allah — He is the Truth."**

Ibn Kathir places this immediately after telling us that Allah is controlling the affairs of all that exists, and that He judges, and there is none to reverse His judgement. *Al-Ḥaqq*, he explains, means the True One, besides whom no one deserves worship. He is the Possessor of the greatest sovereignty; whatever He wills happens and whatever He does not will does not happen. Everything is in need of Him and submits to Him.

**"And what they invoke besides Him, it is false."** — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, the idols and false gods. Everything that is worshipped instead of Him is false, and he gives the reason: because it can neither bring benefit nor cause harm.

**"And verily, Allah — He is the Most High, the Most Great."** Ibn Kathir connects this to *"and He is the Most High, the Most Great"* (42:4) and *"the Most Great, the Most High"* (13:9), and then states the point with force: everything is subject to His might and power; there is no true deity except Him and no Lord besides Him, because He is the Almighty and there is none mightier than He, the Most High and there is none higher than He, the Most Great and there is none greater than He. Exalted, sanctified and glorified be He far above all that the evildoers say.

## Living it

**Keep the measure.** The permission in ayah 60 is a permission for *the like* of what was done — *bi-mithli mā ʿūqiba bihi*. Once retribution has been served in full measure, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes, the two sides stand on even terms, quits. Exceed the injury and you have moved from the wronged party to the wronging one.

**Know the two roads, and be honest about which one you are on.** Ayah 60 licenses a just response. The verses Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gathers — 42:40, 2:237, 42:43 — point to something higher: pardon, putting things right, patient forbearance, which the Qur'an calls true constancy and which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes as a supreme and superior trait. Taking your right is not sin. Letting it go is greatness.

**Do not let a lapse convince you that you have been abandoned.** This is perhaps the most pastoral thing in the passage. Someone who reacted when he could have forgiven may quietly assume he has forfeited Allah's help. *Innallāha la-ʿAfuwwun Ghafūr* is placed at the end of the ayah precisely to close off that despair — Allah will not punish him for this lapse, and will help him if he is wronged again.

**Read your situation against the sky.** Ayah 61 is the antidote to the feeling that the current arrangement is permanent. Night gives way to day and day to night, at Allah's command, on a schedule He alone sets.

**Locate power where it actually is.** Ayah 62 finishes the passage by draining every rival of substance. Whatever people call upon instead of Allah — an idol, a patron, an institution, a scheme — is *bāṭil*, false, because it can neither bring benefit nor cause harm. He is the Truth; He is the Most High; He is the Most Great. If the promise of help in ayah 60 rests on Him, it rests on the only thing that is not going to give way.

passages.title: Rain, ships and life as signs of lordship
passages.tafsir:
Four ayat that ask you to look — at rain falling on dead ground, at ships crossing open sea, at a sky that does not fall, at your own life and death — and to draw the obvious conclusion: the One who does all this is the only one worthy of worship. What holds them together is a single argument, built step by step, from the ground under your feet up to the sky above you and forward to the Day you will be raised.

## The shape of the argument

In Ibn Kathir's commentary these four ayat are handled together, quoted as one block and then unpacked phrase by phrase. The section carries the heading **"Signs of the Power of Allah"**, and his first sentence sets the tone: this is "a further sign of His might and power" — a continuation of the evidence the surah has already been laying out.

Watch how the argument climbs:

- **Ayah 63** — dead earth turns green: Allah acts in the smallest hidden places (*Laṭīf, Khabīr*).
- **Ayah 64** — everything in the heavens and earth is His: He owns it all and needs none of it ("Rich, Worthy of all praise").
- **Ayah 65** — all of it is put at your service, and the sky is held back from crushing you: He is kind to you even in your wrongdoing (*Raʾūf, Raḥīm*).
- **Ayah 66** — He gave you life, will take it, and will give it back again — closing on the verdict *"Verily, man is indeed Kafūrun."*

Four things you have already seen, offered as evidence for one conclusion.

## "Do you not see?" — ayah 63 and ayah 65

Twice in this passage the address begins **أَلَمْ تَرَ** — *"Do you not see…"* (ayah 63, and again ayah 65). It is not asking for information. It is pointing. The evidence is not hidden in a book or a philosopher's argument; it is the weather, the harbour, the graveyard. You have already seen it.

**Rain on dead ground.** Ibn Kathir describes the process concretely: Allah "sends the winds to drive the clouds which deliver rain to the barren land where nothing grows, land which is dry, dusty and desiccated." He links it to what came earlier in this same surah:

> *"but when We send down water on it, it is stirred (to life), and it swells"* (22:5)

Then: *"and then the earth becomes green"* — meaning, as Ibn Kathir puts it, "it becomes green after being dry and lifeless." He notes a detail reported "from some of the people of Al-Hijaz, that the land turns green after rainfall," and closes it with the scholar's honest formula, *"And Allah knows best."*

**Stage after stage.** Of the phrase "and then the earth becomes green," Ibn Kathir says simply that it "indicates the sequence of events and how everything follows on according to its nature." Rain does not become greenery in one leap; it becomes greenery by a process, stage after stage, each stage waiting on the one before it. To make the point he sets beside it the stages of your own making:

> *"Then We made the Nutfah into a clot, then We made the clot into a little lump of flesh"* (23:14)

(The commentary leaves the first stage, *Nutfah*, in Arabic — the word for the earliest stage of the human being named in the ayah, before the clot and the lump of flesh. What matters here is the ordering: one stage, then the next, then the next.)

And he adds that "it was recorded in the Two Sahihs that between each stage there are forty days." The same patient, staged unfolding that turns that first drop into a human being turns a rainstorm into a green field. You were made the way the spring is made.

## *Laṭīf* and *Khabīr* — the One who reaches the buried seed

Why does ayah 63 close with these two names rather than, say, names of sheer power? Ibn Kathir's answer is one of the most beautiful passages in his comment here.

*Laṭīf* is rendered "the Most Kind and Courteous" — and, in the ayah from Luqman he quotes just below, "Subtle": the One whose action is so fine, so delicate, that it reaches into places nothing else can reach. *Khabīr* is "Well-Acquainted with all things," the One whose knowledge goes to the inside of a thing, not just its surface.

Ibn Kathir explains: **"He knows what seeds are in the various regions of the earth, no matter how small they are. Nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him. Each of those seeds receives its share of water and begins to grow."**

Sit with that. The rain does not fall on "the earth" in general. It falls on this seed, and that one, and one buried under a rock on a hillside nobody has walked on — and each gets its share. That is what *Laṭīf Khabīr* means in practice: a knowledge and a gentleness fine enough to find every individual thing.

Ibn Kathir gathers the ayat that say the same:

> *"O my son! If it be equal to the weight of a grain of mustard seed, and though it be in a rock, or in the heavens or in the earth, Allah will bring it forth. Verily, Allah is Subtle, Well-Aware."* (31:16 — Luqman to his son)

> *"not a leaf falls, but He knows it. There is not a grain in the darkness of the earth nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record."* (6:59)

> *"And nothing is hidden from your Lord, the weight of a speck of dust on the earth or in the heaven…"* (10:61)

And he cites *"…so they do not worship Allah, Who brings to light what is hidden in the heavens and the earth"* (27:25) — where the very ayah describing this attribute is set against those who fail to worship Him. The One who reaches the seed under the rock is not someone you can hide a grief from, or a sin.

## Ayah 64: He owns it, and He does not need it

*"To Him belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is on the earth."* Ibn Kathir: **"He owns all things, and He has no need of anything besides Himself, everything is in need of Him and in a state of submission to Him."**

That is the exact sense of the two descriptions closing the ayah: "Rich" — self-sufficient, needing nothing; "Worthy of all praise." The relationship runs one way. Nothing you offer Him adds to Him; everything He gives you, you cannot survive without. This sits between the rain of ayah 63 and the service of ayah 65: before you are told that the world works for you, you are told whose world it is, and that He gains nothing by lending it.

## Ayah 65: what "subjected to you" actually means

*"See you not that Allah has subjected to you all that is on the earth."* Ibn Kathir specifies what is meant: **"animals, inanimate things, crops and fruits,"** and reads it alongside *"And has subjected to you all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth"* (45:13) — adding that "all of this is a blessing and out of His kindness."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here on an objection an honest reader will raise. If everything on earth is "subjugated" to man, why do the mountains, rivers, beasts and birds not follow a single human command?

The answer turns on the word itself. **Taskhīr** — subjugation — is used here, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, in the sense of **"to serve."** "Placing something in the service of someone is also like putting it under his control." The verse means "that all the things mentioned above are all the time working in the service of man by the command of Allah."

And then the commentary makes a striking point about why it was *not* arranged the other way:

> It was well within Allah's power to place these things literally under human command — "but in such a situation man himself would have been the loser, because human natures, desires and needs differ. If a person ordered the river to divert towards a particular direction, and some other person ordered to the contrary, the result would have been utter chaos and confusion."

So, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān concludes, "Allah Ta'ala has retained with Him alone the command of these things, but the benefits to be derived from them accrue to human beings." You get the harvest without the burden of running the seasons. The command stays with the One whose will is one; the benefit comes to the many. Not being in charge of the universe is itself a mercy to you.

**"By His command."** This is why the ships in ayah 65 sail *bi-amrihi*. Ibn Kathir: it is "because He subjugates it to them and makes it easy for them. In the raging sea with its tempestuous waves, the ships sail gently with their passengers and carry them wherever they want to go for trading and other purposes from one land to another, so that they bring goods from here to there, or vice versa, whatever people want or need."

Note the contrast he builds: the sea is *raging*, its waves *tempestuous* — and across it the ship moves *gently*. Nothing has calmed the ocean. What has happened is that the ship has been made easy for its passengers on a force that would otherwise overwhelm them, so that ordinary people can carry ordinary cargo to people who need it. Trade, travel, supply — the ordinary movement of goods from one land to another — is here presented as a standing mercy you have stopped noticing.

**And the sky that does not fall.** *"He withholds the heaven from falling on the earth except by His leave."* Ibn Kathir does not soften this: **"If He willed, He could give the sky permission to fall on the earth, and whoever is in it would be killed, but by His kindness, mercy and power, He withholds the heaven from falling on the earth, except by His leave."**

Every other sign in this passage is something given to you. This one is something withheld from you. The safety you take as the baseline of existence — the ceiling of the world staying where it is, hour after hour, for your entire life — is not a default state. It is an act, continuously performed.

Hence the two names that close the ayah: *Raʾūf, Raḥīm*, "full of kindness, Most Merciful." Ibn Kathir adds the crucial two words: **"meaning, even though they do wrong."** The sky is held up over people who deny the One holding it. He cites:

> *"But verily, your Lord is full of forgiveness for mankind in spite of their wrongdoing. And verily, your Lord is severe in punishment."* (13:6)

Both halves of that ayah are there. The forbearance is real, and it is not indifference.

## Ayah 66: your own body as the final proof

*"It is He, Who gave you life, and then will cause you to die, and will again give you life."*

Ibn Kathir unpacks each link. *"He gave you life"* means **"He gave you life after you were nothing, and brought you into existence."** *"then will cause you to die, and will again give you life"* — the second giving of life is **"on the Day of Resurrection."**

This is the argument closing the circle. It began in ayah 63 with dead ground brought back to green life by water sent from above. It ends with dead people brought back to life by the same Hand. If you have watched the first, you have already watched the answer to your doubts about the second.

Ibn Kathir sets beside it three ayat that state the same sequence, including one where the sequence itself is the rebuke:

> *"How can you disbelieve in Allah? Seeing that you were dead and He gave you life. Then He will give you death, then again will bring you to life and then unto Him you will return."* (2:28)

> *"Say: 'Allah gives you life, then causes you to die, then He will assemble you on the Day of Resurrection about which there is no doubt.'"* (45:26)

> *"They will say: 'Our Lord! You have made us to die twice, and You have given us life twice!'"* (40:11)

Having laid those three side by side, he turns the sequence into a question and puts it to the reader: **"So how can you set up rivals to Allah and worship others besides Him when He is the One Who is independent in His powers of creation, provision and control of the existence?"** If your very existence — start, end, and second start — is entirely in His hands, there is no room left in the picture for a rival to Him.

**"Verily, man is indeed Kafūrun."** Ibn Kathir glosses the word in one word: **"denying."** And that is precisely what the passage has been describing. Rain, ships, an unfallen sky, a life given from nothing: every one of them plainly in view, every one of them passed off as ordinary. The charge is not that the human being lacks evidence. It is that he has the evidence and denies it anyway.

## Living it

- **Let ordinary things function as evidence.** These ayat do not send you searching for a sign; they hand you four you have already seen this week. Rain on a dry patch. A cargo ship. Waking up. The discipline the passage asks for is attention, not information.
- **Read the names as descriptions of your own life.** *Laṭīf Khabīr* is not an abstraction — it is the One who gets water to a seed you never knew existed, and who therefore knows what is buried in you. *Raʾūf Raḥīm* is not sentiment — it is a sky held in place over people who wrong Him, "even though they do wrong."
- **Take the comfort in not being in charge.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is worth carrying: if the world took your orders it would ruin you, because your orders and everyone else's would collide. Allah kept the command and gave you the benefit. That is a mercy to lean on when you cannot control your circumstances.
- **Let ayah 66 settle the question of resurrection.** The One who gave you existence "after you were nothing" is not strained by giving it a second time. The barren land in ayah 63 is the rehearsal; you are the performance.
- **Watch for denial as a habit before it is a creed.** Ibn Kathir's gloss — "denying" — describes a way of living: receiving constantly and acknowledging rarely. The cure the passage implies is the one it keeps modelling: *see*, and then say so.

passages.title: Do not be drawn into their quarrel
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These six ayat are Allah's instruction to His Messenger ﷺ on how to carry himself when opponents try to drag him into an argument about the divine law he has brought. The thread that holds them together is a single strategy: **do not be pulled into the quarrel — keep calling, hand the judgement over to Allah, and remember who is really watching.** Ayah 67 states the principle (every community was given its own prescribed way, so the argument is misconceived); ayah 68 gives the Prophet ﷺ the words to end the exchange; ayah 69 defers the verdict to the Day of Resurrection; ayah 70 grounds that deferral in the totality of Allah's knowledge; and ayat 71–72 turn the mirror on the disputants themselves — people who worship what they cannot justify, whose faces darken at revelation, and who are nearly ready to use their hands.

## Ayah 67: what "mansak" means

**"For every community We appointed a *mansak* which they follow…"**

Ibn Kathir relates from Ibn Jarir that this means every prophet's nation had its own *mansak*. Ibn Jarir explains the root sense: in Arabic *mansik* originally denotes **the place to which a person returns repeatedly**, whether for good or for evil purposes. That is why the rites of Hajj are called *manāsik* — because people return to them and hold fast to them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the same lexical point from Ibn Kathir with a slightly different emphasis: *mansak* means **a place fixed for a specific purpose**, good or bad, and the rites of pilgrimage take the name because each rite has to be performed at the place fixed for it. Maʿārif then adds the other strand of the word's meaning: the dictionary sense is **piety and the worship of Allah**, and it is in that sense that the Qur'anic words *"And show us our ways of worship"* (2:128) are used — *manāsik* there meaning the rules governing worship.

So the word carries a feel of something **fixed, appointed, and habitually returned to** — not a passing custom but a prescribed track that a community walks.

**A deliberate echo, and a deliberate difference.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that almost these same words appeared earlier in this very surah, at ayah 34 — but there *mansak* was used in the context of the Hajj rites and meant the **sacrifice of animals**, whereas here it carries the sense of the rules of slaughter or the general rules of worship. And there is a small grammatical fingerprint of that difference: unlike ayah 34, the present ayah does not open with the connective *wāw* ("and"). It is not continuing the earlier thought; it is starting a fresh one.

## Two readings of the ayah — and why they agree

**The first reading (an occasion of revelation).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī, reports that the idolaters used to engage the Muslims in futile arguments about the slaughter of animals. Their objection had a certain sneering cleverness to it: *you Muslims are permitted to eat the meat of animals you slaughter with your own hands, but forbidden to eat the meat of animals that Allah Himself has killed* — meaning carrion. On this reading, *mansak* here means **the method of slaughter**, and the ayah is the answer: Allah gave each nation a code of laws, and the rules governing slaughter differ from code to code.
