The rules given to the Prophet ﷺ are independent and self-sufficient; it is not permissible to compare them with those of an earlier Sharīʿah, let alone with somebody's own whims and conjectures. And in any case, Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī notes, the use of dead animals as food was forbidden in all the earlier codes too — so to argue with the Prophet ﷺ on that basis is, in Maʿārif's blunt phrase, sheer ignorance.

**The second reading (the majority).** Most commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, take *mansak* here to mean **the general rules of the Sharīʿah**. Sayyidnā Ibn ʿAbbās رضي الله عنه also adopted this second interpretation, and it is the meaning taken by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Kathir, Qurtubi and Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī — and, as Maʿārif observes, the context of the ayah supports it. On this reading the ayah answers a broader objection: the idolaters and disbelievers who dispute the Islamic code of laws *on the ground that their own ancestral religion did not include them*. The reply is that any comparison between an older Book or Sharīʿah and the new one is totally misplaced and irrelevant. Allah granted each nation, in its own time, a special Sharīʿah and a Book binding upon it **until another Book or Sharīʿah arrived** — after which following the new one becomes everyone's duty, and where the new rules conflict with the old, the new prevail and the old stand invalidated. Nobody has the right to raise a dispute about this with the Prophet ﷺ, who is the recipient of the latest Book and Sharīʿah.

**Ibn Kathir's further nuance.** He notes that the phrase can also be read as a statement about *Qadar* — divine decree — comparable to *"For each nation there is a direction to which they face"* (2:148). On that reading, **هُمْ نَاسِكُوهُ** ("which they *Nasikuh*") means "which they must act upon," the pronoun referring back to those who have these ways and ceremonies: they do this **by the will and decree of Allah**. And so, Ibn Kathir concludes, *do not let their dispute with you over that divert you from following the truth.* This is worth pausing on: the fact that people are on different paths is itself within Allah's decree. That knowledge is not meant to unsettle you — it is meant to steady you.

**No real contradiction.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reconciles the two readings elegantly: the ayah may well have been revealed with reference to a specific dispute about the slaughter of animals, but as a general rule **words are interpreted in the sense in which common people understand them, not in reference to a particular event**. So the wording can be construed to apply to all the laws of the Sharīʿah. Either way the essence of both interpretations is one: each nation was given its own particular set of rules, differences of detail genuinely exist, the latest set is binding on all peoples, and issues relating to those differences cannot be raised.

## "So let them not quarrel with you"

**فَلَا يُنَازِعُنَّكَ فِي الْأَمْرِ** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: *they should never quarrel with you in the matter.* The meaning, it explains, is that now that the Prophet ﷺ has brought a new Book and a new code of laws, **no one has the right to dispute them or to create any confusion about them.**

Note the shape of the command. It is not "argue them into silence." It is: *this dispute has no legitimate ground* — and then immediately, **"but invite them to your Lord."** Ibn Kathir explains **إِنَّكَ لَعَلَىٰ هُدًى مُّسْتَقِيمٍ** ("you indeed are on the straight guidance") as meaning a **clear and straight path which will lead you to the desired end**. He pairs it with 28:87, *"And let them not turn you away from the Ayat of Allah after they have been sent down to you — and invite to your Lord."*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sums up the counsel to the Prophet ﷺ: **take no notice of the machinations and disputes raised by the infidels; continue with the mission** — because he was following the path of righteousness whereas his opponents were steeped in error.

## A doubt, and its answer

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious objection. Ayah 67 says Allah granted earlier nations their own Sharīʿah — the Mosaic Code and the Christian Code are instances in point. Could Jews and Christians then argue that their codes, being divine too, should be allowed to exist alongside the Islamic Code?

The answer given is that this is a fallacious argument, because it is a well-established fact that **an earlier Sharīʿah is cancelled by a subsequent one**. And Maʿārif points out that the ayat that follow reinforce exactly this — those who challenge the Islamic Sharīʿah are warned of severe chastisement, beginning with ayah 68.

## Ayah 68: the sentence that closes the argument

**"And if they dispute with you, then say: Allah knows best what you do."**

This is the practical instruction, and it is remarkable for what it does *not* say. The Prophet ﷺ is not told to refute point by point. He is told to step out of the exchange with a single sentence that transfers the file to a higher court.

Ibn Kathir places it alongside 10:41 — *"And if they belie you, say: For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds! You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do!"* The posture is disengagement, not surrender.

But do not mistake mildness for softness. Ibn Kathir states plainly that **"Allah knows best of what you do" is a stern warning and a definite threat**, comparable to 46:8 — *"He knows best of what you say among yourselves concerning it! Sufficient is He as a witness between me and you!"* The sentence sounds like a shrug and lands like a summons.

## Ayah 69: the verdict is scheduled, not skipped

**"Allah will judge between you on the Day of Resurrection about that wherein you used to differ."**

This is what makes the disengagement of ayah 68 bearable rather than bitter. The argument is not being abandoned; it is being **adjourned to the only session that decides anything**. Ibn Kathir links it to 42:15 — *"So unto this then invite, and stand firm as you are commanded, and follow not their desires but say: I believe in whatsoever Allah has sent down of the Book."* Invite, stand firm, do not chase their desires — the same three movements as here.

## Ayah 70: why you can safely leave the judgement to Him

**"Know you not that Allah knows all that is in the heaven and on the earth? Verily, it is all in the Book. Verily, that is easy for Allah."**

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah is telling us **how perfect His knowledge of His creation is, and that He encompasses all that is in the heavens and on earth**. Not even the weight of a speck of dust, or less than that or greater, escapes His knowledge in the heavens or in the earth. He knows all things **even before they happen**, and He has written that in His Book, *al-Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ* — the Preserved Tablet.

Ibn Kathir cites in support what was reported in **Sahih Muslim** from ʿAbdullah bin ʿAmr, who said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"Allah issued His decrees concerning the measurement and due proportion of the creatures fifty thousand years before He created the heavens and the earth, and His Throne was over the water."*

And he cites what was reported **in the Sunan** from a group of the Companions, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> *"The first thing that Allah created was the Pen. He said to it, 'Write!' It said, 'What should I write?' He said, 'Write what will happen,' so the Pen wrote everything that will happen until the Day of Resurrection."*

**"Verily, that is easy for Allah."** The closing phrase is the emotional pivot of the ayah. To a human being, keeping an exhaustive record of every deed of every disputant across every century would be an impossible burden. For Allah it is *yasīr* — easy, effortless, no strain at all. Which is precisely why ayah 68 is not evasion. Nothing gets lost while you walk away from a pointless argument.

## Ayah 71: their position has no evidence behind it

**"And they worship besides Allah others for which He has sent down no authority (*sulṭān*), and of which they have no knowledge."**

Ibn Kathir explains that the idolaters do this **in their ignorance and disbelief**, and that "no authority" means **no proof or evidence** for such behaviour. He compares it with 23:117, *"And whoever calls upon, besides Allah, any other god, of whom he has no proof; then his reckoning is only with his Lord. Surely, the disbelievers will not be successful."*

Then the second clause, **"and of which they have no knowledge"**: Ibn Kathir says they have **no knowledge in the subject that they fabricate lies about**. It is only something **handed down to them from their fathers and ancestors, with no evidence or proof**, and its origins lie in **what the Shayṭān beautified for them and made attractive to them**.

Notice the reversal the passage has performed. They came demanding that the Prophet ﷺ justify a rule of slaughter, or a law that their ancestors never knew. Ayah 71 quietly turns the question around: *what is the evidence for your own position?* There is none — only inheritance and the ornamentation of Shayṭān. The people making the loudest demand for proof were standing on nothing.

**"And for the wrongdoers there is no helper."** Ibn Kathir: **no one to help them against Allah** when He sends His punishment and torment upon them. They may have allies against the believers now; against Allah they will have none.

## Ayah 72: the face gives it away, and the threat that boomerangs

**"And when Our clear Ayat are recited to them, you will notice a denial on the faces of the disbelievers! They are nearly ready to attack with violence those who recite Our Ayat to them."**

Ibn Kathir explains that this happens when **the Ayat of the Qur'an and clear evidence and proof for the Tawhid of Allah are mentioned to them** — when they are told that there is no god besides Allah and that the Messengers spoke the truth. And their reaction is written on their faces before a word is said.

**يَكَادُونَ يَسْطُونَ** — "they are nearly ready to attack with violence." Ibn Kathir describes it as nearly attacking and doing harm to those who bring them proof from the Qur'an, **causing them harm using their tongues and hands**. This is what argument becomes when someone has no evidence and knows it: the case moves from the mind to the fist. That is the state of the very people ayah 67 told the Prophet ﷺ not to be drawn into quarrelling with — and it explains why. There was never a discussion on offer.

**The answer that turns the threat inside out.** Then comes the instruction — Ibn Kathir: *"Say, O Muhammad, to these people"* —

**"Shall I tell you of something worse than that? The Fire which Allah has promised to those who disbelieved, and worst indeed is that destination!"**

Ibn Kathir unpacks it beautifully. **The Fire and the wrath and torment of Allah are far worse than that with which you are trying to scare the believing close friends of Allah in this world.** You are brandishing violence as the worst thing imaginable — let me tell you what is genuinely worse. The punishment in the Hereafter for these very deeds of yours is worse than what you claim you want to do to the believers.

And **"worst indeed is that destination"** — Ibn Kathir: how terrible the Fire is as a final destination and abode, echoing *"Evil indeed it is as an abode and as a place to rest in"* (25:66).

## Living it

The passage is a complete posture for anyone who carries the truth into hostile company.

- **Recognise a quarrel that is not really about evidence.** Ayah 71 exposes the disputants as having neither *sulṭān* nor knowledge, only what was handed down from their forefathers and what Shayṭān made attractive to them; ayah 72 shows the argument sliding towards the fist. Some disputes have no bottom, and Allah's own instruction to His Messenger ﷺ was not to be dragged into them.
- **Do not confuse leaving an argument with abandoning the mission.** The command in ayah 67 is not "be silent" — it is **"invite them to your Lord."** The energy is redirected, not switched off. As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it, take no notice of their machinations and continue with the work.
- **Learn the closing sentence.** *"Allah knows best what you do"* — a phrase that ends the exchange without conceding anything and without descending into it. Ibn Kathir reminds us it is, in truth, a stern warning and a definite threat.
- **Draw your calm from ayah 70.** You can walk away from an unwinnable argument because nothing is being lost. It is all in the Book, and for Allah that is easy.
- **Keep the real stakes in view.** Whatever anyone can threaten you with in this world, ayah 72 names something worse — and it is not aimed at you.

passages.title: They have not valued Allah as He deserves
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Allah addresses all people — *yā ayyuhā al-nās*, "O humanity" — and sets before them a single, devastating illustration: everything they call upon besides Allah could pool all their power and still not produce one fly, nor even recover what a fly steals from them. From that image the passage draws its verdict — *they have not valued Allah as He deserves* — and then turns from the powerlessness of what people worship to the One who genuinely reaches His creation: Allah, who *chooses* messengers from among the angels and from among people, who hears and sees, who knows what lies before and behind them, and to whom every matter returns.

Ibn Kathir sums up the opening in one line: here Allah points out **the insignificance of the idols and the foolishness of those who worship them.** And the four ayat together answer a single question: *who is actually capable?* The parable answers it from below, by showing what these objects of worship cannot do. The closing ayat answer it from above, by showing what only Allah does.

## "A lesson is set forth, so listen to it"

Ibn Kathir explains that this is "a parable of that which is worshipped by those who are ignorant of Allah and who join others as partners with Him," and that the command *fa-stamiʿū lahu* ("so listen to it") means **pay attention and understand** — not merely hear the words, but let them land.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a precise note on the opening phrase *ḍuriba mathal*. Ordinarily that expression is used for quoting an incident as an example. Here it is not used in that sense; rather, the foolishness of idol-worship is illustrated by citing a *parable* — a constructed image whose whole purpose is to make an absurdity visible.

**Why a fly.** The point of the image is its smallness. Ibn Kathir: even if all the idols and false gods they worship "were to come together to create a single fly, they would not be able to do that." Notice the concession built into the wording — *wa-lawi ijtamaʿū lahu*, "even though they combine together for the purpose." The parable does not pit one idol against Allah; it grants them every advantage, lets them cooperate, and *still* the task is out of reach. And the task is not a heaven or a human being. It is a fly, which Ibn Kathir describes as "the weakest and most insignificant of Allah's creatures."

**Then it gets worse.** Creation is one thing; even self-defence is beyond them. *And if the fly snatches away a thing from them, they will have no power to release it from the fly.* Ibn Kathir explains that they are unable to resist it or take revenge against it if it takes anything from the good and perfumed thing on which it lands; "if they wanted to recover that, they would not be able to."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the everyday scene concrete: these idols cannot even protect the offerings of food which their worshippers bring them daily against the inroads of flies. And then it presses the obvious question — **then how can they protect you from any calamity?**

## "So weak are the seeker and the sought"

The ayah closes with a short, hard clause: *ḍaʿufa al-ṭālib wa-l-maṭlūb* — feeble are the one who seeks and the one who is sought. The commentators differ on who is who, and the difference is worth knowing, because each reading yields a different sting.

- **Ibn ʿAbbās** said: "The seeker is the idol and the sought is the fly." Ibn Kathir notes that this was the view favoured by **Ibn Jarīr**, and that it is what is apparent from the context — the idol is the one trying, and failing, to retrieve what the fly took.
- **As-Suddī and others** said: "The seeker is the worshipper, and the sought is the idol." On this reading the weakness moves up a level — the worshipper who comes seeking, and the object he seeks from.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic of that second sense plainly: if the object of worship is so utterly weak and powerless, those worshipping it must be more so. A person cannot be stronger than what he leans on.

## From the Sunnah: "Let them create an ant, or a fly"

Ibn Kathir brings the parable's theme in the Prophet's ﷺ own teaching. **Imam Ahmad** recorded that **Abū Hurayrah** recorded the *marfūʿ* report — *marfūʿ* meaning a report traced up to the Prophet ﷺ — that Allah says: *"Who does more wrong than one who tries to create something like My creation? Let them create an ant or a fly or a seed like My creation!"*

Ibn Kathir adds that this was also recorded by **the authors of the Two Ṣaḥīḥs**, via ʿUmārah, from Abū Zurʿah, from Abū Hurayrah, who said that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: *"Who does more wrong than one who tries to create (something) like My creation? Let them create an ant, let them create a grain of barley."*

The challenge is the same as the parable's, and the smallness is the whole argument: an ant, a fly, a grain of barley.

## The verdict: "They have not valued Allah as He deserves"

*Mā qadarū Allāha ḥaqqa qadrih.* Ibn Kathir glosses it: "they have not recognized the might and power of Allah when they worship alongside Him those who cannot even ward off a fly, because they are so weak and incapable." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it in terms of both foolishness and ingratitude: these people are so foolish and ungrateful that they did not recognise the power of Allah Taʿālā, and placed their helpless idols at the same level with Him.

This is the hinge of the passage. Shirk — associating others with Allah in worship — is presented here as a **failure of estimation**: a catastrophic misjudgement of who Allah is. To set anything alongside Him is, by that very act, to have measured Him wrongly.

**Then His two names close the ayah.**

*Al-Qawiyy* — the All-Strong. Ibn Kathir: "He is the All-Strong Who, by His might and power, created all things." He brings other ayat alongside it to fill out the sense: *And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him* (30:27); *Verily, the punishment of your Lord is severe and painful. Verily, He it is Who begins and repeats* (85:12–13); *Verily, Allah is the Provider, Owner of power, the Most Strong* (51:58). Strength here is not an abstraction — it is originating, repeating, and providing.

*Al-ʿAzīz* — the All-Mighty. Ibn Kathir: "He has subjugated and subdued all things, and there is none that can resist Him or overcome His might and power, and He is the One, the Subduer." Set that against the fly: on one side, objects of worship that cannot retrieve a stolen drop of perfume; on the other, the One whom nothing in existence can resist.

*(A note in my own words, not from the commentaries quoted above: these are names Allah gave Himself, and the way of Ahl al-Sunnah is to affirm them as they came — without likening His strength to the strength of creatures, and without emptying the words of their meaning.)*

## The turn: how Allah actually reaches His creation

Having shown the impotence of what people call upon, the passage turns to the real channel between Allah and mankind. **Allah *chooses*** — the ayah's own verb, *yaṣṭafī*. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah tells us He chooses Messengers from His angels as He wills, by His law and decree, and chooses Messengers from mankind to convey His Message. The idols in the parable could not so much as retrieve a stolen thing; Allah appoints both the angelic carriers of revelation and the human beings who deliver it.

**"Verily, Allah is All-Hearer, All-Seer."** Ibn Kathir: this means He hears all that His servants say, and He sees them and knows who among them is deserving of that. He cites: *Allah knows best with whom to place His Message* (6:124). The choice rests on a knowledge of people that no observer could match.

**"He knows what is before them, and what is behind them."** Ibn Kathir reads this of the messengers: He knows what will happen to His Messengers and the Message He sent them with, for none of their affairs are hidden from Him. He brings *The All-Knower of the Ghayb — the Unseen, what is beyond all created perception — and He reveals to none His Ghayb* (72:26) through to *and He keeps count of all things* (72:28), and concludes: so He, may He be glorified, is **guarding** them, and is **Witness** to what is said about them; He is **protecting them and supporting them.** He then cites the promise made explicit to the Prophet ﷺ: *O Messenger! Proclaim what has been sent down to you from your Lord. And if you do not, then you have not conveyed His Message. Allah will protect you from mankind* (5:67).

**"And to Allah return all matters."** The passage ends where every matter ends — with the One who is All-Strong, All-Mighty, All-Hearing, All-Seeing, and from whom no affair is hidden.

## Living it

**Ask what you actually lean on.** The parable's method is to measure a claimed source of help against the smallest real task. Anything a person turns to with the reliance that belongs to Allah alone can be put in the same sentence: could it create a fly? Could it get back what a fly took?

**Treat mis-estimating Allah as the root problem.** *They have not valued Allah as He deserves* names the disease beneath the symptom. Growth in tawḥīd — holding Allah alone as the true deity and directing worship to Him alone — is largely growth in rightly weighing Him: His strength (*al-Qawiyy*) and the might nothing can resist (*al-ʿAzīz*).

**Take the command literally.** *So listen to it* — Ibn Kathir says: pay attention and understand. The parable only works on someone willing to actually picture it.

**Rest in the last ayah.** If Allah knows what is before and behind His messengers, guards them, is Witness to what is said about them, and protects and supports them — and if to Him all matters return — then the believer carrying that same Message into an unwelcoming room is not carrying it alone.

passages.title: Bow, prostrate, and strive as He deserves
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat close Sūrah al-Hajj. They are a final address to the believers: worship Him with your bodies, strive for Him with everything you have, and know who you are and Whose you are. Ayah 77 is the command to worship; ayah 78 is the command to strive, followed by four reasons that make both commands bearable and honourable: Allah chose you, He put no crushing burden on you, He named you, and He remains your Protector.

## Ayah 77: bodies before arguments

"O believers! Bow down, prostrate yourselves, worship your Lord, and do good — that you may be successful."

Notice the order. Before any theology or any battlefield, Allah names two physical postures: rukūʿ (bowing) and sujūd (prostration). Then He widens out — "worship your Lord" — and widens again — "do good": from the specific act, to the whole worshipping life, to every act of benefit. The Tafsir Ibn Kathir excerpt carries these two ayat under a single section heading, "The Command to worship Allah and engage in Jihad," treating them as one instruction with two halves.

**Is this a verse of prostration?** It affects what you do when you recite it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains: verse 18 of this sūrah is a verse of sajdah by the consensus of the jurists — whoever recites it or hears it recited must make a prostration. The present verse is disputed. Imam Abu Hanifah, Imam Malik and Sufyan al-Thawrī (may Allah have mercy on them) held that it is not a verse of recitation-prostration, and their reasoning is linguistic: here "prostrate" comes paired with "bow," and that pairing signals the ordinary sajdah performed inside the prayer, not a standalone prostration of recitation. They point to a case all scholars agree on — the words "And prostrate and bow down with those who bow" (3:43) — where the sajdah is unanimously understood as the prayer's own prostration.

Imam al-Shāfiʿī and Imam Ahmad (may Allah have mercy on them) held the contrary view, citing a hadith according to which Sūrah al-Hajj has a position of greater merit than other sūrahs because of two verses of sajdah occurring in it. Ibn Kathir gives that report from ʿUqbah bin ʿĀmir, that the Prophet ﷺ said, "Sūrat al-Hajj has been blessed with two Sajdahs" — while noting that the added clause, "so whoever does not prostrate them should not read them," is considered unauthentic. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that Imam Abu Hanifah questioned the authenticity of this hadith.

This is a genuine difference among the imams. Follow what your madhhab or your teacher tells you; do not treat either side as an error.

## Ayah 78: "strive as He deserves"

**وَجَاهِدُوا فِي اللَّهِ حَقَّ جِهَادِهِ** — "And strive hard in Allah's cause as you ought to strive."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word. *Jihād* and *mujāhadah* mean to exert one's utmost effort to achieve an objective and to take pains for it. Warfare against the disbelievers is called jihād precisely because the Muslims make supreme efforts in it.

Then the qualifier: **ḥaqqa jihādihi**, "a struggle that is due to Him." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that this means all such effort and sacrifice must aim solely at winning the favours and goodwill of Allah, free of every consideration of worldly reward — such as fame or spoils of war. The measure of your striving is not how hard it looked to others but Whom it was for. Ibn Kathir sets this phrase beside a twin from Āl ʿImrān: "Have taqwā of Allah as is His due" (3:102). Both refuse to name a ceiling. They do not say "strive a lot": they say strive by a standard set by Him, not by you.

**What does the striving cover?** The answers are complementary; better to hold them together than pick one.

- **Ibn Kathir:** "with your wealth and your tongues and your bodies." Three currencies — what you own, what you say, what you can physically do. Everyone has at least one.
- **Ibn ʿAbbās** (as reported in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān): to strive to the utmost of one's capacity in the course of jihād, unmindful of all criticism.
- **Some other commentators:** that one exerts his utmost effort in carrying out the acts of worship and in full obedience to the rules of the Sharīʿah, in all sincerity.
- **Al-Ḍaḥḥāk and Muqātil:** that it means to act in Allah's obedience and worship as is due to Him.
- **ʿAbdullāh Ibn al-Mubārak:** that jihād here means to strive against the *nafs* — the self and its baser desires.

On that last view, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that Imam al-Baghawī supported it with a hadith he has from Jābir Ibn ʿAbdullāh that when a group of Companions returned from jihād, the Prophet ﷺ said they had returned from a smaller jihād to a greater jihād — meaning that the fight against the temptations of the self and its baser desires never ceases. **Be careful with this report:** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān itself states that al-Bayhaqī also related it and was of the opinion that it has some weak narrators. Tafsīr Mazharī adopted this interpretation and observed that the Muslims were in fact fighting the coarse desires of the self even while engaged in jihād against the disbelievers — the point of the hadith placing it *after* their return being that this inner fight, though it continued on the battlefield, could be brought to fruition only under the watchful eye of a perfect spiritual guide, the Prophet ﷺ himself.

So the passage does not permit either extreme: not a religion of exertion without inwardness, and not an inwardness that never costs you anything.

## "He has chosen you"

**هُوَ اجْتَبَاكُمْ.** Ibn Kathir paraphrases the address: O Ummah of Islam, Allah has selected you and chosen you over all other nations, favoured you, blessed you, and honoured you with the noblest of Messengers and the noblest of Laws.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān places this choosing in a longer chain of choosing, reporting from Wāthilah Ibn al-Asqaʿ (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said Allah chose Kinānah from the children of Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him), then chose Quraysh from Kinānah, then Banū Hāshim from Quraysh, and from Banū Hāshim He chose him ﷺ (Muslim, via Mazharī). Selection is how Allah has always worked; you are standing at the end of that line, not at its beginning.

Note the logic of the sentence: the choosing is given as the *reason* for the striving. You are not striving to earn the status. The status is already given; the striving is what you do with it.

## "He has not laid upon you in religion any hardship"

**وَمَا جَعَلَ عَلَيْكُمْ فِي الدِّينِ مِنْ حَرَجٍ.** Ibn ʿAbbās glossed *ḥaraj* simply: "This means difficulty."

This clause arrives immediately after a command to strive to the very limit — and that is deliberate. The limit is real, but the limit is *yours*. Ibn Kathir puts it precisely: He has not given you more than you can bear, and He has not obliged you to anything causing difficulty without creating for you a way out. Then he demonstrates it from the prayer — the most important pillar of Islam after the two testimonies of faith:

- Four rakʿahs when settled, shortened to two when travelling.
- According to some imams, only one rakʿah is obligatory at times of fear, as was recorded in the hadith.
- A person may pray while walking or riding, facing the qiblah or otherwise.
- Optional prayers while travelling may be prayed facing the qiblah or not.
- A sick person is not obliged to stand: he may pray sitting, and if unable, lying on his side.

And, Ibn Kathir adds, there are other exemptions and dispensations which may apply to the obligatory prayers and to other duties. The pillar bends to the person; it does not break, and the person is not broken by it. He cites the Prophet's ﷺ own words that he was sent with the easy Ḥanīfī way (*al-ḥanīfiyyah al-samḥah*), and his instruction to Muʿādh and Abū Mūsā when he sent them as governors to Yemen: "Give good news and do not repel them. Make things easy for the people and do not make the things difficult for them." (Ibn Kathir cites these two reports without naming their collections, adding that there are many similar hadiths.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the same clause from three further angles:

1. **Repentance.** From this, some scholars concluded that in Islam there is no sin which cannot be forgiven and lifted from a person before the punishment of the Day of Resurrection if he repents for it truly — whereas among earlier nations there were certain sins that repentance did not erase.
2. **Ibn ʿAbbās's reading:** *ḥaraj* refers to the rigid, harsh laws that applied to the Banū Isrāʾīl, for which the Qur'an uses the words *iṣr* (burden) and *aghlāl* (shackles). Others interpreted it as hardship beyond human endurance. Either way, Islam has no rule that is unbearable in itself — though it certainly has rules that entail strenuous effort. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes: education, commerce and industry are all fields where success depends on unremitting labour, and nobody calls them impossible. Difficulty from unfamiliarity with the task or an unfavourable environment is not *ḥaraj*; it can be overcome by sustained hard work.
3. **Qāḍī Thanāʾullāh in Tafsīr Mazharī:** since Allah has chosen the Muslims for His favours out of all nations, they themselves willingly opt for the severest hardship in His service — so hardships do not deter their resilience; they endure them willingly and happily. He brings the hadith related by Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said the coolness of his eyes lay in the prayer (Ahmad and Nasāʾī). The obligation that could have been felt as a weight was, for him ﷺ, the place he rested his eyes.

## "The religion of your father Ibrahim"

**مِّلَّةَ أَبِيكُمْ إِبْرَاهِيمَ.** Ibn Jarīr, as quoted by Ibn Kathir, offered two readings. It may refer back to the ease just mentioned: He has laid no difficulty on you — on the contrary He has made it easy for you, like the religion of your father Ibrāhīm. Or it may carry the sense of a command: *adhere to* the religion of your father Ibrāhīm. Ibn Kathir adds that this second reading matches "Say: Truly, my Lord has guided me to a straight path, a right religion, the religion of Ibrāhīm, a ḥanīf" (6:161).

Who is "your father"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives two answers. The words are addressed to the Quraysh, who descend from Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him) — and all other people who follow them become entitled to the favours Allah granted them; it cites the hadith that all people follow Quraysh in this faith, the believers among them following the believers of Quraysh and the disbelievers following the disbelievers (Bukhārī and Muslim, via Mazharī). Others say "your father Ibrāhīm" addresses all Muslims, in the sense that the Prophet ﷺ was the spiritual father of every Muslim and had himself descended from Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him).

## "He has named you Muslims"

**هُوَ سَمَّاكُمُ الْمُسْلِمِينَ مِن قَبْلُ وَفِي هَٰذَا.** Who did the naming? The commentators differ.

Ibn Kathir reports through Imam ʿAbdullāh bin al-Mubārak, from Ibn Jurayj, from ʿAṭāʾ, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that "He named you Muslims before" refers to **Allah**, may He be glorified — and that this was also the view of Mujāhid, ʿAṭāʾ, al-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Suddī, Muqātil bin Ḥayyān and Qatādah. Mujāhid said: Allah named you Muslims before, in the previous Books and in *al-Dhikr*; and "in this" means the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir supports this by the flow of the sentence itself — the two clauses just before it, "He has chosen you" and "has not laid upon you in religion any hardship," both have Allah as the actor. Allah mentioned this Ummah and praised it long ago in the Books of the Prophets, which were recited to the rabbis and monks.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān records the other view: that **Ibrāhīm** (peace be upon him) named the followers of the Prophet ﷺ and all other believers "Muslims" even before the Qur'an, as is evident from his supplication recorded in the Qur'an — "O our Lord, make us both submissive to You, and of our progeny a people submissive to You" (2:128). The name was not given directly by him, but since he had suggested it before the Qur'an was revealed and the Qur'an then adopted it, the naming is attributed to him.

**Why the name matters.** Under this ayah, Ibn Kathir records that An-Nasāʾī narrated from al-Ḥārith al-Ashʿarī that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Whoever adopts the call of Jāhiliyyah will be one of those who will crawl on their knees in Hell." A man said, "O Messenger of Allah, even if he fasts and performs Salah?" He said, "Yes, even if he fasts and performs Salah. So adopt the call of Allah whereby He called you Muslims and believers and servants of Allah." The names Allah gave — Muslims, believers, servants of Allah — are meant to be the banner people rally under, and prayer and fasting do not cancel out a rival loyalty.

## Witnesses over mankind

**لِيَكُونَ الرَّسُولُ شَهِيدًا عَلَيْكُمْ وَتَكُونُوا شُهَدَاءَ عَلَى النَّاسِ.** Ibn Kathir explains: thus Allah made you a just and fair nation, the best of nations, whose justice all other nations will testify to — for on the Day of Resurrection all the nations will acknowledge this community's leadership and precedence. On that Day the testimony of its members will be accepted as proof that the Messengers conveyed the Message of their Lord to their peoples — and the Messenger ﷺ will testify that he conveyed it to you.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the scene from a hadith which Bukhārī and others related on the authority of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allah be pleased with him): the Prophet ﷺ will depose that he conveyed the commands of Allah to his Ummah, and the Ummah will acknowledge it. When the other prophets make similar depositions, their nations will deny them — and this Ummah will come forward and bear witness that all the prophets did indeed convey their Lord's commands. Challenged on the ground that they did not even exist in those earlier times, they will reply that they learned it from their own Prophet ﷺ, whose truthfulness and integrity was admitted by all.

That is the weight behind the word "witness." Being chosen is not decoration; it is being called to the stand.

## What it asks of you: pray, give, hold on

**فَأَقِيمُوا الصَّلَاةَ وَآتُوا الزَّكَاةَ.** After those blessings comes the response. Ibn Kathir: respond to this great blessing with gratitude, by fulfilling your duties towards Allah, doing what He enjoined and avoiding what He forbade; and among the most important of these are establishing regular prayer and giving zakāh. Zakāh, he adds, is a form of beneficence towards Allah's creatures: He has enjoined upon the rich to give a little of their wealth to the poor each year, to help the weak and needy.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains why these two are singled out from all the commands: prayer is the most important of the obligations performed by the body, and zakāh the most important of the commands concerning wealth — but the idea is that every command Allah has enjoined be obeyed. Between them they claim both of the things a person guards most: his time and his money.

**وَاعْتَصِمُوا بِاللَّهِ** — "and hold fast to Allah." The verb is one of gripping something to keep from falling. Ibn Kathir: seek the help and support of Allah, put your trust in Him, and get strength from Him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: place your trust in Allah alone in all affairs and seek help from none but Him; and from Ibn ʿAbbās, that it means seeking Allah's protection from all things loathsome in this world and the Hereafter. Others took it to mean holding fast to the Qur'an and the Sunnah, quoting the hadith that the Prophet ﷺ left behind two things which, held to, would keep you from ever going astray: the Book of Allah and the Sunnah of His Messenger (related by Mālik in the Muwaṭṭaʾ in *mursal* form — that is, with a gap in the chain — as Mazharī notes).

## The last words of the sūrah

**هُوَ مَوْلَاكُمْ فَنِعْمَ الْمَوْلَىٰ وَنِعْمَ النَّصِيرُ.** *Mawlā* is your Patron, the One who takes charge of you. Ibn Kathir: He is your Protector and your Helper, the One who will cause you to prevail against your enemies — the best Mawlā and the best Helper.

The sūrah that commanded striving to the very limit ends not with your effort but with His guarantee: the One you are striving for is the One holding you up. Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on Sūrat al-Hajj here, with a prayer for the Prophet ﷺ, his family and his Companions, and for those who follow them in truth until the Day of Resurrection.

**Carry away three things.** Worship with your body before you argue about religion (ayah 77). Measure your striving by what He deserves, not by what impresses people — and let it reach your own desires, not only the world outside (ayah 78). And when that standard sounds impossible, re-read the very next clause: *He has not laid upon you in religion any hardship*.
